The reminder letter was criticised as "coercive", although recipients faced no penalty of any kind and could ignore it without consequence.
The finding was presented as "generalisable", having been obtained on a single street in one town and never tested anywhere else.
The analysis was described as "pre-registered", with the primary outcome chosen after the team had examined the collected data.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Enrolment operates by "default": eligible residents are placed in the scheme automatically and stay in it unless they ask to leave.**

A "default" is the outcome that takes effect when a person makes no active choice, which is why defaults exert such influence on participation rates. The colon describes that arrangement precisely: automatic placement, with continued membership for anyone who does nothing. An opt-in scheme would reverse the default and leave inaction meaning non-participation.

Automatic inclusion unless the person acts is the definition of an opt-out default, so the term is used correctly here.

**B) The evaluation rests on a "counterfactual", an estimate of what the same households would have done had no appointment reminder arrived.**

A "counterfactual" is a statement of what would have happened under conditions that did not in fact obtain, and every claim about an effect depends on one. The appositive states that structure exactly, since the comparison is with the same households in a world without the reminder. The counterfactual is estimated rather than observed, which is why control groups exist.

An estimate of the unobserved alternative course of events is what the term names, so the sentence uses it properly.

**C) The reminder letter was criticised as "coercive", although recipients faced no penalty of any kind and could ignore it without consequence.**

Coercion works by removing acceptable alternatives, typically through force, threat or penalty, so the person is left with no real option but to comply. The concessive clause withdraws exactly that element: no penalty, and no consequence for ignoring the letter. Nudges may still be criticised as manipulative, which is a different and more interesting objection.

A letter that can be binned without cost leaves the choice intact, so the criticism reaches for a word the facts do not support.

**D) The finding was presented as "generalisable", having been obtained on a single street in one town and never tested anywhere else.**

A result is "generalisable" when there is reason to expect it to hold beyond the particular sample and setting that produced it, which usually means variation across sites or populations. One street in one town, never replicated, provides no such variation and no evidence about other contexts. Internally valid is the most such a study can claim: it may describe that street accurately and say nothing about anywhere else.

A single untested site supplies no ground for extending the result, so the presentation claims a reach the design cannot support.

**E) The analysis was described as "pre-registered", with the primary outcome chosen after the team had examined the collected data.**

"Pre-registration" means the hypotheses and analysis plan are lodged publicly before the data are seen, which is what stops the outcome measure from being selected to fit the result. Choosing the primary outcome after looking at the data is the practice pre-registration exists to prevent. An exploratory analysis is a legitimate thing to report, provided it is labelled as one.

An outcome selected once the data were in hand cannot have been registered in advance, so the description claims a safeguard the study did not apply.
tasks.solution_overview: Evaluation vocabulary is built to keep claims honest: what happens when nobody chooses, what the comparison group stands for, whether pressure was really applied, how far a result may travel, and when the analysis plan was fixed. Each term names a condition, and each sentence reports enough of the design to test it. Where the reported design fails the condition, the write-up has claimed a standard the study did not meet.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five lines from hospital and veterinary policy on antibiotic resistance. Decide whether each quoted term fits the practice the sentence describes.
statements: The hospital calls the programme "stewardship", governing which agents may be used, at what dose, for how long and on whose authority.
Routine dosing across a herd applies "selective pressure", handing an advantage to any resistant strain in every generation that follows.
Colistin is treated as a "last-resort" agent, held back for infections that every other available antibiotic has failed to clear.
The prescription was defended as "broad-spectrum", chosen because the laboratory had already identified the single organism responsible.
Resistance also spreads by "horizontal" transfer, passing between unrelated bacteria rather than only from a cell to its descendants.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hospital calls the programme "stewardship", governing which agents may be used, at what dose, for how long and on whose authority.**

"Stewardship" describes the careful management of a shared resource on behalf of others, and antimicrobial stewardship applies that idea to drugs whose effectiveness is depleted by use. The list of controls gives the programme its substance: agent, dose, duration and authorisation, the four levers such schemes actually pull. The word carries the sense of holding something in trust rather than merely restricting it.

Managing a shared and exhaustible resource through explicit controls is exactly what the term denotes, so it fits this programme.

**B) Routine dosing across a herd applies "selective pressure", handing an advantage to any resistant strain in every generation that follows.**

"Selective pressure" is any factor that makes some variants reproduce more successfully than others, so that their frequency rises over generations. Continuous antibiotic exposure is the textbook case, since susceptible bacteria are removed and resistant ones inherit the space. The phrase describes a differential advantage rather than the creation of a mutation.

Continuous exposure that favours resistant variants generation after generation is selection in the strict sense, so the phrase is correctly used.

**C) Colistin is treated as a "last-resort" agent, held back for infections that every other available antibiotic has failed to clear.**

A "last-resort" drug is kept in reserve for cases where the alternatives have already been tried and have failed, which is why access to it is restricted rather than encouraged. The sentence states both parts of that policy: deliberate withholding, and the clinical situation that releases it. Reserving such agents preserves their usefulness by limiting the exposure that breeds resistance.

An agent held back until everything else has failed is a last resort in the literal sense, so the description holds.

**D) The prescription was defended as "broad-spectrum", chosen because the laboratory had already identified the single organism responsible.**

A "broad-spectrum" antibiotic acts against a wide range of bacteria, which is why it is the right choice while the organism is still unknown. Once the laboratory has named the organism, prescribing practice moves the other way, to the narrowest agent that covers it, precisely to spare everything else. The reason offered here therefore argues against the choice it is meant to justify.

A known organism calls for narrow targeted therapy rather than wide coverage, so the defence undercuts itself.

**E) Resistance also spreads by "horizontal" transfer, passing between unrelated bacteria rather than only from a cell to its descendants.**

"Horizontal" gene transfer moves genetic material sideways between organisms that are not parent and offspring, often across species boundaries. The sentence supplies the contrast that defines the term, setting transfer between unrelated bacteria against inheritance down a line of descent. Vertical transmission is the name for that second route.

Movement between unrelated cells rather than along a line of descent is exactly what the term specifies, so it is used correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Resistance policy has its own precise vocabulary: governing how drugs are used, the pressure that favours resistant strains, the reserve agent held back, the breadth of an agent's coverage, and the route by which resistance genes travel. Read the clinical or biological detail beside each term and ask whether it satisfies the condition the word sets. Timing matters as much as meaning here: what was already known when the choice was made, and what had already been tried.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five lines from studies that track birds across oceans. Decide whether each quoted term describes the pattern the sentence reports.
statements: The birds show strong site "fidelity", returning to the same ledge within a metre or so year after year.
The tag record shows steady "attrition", with fewer transmitters reporting in each successive month of the crossing.
The route is "circumpolar", carrying the birds right around the southern ocean rather than back and forth along one meridian.
Movements of the species are "irruptive": in most winters the birds stay north, and in a few they appear far south in enormous numbers.
The distances are "prodigious", with one tagged bird logging ninety thousand kilometres in a single year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The birds show strong site "fidelity", returning to the same ledge within a metre or so year after year.**

Site "fidelity" is the tendency of an animal to return to the same location across seasons or years, and its strength is measured by how precisely the return is made. The sentence supplies that measurement, since a metre on the same ledge is about as exact as such returns get. The word describes attachment to a place rather than to a mate, which is a separate use of the same term.

Precise annual return to one spot is the behaviour the term names, so it is applied correctly here.

**B) The tag record shows steady "attrition", with fewer transmitters reporting in each successive month of the crossing.**

"Attrition" is gradual loss from a group by a continuing process rather than a single event, whether through failure, detachment or death. Month-by-month decline in the number of reporting tags fits that pattern exactly, and the word is standard in describing sample loss over a study. A sudden collapse in reports would need a different account, since attrition implies erosion.

Steady month-on-month loss from the reporting sample is attrition in the ordinary technical sense, so the description holds.

**C) The route is "circumpolar", carrying the birds right around the southern ocean rather than back and forth along one meridian.**

"Circumpolar" describes a distribution or a track that encircles one of the poles, and the sentence makes the geometry explicit by contrast. Travelling around the southern ocean is circular movement about the pole, whereas a there-and-back journey along a single meridian would be latitudinal. The word describes the shape of the route, not its length.

A track that goes right around the pole is circumpolar in the plain geographical sense, so the term fits.

**D) Movements of the species are "irruptive": in most winters the birds stay north, and in a few they appear far south in enormous numbers.**

An "irruptive" species moves in occasional mass irruptions rather than on a regular annual schedule, usually when food supplies fail. The colon reports that irregularity in the form ornithologists use: most years nothing, occasional years an enormous influx. Regular migration would show the same journey each season, which is the pattern the sentence rules out.

Occasional mass movements against a background of staying put is precisely what the term describes, so the wording stands.

**E) The distances are "prodigious", with one tagged bird logging ninety thousand kilometres in a single year.**

"Prodigious" means impressively great in extent, and the word carries a note of astonishment that ordinary large does not. Ninety thousand kilometres in a year is more than twice around the planet, which is the kind of figure the adjective exists for. The sentence earns the word by supplying the number rather than leaving the reader to take the claim on trust.

A single year's travel of that magnitude is remarkable by any measure, so the adjective is justified here.
tasks.solution_overview: Migration research needs words for faithfulness to a place, steady loss from a sample, the geometry of a route, irregular mass movements and sheer scale. Each is answerable to a number or a pattern in the record, so read the figures attached to it. Where the tagging data show the exact behaviour the term specifies, the technical word is doing work that a general one could not.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five lines from conservation reports on paintings and panels. Decide whether each quoted term describes the object or the treatment as the sentence reports it.
statements: The treatment is described as "reversible", using an adhesive that cannot be removed later without lifting the paint layer with it.
Centuries of "accretion" had darkened the surface: varnish, soot, and successive layers of well-meant retouching.
The panel's "provenance" is secure, with nothing at all known of its whereabouts between 1620 and its reappearance in a private collection in 1932.
The forgery is a "pastiche" in the strict sense, invented wholly from the forger's imagination without reference to any earlier work.
A "lacuna" runs across the sitter's hand, a loss where the paint layer has gone entirely and only ground remains.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The treatment is described as "reversible", using an adhesive that cannot be removed later without lifting the paint layer with it.**

A "reversible" treatment can be undone without damage, leaving the object as it was before, which is why reversibility is a founding principle of modern conservation. An adhesive that takes the paint with it fails that test in the most direct way available, since the removal itself causes the loss. Irreversible interventions are sometimes accepted, but they are never described this way.

A treatment that destroys the paint on removal cannot be undone, so the description claims exactly what the material rules out.

**B) Centuries of "accretion" had darkened the surface: varnish, soot, and successive layers of well-meant retouching.**

"Accretion" is material added gradually in layers over time, and in conservation it names everything that has accumulated on a surface since the artist left it. The list after the colon is exactly that inventory, mixing deliberate additions with accidental deposits. Accretion is distinct from the original paint, which is why removing it is a defensible aim.

Layer upon layer added over centuries is precisely what the noun describes, so it fits this surface.

**C) The panel's "provenance" is secure, with nothing at all known of its whereabouts between 1620 and its reappearance in a private collection in 1932.**

"Provenance" is the documented chain of ownership and location from the object's creation to the present, and its security depends on that chain being unbroken. A gap of three centuries is the largest possible break, and gaps of this kind are exactly where losses and forgeries are hidden. Attribution is a separate question, since a work can be confidently attributed and still have a broken provenance.

Three unrecorded centuries leave the chain of ownership open at its widest point, so the provenance is anything but secure.

**D) The forgery is a "pastiche" in the strict sense, invented wholly from the forger's imagination without reference to any earlier work.**

A "pastiche" is assembled from borrowed elements, imitating the manner of an artist or combining motifs taken from existing works. Invention owing nothing to any earlier work is the opposite procedure, since there is nothing borrowed to assemble. Such a piece might be a forgery in style, but it is an original composition rather than a pastiche.

A work that copies nothing has no borrowed parts to assemble, so the strict sense of the term cannot apply to it.

**E) A "lacuna" runs across the sitter's hand, a loss where the paint layer has gone entirely and only ground remains.**

A "lacuna" is a gap where original material is missing, whether in a manuscript, a mosaic or a paint film. The appositive gives the condition that qualifies it here: the paint layer has gone, leaving bare ground rather than damaged pigment. Abrasion or discoloured retouching would be different conditions, since in both cases some original material survives.

Total loss of the paint layer down to the ground is a lacuna in the conservator's sense, so the term is used properly.
tasks.solution_overview: Conservation vocabulary carries strict commitments: whether a treatment can be undone, what has built up on a surface, how complete an object's documented history is, what kind of imitation a forgery attempts, and what is missing from a paint layer. Read the factual clause and ask whether it satisfies the condition or quietly cancels it. Documented history is judged by whether the chain of records is unbroken, not by how confident the report sounds.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five lines from seed banks and plant collections. Decide whether each quoted term fits the material or the method the sentence describes.
statements: Cocoa seed is "recalcitrant": it cannot be dried and frozen as wheat can, and dies within weeks of leaving the pod.
The collection preserves a "landrace", a local population shaped over generations by farmers rather than bred at a research station.
The hybrid line is "true-breeding", producing a second generation that varies widely from the parent plants in height and yield.
The accession was logged as "viable" after a germination test in which none of the two hundred seeds sprouted.
Some varieties are conserved "in situ", left growing in the fields where they developed rather than held as frozen samples.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Cocoa seed is "recalcitrant": it cannot be dried and frozen as wheat can, and dies within weeks of leaving the pod.**

In seed science, "recalcitrant" is a technical classification for seed that does not survive drying and freezing, in contrast to orthodox seed, which does. The colon supplies both halves of that definition: conventional storage is impossible, and viability is lost within weeks. The everyday sense of stubborn resistance survives faintly, since such species resist the standard method.

Seed that cannot be dried or frozen and dies quickly is recalcitrant in the exact technical sense, so the term is right.

**B) The collection preserves a "landrace", a local population shaped over generations by farmers rather than bred at a research station.**

A "landrace" is a traditional variety developed through generations of farmer selection in one locality, and it is typically diverse rather than uniform. The appositive states both defining features, the local origin and the absence of formal breeding, and sets them against the modern cultivar. Landraces matter to seed banks precisely because they carry variation that formal breeding has narrowed.

Farmer selection in a particular place over generations is the whole content of the term, so it is correctly applied.

**C) The hybrid line is "true-breeding", producing a second generation that varies widely from the parent plants in height and yield.**

A "true-breeding" line produces offspring resembling the parents in the traits concerned, generation after generation, because the relevant loci are homozygous. Wide variation appearing in the second generation is the classic signature of a hybrid segregating, which is the opposite behaviour. It is the reason farmers cannot save seed from hybrid varieties and expect the same crop.

Offspring that scatter away from the parental type are not breeding true, so the description defeats the label attached to it.

**D) The accession was logged as "viable" after a germination test in which none of the two hundred seeds sprouted.**

Seed is "viable" when it is alive and capable of germinating, and the germination test is exactly the procedure used to establish that. A test in which no seed out of two hundred sprouted is the strongest available evidence for the opposite conclusion. Viability is a matter of measured germination rather than of how the seed looks or how carefully it has been stored.

A germination rate of zero is the record of a dead accession, so the entry contradicts the test it claims to rest on.

**E) Some varieties are conserved "in situ", left growing in the fields where they developed rather than held as frozen samples.**

"In situ" conservation keeps organisms in the place where they occur, so that they continue to adapt in their original setting. The sentence supplies the contrast on which the term depends, setting living fields against frozen storage, which is the ex situ alternative. The phrase describes location rather than method, and the two strategies are usually pursued together.

Maintaining varieties in their original growing places is exactly what the phrase specifies, so it fits this description.
tasks.solution_overview: Conservation genetics uses terms that specify how seed behaves in storage, where a variety came from, how uniformly it breeds, whether it can still germinate and where it is being kept. Each word sets a condition, and each sentence supplies the germination result, the breeding behaviour or the storage arrangement that tests it. A technical sense can run against the everyday one, so let the reported detail decide rather than the word's ordinary flavour.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five lines from security policy on controlled technologies. Decide whether each quoted term matches the arrangement the sentence describes.
statements: The microscope was listed as "dual-use", though it has no application beyond routine hospital diagnosis.
The rule was described as "extraterritorial", applying only to conduct that takes place inside the issuing state's own borders.
One factory has become a "chokepoint": nearly every advanced design in the world must pass through its machines at some stage.
The controls were presented as "reciprocal", imposed on a state that had taken no comparable measure against the country imposing them.
The prohibition is "de jure" only, resting on informal pressure from officials with nothing whatever written into law.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The microscope was listed as "dual-use", though it has no application beyond routine hospital diagnosis.**

A "dual-use" item is one with both civilian and military or weapons-related applications, which is precisely why such items attract export control. An instrument with no application beyond hospital diagnosis has a single civilian use and fails the definition at the first step. The listing decision may still be arguable, but not on this ground.

One civilian application and nothing else leaves no second use to speak of, so the classification does not fit this instrument.

**B) The rule was described as "extraterritorial", applying only to conduct that takes place inside the issuing state's own borders.**

An "extraterritorial" rule reaches conduct beyond the borders of the state that made it, which is what makes such rules diplomatically contentious. A measure confined to conduct at home is ordinary domestic regulation and raises none of those questions. The word describes the geographical reach of a rule, not how strict it is.

A rule that stops at the border reaches nothing extraterritorially, so the description misstates its scope.

**C) One factory has become a "chokepoint": nearly every advanced design in the world must pass through its machines at some stage.**

A "chokepoint" is a narrow passage through which traffic must pass, so that whoever controls it controls the flow; the term moved from geography into supply-chain analysis without changing shape. The colon supplies the two features that define it, a single point and no way around it. That is why chokepoints attract regulatory attention out of all proportion to their size.

A single unavoidable passage that everything must go through is a chokepoint in the exact sense, so the term is well used.

**D) The controls were presented as "reciprocal", imposed on a state that had taken no comparable measure against the country imposing them.**

"Reciprocal" measures answer equivalent measures taken by the other side, and the mutuality is the whole justification for the word. The sentence removes that basis by reporting that the other state had taken no comparable step, which leaves the controls first in the sequence rather than answering anything. Unilateral or pre-emptive would describe what actually happened.

There is nothing to reciprocate when the other side has not acted at all, so the presentation dresses a first move as a reply.

**E) The prohibition is "de jure" only, resting on informal pressure from officials with nothing whatever written into law.**

A "de jure" prohibition exists in law, set down in an instrument that can be pointed to, challenged and enforced through the courts. Informal pressure with nothing written down is the opposite footing: the restriction operates in practice while having no legal existence at all. De facto is the tag for a situation that holds in fact without legal foundation.

A ban that exists only in officials' behaviour has no legal basis to appeal to, so the Latin tag chosen here is the wrong one of the pair.
tasks.solution_overview: Control regimes depend on terms of art: goods with both civilian and military application, rules that reach conduct abroad, single points through which everything must pass, measures answering measures, and prohibitions with or without a legal basis. Read the clause describing where the rule bites, what the item is used for, and whether anything was written into law. Two Latin tags in this field differ only on that last point, and one of them is tested here.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five lines from work on how an ice sheet might fail. Decide whether each quoted term describes the model or the physics the sentence reports.
statements: The projection is "deterministic", presented as a spread of two thousand runs with a probability attached to each outcome.
The ice sheet's response is "nonlinear": a small additional warming past the threshold produces a loss far larger than the increment before it.
The system shows "hysteresis", so the ice does not return at the same temperature at which it was lost.
Cloud behaviour is "parameterised", represented by a simplified rule because the processes are far smaller than the model's grid cells.
The high-end scenario is "plausible" rather than likely, physically consistent but resting on assumptions few researchers expect to hold.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The projection is "deterministic", presented as a spread of two thousand runs with a probability attached to each outcome.**

A "deterministic" model returns a single outcome for a given set of inputs, with no randomness in the process and no distribution at the end. Two thousand runs with probabilities attached to the outcomes is the signature of a probabilistic or ensemble approach, built precisely to represent uncertainty. The distinction concerns how the model treats uncertainty rather than how sophisticated it is.

An ensemble carrying probabilities is by construction not a single-answer model, so the description contradicts the output it reports.

**B) The ice sheet's response is "nonlinear": a small additional warming past the threshold produces a loss far larger than the increment before it.**

A response is "nonlinear" when the output is not proportional to the input, so equal increments of forcing produce unequal effects. The colon supplies exactly that behaviour, with a small step past a threshold yielding a disproportionate loss. Thresholds are the most familiar source of nonlinearity in the cryosphere, which is why they dominate discussion of ice-sheet risk.

Effects that grow out of proportion to their cause is what the term names, so it describes this response accurately.

**C) The system shows "hysteresis", so the ice does not return at the same temperature at which it was lost.**

"Hysteresis" is present when a system's state depends on its history, so the return path differs from the outgoing one and thresholds are not symmetric. The sentence gives the standard test in a single clause: recovery requires conditions different from those under which the loss occurred. It is the reason some changes are described as effectively irreversible on human timescales.

A return path that does not retrace the outward one is hysteresis in the exact sense, so the term is correctly applied.

**D) Cloud behaviour is "parameterised", represented by a simplified rule because the processes are far smaller than the model's grid cells.**

To "parameterise" a process is to replace its explicit physics with a simplified relationship, which is necessary whenever the process is smaller than the model can resolve. The sentence names both the substitution and the reason for it, and the scale mismatch is the standard justification. Resolved processes are computed directly, which is the contrast the term implies.

A sub-grid process represented by a simplified rule is parameterised in the exact modelling sense, so the wording holds.

**E) The high-end scenario is "plausible" rather than likely, physically consistent but resting on assumptions few researchers expect to hold.**

"Plausible" says that something could happen without asserting that it probably will, which is why the sentence sets it against "likely" rather than against "impossible". The two clauses that follow supply the grounds on each side: physical consistency earns the plausibility, and doubted assumptions withhold the probability. The distinction is standard in risk assessment, where possible-but-improbable outcomes still matter.

Physical coherence without expected occurrence is exactly the space the word occupies, so it is well chosen here.
tasks.solution_overview: Modelling vocabulary states what kind of claim is being made: one outcome or a distribution of them, a response proportional to its cause or not, a path that retraces itself or does not, a process resolved directly or represented by a rule, and a scenario that is possible rather than expected. Read the methodological detail beside each word and hold the term to it. How a model treats uncertainty is declared by the form of its output, so read that form before accepting the label.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five lines from histories of underground labour. Decide whether each quoted term matches the working conditions the sentence describes.
statements: The work was "arduous": eight hours of hewing on the side, in a seam too low for a man to stand upright.
The barracks were "insalubrious", damp, unventilated, and shared in turn by men working three shifts around the clock.
The agreement was "tacit", never written down and never announced, yet observed by both sides for thirty years.
Pay was not "commensurate" with the risk, a few pence above surface rates for work that killed one man in twenty.
Dust disease was "insidious", advancing without symptoms for decades before the first breathlessness appeared.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The work was "arduous": eight hours of hewing on the side, in a seam too low for a man to stand upright.**

"Arduous" describes work demanding sustained and severe physical effort, and it belongs to a formal register that suits historical narrative. The detail after the colon earns the adjective by specifying both the duration and the posture forced on the hewer. Difficult would be vaguer, since it says nothing about the bodily cost the word implies.

Hours of heavy labour in a seam that forbids standing is arduous in the fullest sense, so the description is apt.

**B) The barracks were "insalubrious", damp, unventilated, and shared in turn by men working three shifts around the clock.**

"Insalubrious" means unhealthy to live in, and the word is normally applied to housing, air or a district rather than to people. Damp, unventilated rooms occupied continuously by rotating shifts describes conditions unhealthy by every nineteenth-century measure. The formal register is doing real work here, since the term makes a claim about health rather than about comfort.

Accommodation that damages the health of those living in it is what the adjective names, so it fits these barracks.

**C) The agreement was "tacit", never written down and never announced, yet observed by both sides for thirty years.**

Something "tacit" is understood without being stated, so it is real in its effects while leaving no explicit record. The sentence gives both halves of that condition: nothing written or announced, and consistent observance over three decades. An agreement that was merely informal might still have been spoken aloud, which is the distinction the word preserves.

An understanding honoured for thirty years without ever being stated is tacit in the exact sense, so the term is right.

**D) Pay was not "commensurate" with the risk, a few pence above surface rates for work that killed one man in twenty.**

"Commensurate" means proportionate to something else, corresponding in scale, and it normally takes "with" before the thing compared. The sentence sets the two quantities side by side, a marginal premium against a mortality rate of one in twenty, so the reader can see the disproportion. The negation is what the evidence supports, since the comparison shows the two scales failing to match.

A few pence set against a death rate of that order is plainly out of proportion, so the denial of commensurability is well founded.

**E) Dust disease was "insidious", advancing without symptoms for decades before the first breathlessness appeared.**

"Insidious" describes harm that develops gradually and unnoticed, doing its damage before anything reveals it, and the medical use of the word keeps that sense exactly. Decades of silent progression followed by a late first symptom is the pattern the term was made for. Aggressive would describe speed instead, which is precisely what this disease did not have.

Long concealed progression that surfaces only when the damage is done is insidious in the strict sense, so the word fits.
tasks.solution_overview: Historical writing about labour needs words for effort, environment, unwritten agreements, the fit between pay and risk, and disease that develops unnoticed. Each carries a register as well as a meaning, and the sentences here supply the concrete detail that earns it. Reading the evidence clause first shows how a formal word can be exactly right rather than merely elevated.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: A closing set of five lines from different fields. Decide whether each quoted term is used in the sense the surrounding sentence requires.
statements: The rise in recorded cases was called "exponential", adding the same fixed number of new patients every week for a year.
Wages had risen in "nominal" terms only, buying noticeably less at the end of the decade than at the beginning.
The 1908 edition is "canonical", the text later scholars cite by default and against which variant readings are measured.
Whether the treaty still bound the island became "moot" once the state that had signed it ceased to exist.
The claim was treated as "axiomatic", accepted only after three separate laboratories had confirmed it experimentally.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rise in recorded cases was called "exponential", adding the same fixed number of new patients every week for a year.**

"Exponential" growth multiplies by a constant factor in each period, so the absolute increase itself grows and doubling times can be quoted. A fixed number of new cases each week is a constant absolute increase, which is linear growth however large the weekly figure happens to be.

**Trap:** Exponential is borrowed constantly to mean merely fast; the test is whether the increase itself keeps growing, not whether the total is alarming.

The same increment every week describes a straight line rather than a curve, so the term misstates the shape of this rise.

**B) Wages had risen in "nominal" terms only, buying noticeably less at the end of the decade than at the beginning.**

A "nominal" figure is stated at the prices of the day, with no adjustment for inflation, which is why nominal growth can coexist with falling purchasing power. The sentence reports precisely that combination, since the number went up while what it bought went down. Real terms is the counterpart, and it is the adjusted measure that answers questions about living standards.

An unadjusted increase that leaves workers able to buy less is exactly what the qualifier warns of, so the wording is correct.

**C) The 1908 edition is "canonical", the text later scholars cite by default and against which variant readings are measured.**

A "canonical" text is the accepted standard version within a field, the one that other versions are compared against rather than merely one among many. The appositive supplies both marks of that status: default citation, and use as the reference point for variants. Definitive would claim finality, whereas canonical describes the position a text holds in scholarly practice.

Being the reference against which other readings are judged is what confers canonical status, so the term is used correctly.

**D) Whether the treaty still bound the island became "moot" once the state that had signed it ceased to exist.**

A question is "moot" when it no longer has any practical consequence, so that deciding it would settle nothing for anyone. The disappearance of the signatory state removes the party the obligation ran to, which is the standard way a live legal question becomes academic. The word says nothing about how interesting the question remains to historians.

A question with no remaining practical effect is moot in the established sense, so the sentence uses it properly.

**E) The claim was treated as "axiomatic", accepted only after three separate laboratories had confirmed it experimentally.**

Something "axiomatic" is taken as self-evident and assumed at the outset, which is exactly why axioms are not derived from evidence within the system that rests on them. A claim accepted only after three laboratories confirmed it has been established empirically, which is the opposite route to acceptance. Well-corroborated or firmly established is the description the evidence supports.

A proposition earned through repeated experiment is demonstrated rather than assumed, so the word misdescribes how this claim came to be accepted.
tasks.solution_overview: These last items come from separate disciplines but reward the same reflex: take the word to its technical definition, then read the clause that reports the growth pattern, the price adjustment, the textual authority, the practical consequence or the status of the claim. One of them turns on how a proposition is held, assumed at the outset or earned through evidence, and that distinction decides the item. Where the surrounding detail belongs to the neighbouring term, that neighbour is the word the sentence needed.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five lines from a central bank's policy commentary. Decide whether each phrase is the combination monetary-policy writing actually uses.
statements: Policymakers voted to harden monetary policy after core inflation proved unexpectedly sticky.
The committee's guidance was designed to anchor inflation expectations before the autumn wage round.
Officials insisted that a further quarter-point rise would not provoke a soft landing in the labour market.
The bank continued to withdraw liquidity out of the money market through weekly repo operations.
Rate-setters said they would hold the ground on rates until inflation returned to target.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Policymakers voted to harden monetary policy after core inflation proved unexpectedly sticky.**

Monetary policy is tightened or loosened, and that antonym pair is fixed: a tightening cycle, an easing cycle, tighter conditions. "Harden" governs attitudes and positions rather than instruments — a stance hardens, a line hardens, rhetoric hardens — so it cannot take the policy setting itself as its object. Sticky core inflation is exactly the trigger a tightening decision reports, which shows the noun and the reason are right and only the verb has slipped.

**Trap:** A hawkish tone can harden; the policy it announces tightens.

The decision described is a rate rise in response to persistent inflation, so the wording a minute would carry is "voted to tighten monetary policy."

**B) The committee's guidance was designed to anchor inflation expectations before the autumn wage round.**

Expectations are anchored, and the metaphor is so entrenched that its failure has its own name: de-anchored expectations. Guidance is the standard instrument credited with doing the anchoring, since the point of publishing a path for rates is to fix what households and firms assume about future prices. Wage bargaining is in turn the classic channel through which those assumptions become actual inflation.

Verb, object and timing all sit inside one settled frame here, so the sentence reads exactly as a policy commentary would write it.

**C) Officials insisted that a further quarter-point rise would not provoke a soft landing in the labour market.**

A soft landing is engineered, achieved or delivered, because the phrase names the outcome policymakers are steering towards: inflation falls without a collapse in employment. "Provoke" governs unwelcome reactions — provoke a backlash, provoke a sell-off, provoke a run — so attaching it to the one result every central banker wants inverts the evaluation the sentence needs.

**Trap:** The verb, not the noun, carries the judgement; check whether the outcome is desired before choosing it.

Officials were reassuring their audience rather than disowning a success, so the line they would actually give is "would still deliver a soft landing in the labour market."

**D) The bank continued to withdraw liquidity out of the money market through weekly repo operations.**

Liquidity is drained from a market or withdrawn from it, and the mirror image is injecting liquidity into it; the operational vocabulary keeps to that in-and-out pair with "from" and "into." "Out of" belongs to physical extraction — tipping water out of a jug — and after "withdraw" the settled preposition is simply "from."

**Tip:** Inject liquidity into a market, drain it from one.

The repo operations described are the standard way of absorbing cash, so the phrase an operations desk would use is "drain liquidity from the money market."

**E) Rate-setters said they would hold the ground on rates until inflation returned to target.**

Two real idioms have been welded together here: "hold the line on rates," which is what a committee does when it refuses to move, and "stand one's ground," which is what a person does under pressure. Each is fine on its own, but "hold the ground" belongs to neither, and the military sense of holding ground needs territory rather than a policy setting.

The committee is refusing to shift its rate until a condition is met, so the natural version is "hold the line on rates until inflation returned to target."
tasks.solution_overview: Central-bank prose is unusually formulaic, so each line can be checked against the phrase a published policy statement would print. Watch which verbs belong with the stance itself, which belong with expectations, and which belong with operations in the money market, because each of those three slots has its own settled partner. Two of the traps here are blends of two genuine idioms, so say the whole phrase aloud and ask which half has been borrowed from somewhere else.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Five lines from a labour-market briefing on shortages and pay. Decide whether each verb sits with its noun the way employment economics words it.
statements: A shrinking pool of applicants has narrowed the labour market in several regions.
Two years of rapid inflation ate away real wages across the private sector.
Vacancy data suggest that acute skill shortages are bidding up wages in construction.
The minimum wage increase was expected to squeeze out the wage premium enjoyed by shift supervisors.
Firms facing chronic shortages have begun to poach staff from smaller regional rivals.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A shrinking pool of applicants has narrowed the labour market in several regions.**

A labour market tightens when workers are scarce and loosens when they are plentiful, and the adjective follows the same logic in "a tight labour market." "Narrow" needs an object with two measurable edges — a gap, a lead, a spread, a margin — and a market is not that sort of object, which is why nobody reports a narrow labour market either.

**Tip:** Gaps narrow; markets tighten.

The sentence describes scarcity pushing employers into competition, so the standard reading is "has tightened the labour market in several regions."

**B) Two years of rapid inflation ate away real wages across the private sector.**

Inflation erodes real wages, or eats away at them, and that second phrase is fixed with its preposition: "eat away" never governs a bare object. Removing "at" leaves a pattern English does not have, even though the metaphor of slow consumption is the right one for what rising prices do to the purchasing power of pay.

**Trap:** Eat into and eat away at both need their preposition; only the plain verb eat takes a direct object.

The sense is right but the pattern is broken, so the sentence needs "ate away at real wages" or, in more formal reporting, "eroded real wages."

**C) Vacancy data suggest that acute skill shortages are bidding up wages in construction.**

When competing buyers force a price higher, English says they bid it up, and the phrase transfers from auctions to housing, commodities and labour without changing shape. Shortages are the standard subject of that verb in pay reporting, because scarce skills are precisely what rival employers compete over, and vacancy figures are the evidence normally cited for the claim.

The mechanism and the phrase that names it match exactly here, so the wording is what a labour-market briefing would print.

**D) The minimum wage increase was expected to squeeze out the wage premium enjoyed by shift supervisors.**

A differential is compressed or eroded when a rising floor catches up with the grade above it, and "wage compression" is the technical name for that effect. "Squeeze out" means to force something or someone out of a market altogether — smaller rivals get squeezed out — so it describes expulsion rather than the shrinking of a gap.

What the rise threatens is the size of the supervisors' advantage rather than its existence, so the line should read "compress the wage premium enjoyed by shift supervisors."

**E) Firms facing chronic shortages have begun to poach staff from smaller regional rivals.**

Poaching is the settled term for hiring away another employer's workers, and it keeps the preposition "from" for the firm that loses them. The word carries a mild accusation of unfairness, which fits a sentence about large employers turning on smaller competitors during a shortage.

Both the verb and the pattern around it are the ones this situation calls for, so the sentence stands as competent reporting.
tasks.solution_overview: Labour economics describes scarcity, pay erosion and competition for staff with a small set of verbs that have hardened into terms of art. Ask what English does to a market when workers are scarce, what inflation does to the buying power of pay, and what happens to the differential between two grades when the floor rises. One trap is a missing preposition rather than a wrong verb, so read each phrase for its complete pattern and not just its headline word.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Five lines from coverage of a company's results season. Decide whether each phrase matches the wording of financial reporting.
statements: The retailer made a profit warning three weeks before the Christmas trading update.
Management admitted that the write-down would dent operating margins in the second half.
Quarterly revenue overtook analysts' forecasts by the widest margin in three years.
The board declined to reinstate the dividend until leverage fell below two times earnings.
Auditors questioned whether the group had been smoothing earnings across reporting periods.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The retailer made a profit warning three weeks before the Christmas trading update.**

A profit warning is issued, and that verb covers the whole family of formal market announcements: firms issue guidance, issue a statement, issue a trading update. "Make" governs the outcome itself rather than the announcement of it, which is why a company makes a profit but issues the warning that it will not.

**Tip:** Make the result, issue the announcement about it.

What the retailer released was a formal notice to the market, so the phrase financial pages use is "issued a profit warning."

**B) Management admitted that the write-down would dent operating margins in the second half.**

Margins are dented, squeezed, eroded or wiped out, and "dent" is the mild member of that set: it signals visible but survivable damage rather than collapse. A write-down is exactly the sort of one-off charge that produces that scale of effect, and pairing it with the softest verb in the family is how management would play the news down.

The strength of the verb matches the size of the event it reports, so the sentence works as written.

**C) Quarterly revenue overtook analysts' forecasts by the widest margin in three years.**

Results beat, exceed or come in ahead of forecasts, and "beat expectations" is so standard that a results-day headline barely needs anything else. "Overtake" requires two things travelling in the same direction, one catching the other, which is why cars and runners overtake but figures compared at a single moment do not.

**Trap:** A forecast is a benchmark, not a moving rival, so the verb of pursuit does not fit.

The comparison is between one quarter's figure and the consensus estimate for it, so the line should read "beat analysts' forecasts by the widest margin in three years."

**D) The board declined to reinstate the dividend until leverage fell below two times earnings.**

A dividend is cut, suspended or passed when a company is under strain, and reinstated when it resumes; "reinstate" carries exactly the sense of restoring something that was previously withdrawn. Tying that restoration to a leverage test is the usual condition boards attach, since lenders expect debt to come down before cash flows back to shareholders.

The verb presupposes a payment that had been stopped, which is precisely the situation described, so this line reads as a competent results report.

**E) Auditors questioned whether the group had been smoothing earnings across reporting periods.**

Earnings smoothing is the technical name for shifting income between periods to make a jagged series look steady, and the verb keeps its plain form with "earnings" as its object. It belongs to the same family as window dressing and creative accounting, all of which describe presentation rather than outright fabrication, and auditors are the natural subject of the doubt.

The phrase names a recognised practice in the terms the profession uses for it, so the sentence holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Results reporting runs on announcements, comparisons and payout decisions, each with its own fixed verb. Ask which announcements are issued rather than made, what a company does when figures come in above the consensus, and what happens to a dividend that was suspended and is now restored. Two of the phrases are technical accounting terms, so judge them on what the practice actually is rather than on how the words sound.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five lines from a trade-policy digest on barriers, balances and duties. Decide whether each combination is the one trade writing supplies.
statements: Exporters complained that the new certification rules erect non-tariff barriers against processed food.
The ministry announced that it would lay an embargo on timber from the disputed region.
The economy ran a persistent current-account deficit financed by short-term portfolio inflows.
Negotiators agreed to phase out tariffs on industrial goods over a period of seven years.
The commission voted to levy anti-dumping duties on subsidised steel imports.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Exporters complained that the new certification rules erect non-tariff barriers against processed food.**

Barriers are erected, raised or put up, since the metaphor treats them as structures blocking a route to market; the mirror phrase is dismantling or lowering them. Non-tariff barriers are precisely the sort built out of paperwork rather than tax — standards, licences, certification schemes — so a rule about certificates is the natural subject.

The metaphor and the technical term fit together as trade writing normally joins them, so this line stands.

**B) The ministry announced that it would lay an embargo on timber from the disputed region.**

An embargo is imposed on goods, or placed on them, and the same verbs serve sanctions, tariffs and quotas: the state applies a restriction from above. "Lay" belongs to a narrow set of legal and formal objects — lay charges, lay claim to something, lay down conditions — and it has never governed trade restrictions.

**Tip:** Sanctions, embargoes and quotas are all imposed on their target.

The ministry is announcing a ban on a category of imports, so the wording a trade report would carry is "impose an embargo on timber from the disputed region."

**C) The economy ran a persistent current-account deficit financed by short-term portfolio inflows.**

Countries run deficits and surpluses, exactly as companies run losses; the verb turns the balance into something maintained over time rather than a single event. "Persistent" is the standard adjective for a gap that fails to correct itself, and financing by portfolio inflows is the classic description of a deficit covered by volatile capital.

Every element of the phrase belongs to balance-of-payments writing, so the sentence is idiomatic as it stands.

**D) Negotiators agreed to phase out tariffs on industrial goods over a period of seven years.**

Tariffs are phased out when they fall to zero in scheduled steps, and the phrase carries its gradualism inside it, which is why a timetable follows so comfortably. Its partners are the same shape: phase in a rule, phase down a subsidy, with the particle marking the direction of the change.

A schedule stretching over seven years is exactly what this phrasal verb was made to describe, so the line is sound.

**E) The commission voted to levy anti-dumping duties on subsidised steel imports.**

Duties, tariffs and taxes are levied on goods by an authority, and "levy" is the formal member of a set that also includes impose and charge. Anti-dumping duties are the technical response to goods sold below a fair price, so the object of the verb is the standard one and the preposition "on" points at the imports being taxed.

The authority, the charge and the target line up as trade law arranges them, so this wording holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Trade writing treats barriers as structures, balances as things a country runs, and duties as charges a state puts on goods, and each of those images fixes its own verb. Check whether the verb belongs to the vocabulary of building, of accounting or of taxation, and whether the state is the party doing it. Only one line borrows a verb from a different family altogether, so compare each phrase with the version a trade ministry would publish.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Five lines from an audit file and the notes to a set of accounts. Decide whether each phrase is the fixed expression accounting uses.
statements: The auditors issued a qualified opinion after failing to obtain evidence on year-end inventory.
The distributor's collapse forced the group to write off bad debts worth twelve million.
Depreciation on the new fleet is charged on a straight-line basis over eight years.
The group recognises revenue only when control of the goods passes to the customer.
Analysts prefer cash flow because generous accruals can flatter reported earnings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The auditors issued a qualified opinion after failing to obtain evidence on year-end inventory.**

An audit opinion is issued, and the adjective in front of it is a graded technical scale: unqualified, qualified, adverse, or a disclaimer of opinion. A qualification is exactly what an auditor gives when one area of the accounts cannot be verified, and unverifiable stock is the textbook example, since inventory has to be counted at a moment that has already passed.

**Tip:** Qualified here means limited, not accredited.

The verb, the technical term and the reason given all match audit practice, so this line reads exactly as the report would.

**B) The distributor's collapse forced the group to write off bad debts worth twelve million.**

Debts that will never be collected are written off, which removes them from the books entirely, as against writing an asset down to a lower value that it still carries. "Bad debts" is the settled label for irrecoverable receivables, and a customer's insolvency is the standard trigger for accepting that the money is gone.

A collapse leaves nothing to recover, so the total write-off the sentence describes is the correct treatment and the correct phrase for it.

**C) Depreciation on the new fleet is charged on a straight-line basis over eight years.**

Depreciation is charged, and the method is introduced with "on a straight-line basis" or "on a reducing-balance basis"; the preposition and the article are both fixed inside that formula. Spreading the cost of vehicles evenly across their useful life is the ordinary choice, and eight years is a plausible life for a fleet.

The standard verb, the standard frame for the method and a sensible life all sit together here, so the note is properly worded.

**D) The group recognises revenue only when control of the goods passes to the customer.**

Revenue is recognised, and recognition is the formal act of admitting an item into the financial statements at a particular moment. Modern standards tie that moment to the transfer of control rather than to delivery or invoicing, so "control passes to the customer" is the very test the rule sets out.

The accounting term and the trigger written into the standard appear here in their normal form, so the policy note holds.

**E) Analysts prefer cash flow because generous accruals can flatter reported earnings.**

Figures are flattered when accounting choices make performance look better than the underlying business warrants, and "flatter the numbers" or "flatter earnings" is the usual way of saying it without alleging fraud. Accruals are the standard suspect because they bring income forward and push costs back, which is precisely why analysts fall back on cash.

The verb carries the mild scepticism the sentence needs, and its object is the one it normally takes, so the line is well formed.
tasks.solution_overview: Accounting language is close to a legal vocabulary: each procedure has one accepted wording and variation is treated as error. Test each line against what an auditor's report or a note to the accounts would actually say about opinions, irrecoverable balances, depreciation methods and the moment income enters the books. Where a phrase already exists as a term of art, the question is whether the sentence has used it in its proper technical sense.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Five lines from a corporate-finance memo on a leveraged buyout. Decide whether each phrase is the combination deal reporting actually uses.
statements: The sponsors plan to gear the acquisition with a mixture of senior and mezzanine debt.
Underwriters struggled to float the high-yield notes with institutional buyers.
Covenant packages were designed to ring-fence cash into debt service before dividends.
Rating agencies threatened to place the issuer on credit watch with negative implications.
Management promised to deleverage the balance sheet within eighteen months of closing.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The sponsors plan to gear the acquisition with a mixture of senior and mezzanine debt.**

Companies and balance sheets are geared or leveraged, and a purchase is financed or funded with a given mix of debt; "gear" does not take the acquisition itself as its object. The related noun "gearing" names the resulting ratio, which is why writers talk of high gearing and of a highly geared company rather than of gearing a deal.

**Trap:** Gear the company, finance the acquisition — keep the verb and the object matched.

What the sponsors are loading with borrowed money is the target, so the line a term sheet would carry is "finance the acquisition with a mixture of senior and mezzanine debt."

**B) Underwriters struggled to float the high-yield notes with institutional buyers.**

A company floats when it lists its equity on an exchange, and the noun "flotation" belongs to that IPO ceremony rather than to a bond syndication. High-yield notes are placed with investors, or the issue is syndicated, and both of those verbs describe finding buyers for already designed paper rather than bringing a new company to market.

**Tip:** Float shares in an IPO; place notes in a bond issue.

The underwriters were trying to sell debt to institutions, so the natural wording is "struggled to place the high-yield notes with institutional buyers."

**C) Covenant packages were designed to ring-fence cash into debt service before dividends.**

Cash and assets are ring-fenced from other claims, or earmarked for a particular use; the first pattern protects something against diversion and the second assigns it to a purpose. "Into" belongs to verbs of transfer such as inject and channel, and it cannot follow ring-fence, which is about drawing a protective boundary rather than pouring money somewhere.

The covenants are meant to keep cash reserved for creditors, so the phrase English supplies is either "ring-fence cash from dividend leakage" or "earmark cash for debt service."

**D) Rating agencies threatened to place the issuer on credit watch with negative implications.**

An issuer is placed on credit watch, or put on review for a possible downgrade, and the formula "with negative implications" is the agencies' own stock phrase for the direction of the signal. The wording stops short of an actual cut in the rating, which is exactly the intermediate warning the sentence describes.

The technical ceremony and its fixed wording both appear here in their normal form, so the sentence reads as a ratings bulletin would.

**E) Management promised to deleverage the balance sheet within eighteen months of closing.**

Balance sheets are deleveraged when debt is paid down relative to assets or earnings, and the verb is now standard in post-deal reporting. A timetable after closing is the usual promise sponsors make to rating agencies and lenders, since the leverage that funded the buyout is meant to be temporary.

The verb, the object and the horizon all belong to one familiar frame, so this line holds as written.
highlights: place the issuer on credit watch
tasks.solution_overview: Leveraged deals speak a dialect of their own: how debt is loaded onto a company, how paper finds buyers, how cash is protected for creditors, and how rating agencies signal concern each have a preferred wording. Ask which verbs take the company or the balance sheet as their object, and which take the securities or the rating itself. Two of the traps borrow a verb from a neighbouring capital-markets ritual, so check whether the object still matches the ceremony you named.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five lines from a competition-authority case file. Decide whether each phrase matches the wording of antitrust and merger review.
statements: Regulators warned that the merger would raise a dominant position in regional logistics.
The authority threatened to open a formal probe into alleged predatory pricing.
Rivals claimed the incumbent had broken a dominant position to shut out new entrants.
Clearance was granted only after the buyer agreed to divest overlapping depots.
The fine was designed to strip the cartelists of their illicit gains.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Regulators warned that the merger would raise a dominant position in regional logistics.**

A dominant position is created, acquired or strengthened, and EU merger control even prints the paired formula "create or strengthen a dominant position." "Raise" belongs with barriers, concerns, objections and prices — raise a barrier, raise concerns — and it cannot take a market position as its object.

**Trap:** Raise barriers to entry; create or strengthen a dominant position.

The fear in the file is that the merged firm would hold unlawful market power, so the wording a decision would carry is "create or strengthen a dominant position in regional logistics."

**B) The authority threatened to open a formal probe into alleged predatory pricing.**

Investigations, probes and inquiries are opened, and "open a probe into" is the standard journalistic and official pairing for starting one. Predatory pricing is a classic antitrust allegation, so the object of the inquiry is the one competition writing expects.

The verb, the formality marker and the preposition all sit where they should, so this line reads as a case update would.

**C) Rivals claimed the incumbent had broken a dominant position to shut out new entrants.**

What a powerful firm does wrongly is abuse a dominant position, and "abuse of dominance" is the legal label for that offence. "Break" governs laws, rules and agreements — break the law, break a covenant — and a position is held or abused rather than broken.

**Tip:** Break the rules; abuse the position those rules protect against.

The rivals are alleging exclusionary conduct by a powerful incumbent, so the phrase the complaint needs is "abused a dominant position to shut out new entrants."

**D) Clearance was granted only after the buyer agreed to divest overlapping depots.**

Assets are divested when a merger remedy requires their sale, and "divestiture" is the technical name for that cure. Overlapping sites are the classic candidates, because selling them restores a competitor where the overlap would otherwise have removed one.

The remedy verb and the type of asset it takes are exactly the ones merger control uses, so the sentence stands.

**E) The fine was designed to strip the cartelists of their illicit gains.**

Fines and confiscation orders strip offenders of gains, deprive them of profits, or force them to disgorge what they made; all three verbs treat the illicit money as something to be taken away. Cartels are the textbook subject of that logic, since the whole point of the penalty is to make collusion unprofitable.

The verb and the prepositional pattern "strip X of Y" are the ones this remedial purpose calls for, so the wording holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Competition writing has a near-legal vocabulary for market power, investigations and remedies, and most of its verbs are fixed. Ask what English says when a firm already holds power and misuses it, what an authority does when it starts an inquiry, and what a buyer must sell to win clearance. One trap borrows a verb that belongs with prices or barriers rather than with dominance itself, so check whether the object still matches the verb's usual family.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Five lines from a macro briefing on fiscal stance and public debt. Decide whether each phrase is the combination public-finance writing uses.
statements: Ministers promised to rein in public spending once the emergency support expired.
The treasury refused to water down the fiscal rules ahead of the autumn statement.
Debt-service costs began to crowd out capital investment in transport and housing.
A sudden stop in foreign buying could trigger a disorderly sell-off in government bonds.
Opposition MPs accused the chancellor of massaging the books to meet the deficit target.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Ministers promised to rein in public spending once the emergency support expired.**

Spending is reined in, curbed or brought under control, and "rein in" is the liveliest of those options without leaving the register of serious reporting. Emergency support that is allowed to expire is exactly the moment at which that restraint is usually promised.

The metaphor of holding back a horse and the object "public spending" are a standard pairing in fiscal commentary, so the sentence is sound.

**B) The treasury refused to water down the fiscal rules ahead of the autumn statement.**

Rules, standards and commitments are watered down when their force is diluted, and fiscal rules are a frequent object of that suspicion. Refusing the dilution is the stance a hawkish treasury claims before a budget, so the verb and the political moment fit.

The phrase is the one budget commentary habitually uses for softening a constraint, so this line holds.

**C) Debt-service costs began to crowd out capital investment in transport and housing.**

Crowding out is the textbook name for public borrowing or debt interest absorbing resources that would otherwise fund private or productive investment. Capital spending on infrastructure is the classic victim of that squeeze when interest bills rise.

The technical term and the type of spending it threatens appear here in their normal configuration, so the wording is exact.

**D) A sudden stop in foreign buying could trigger a disorderly sell-off in government bonds.**

Bond markets suffer orderly or disorderly sell-offs, and "disorderly" is the label officials reach for when prices gap and liquidity vanishes. A sudden stop in capital inflows is the standard shock that sets that process off in emerging and advanced markets alike.

Both halves of the sentence — the capital-flow trigger and the market outcome — belong to one established frame, so the line reads as a risk briefing would.

**E) Opposition MPs accused the chancellor of massaging the books to meet the deficit target.**

Two real phrases have been welded together: "massage the figures," which is how budget criticism describes soft presentation of a forecast, and "cook the books," which is the corporate-fraud charge for falsifying accounts. "Massage the books" belongs to neither pattern, and books in the fraud sense are not what a chancellor publishes before a fiscal event.

**Trap:** Blend detection — if each half of the phrase comes from a different idiom, the whole is usually wrong.

The attack is on optimistic presentation of the public finances, so the line that fits the register is "massaging the figures to meet the deficit target."
tasks.solution_overview: Public-finance English mixes technical terms of art with a few settled metaphors for restraint, dilution and market stress. Ask what a government does to spending when it wants control, what happens to private investment when public borrowing soaks up savings, and what a bond market does when confidence snaps. One line blends two genuine idioms of fiscal criticism, so check whether the verb and the noun still belong to the same fixed phrase.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Five lines from equity-research notes on valuation and shareholder returns. Decide whether each phrase is the one markets writing supplies.
statements: The shares still trade on a steep premium to the sector on every forward multiple.
Management pledged to reimburse capital to shareholders through buybacks and a special dividend.
A rights issue was floated to plug the hole left by the failed overseas expansion.
The stock re-rated sharply once the new margin targets looked credible to the market.
Analysts warned that a further profit warning could wipe the floor with the rating.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The shares still trade on a steep premium to the sector on every forward multiple.**

Shares trade at a premium to a benchmark, or at a discount to it, and that preposition is fixed; the same pattern covers trade at a multiple of earnings. "On" belongs to different market phrases — trade on an exchange, trade on rumour — and it cannot introduce the size of the premium.

**Tip:** Trade at a price, at a premium, at a discount; trade on an exchange.

The comparison with the sector is a valuation gap, so the wording a note would print is "trade at a steep premium to the sector."

**B) Management pledged to reimburse capital to shareholders through buybacks and a special dividend.**

Surplus cash is returned to shareholders, and "return of capital" is the technical label for distributions that are not ordinary dividends. "Reimburse" means paying someone back for an expense they have already met — reimburse travel costs — so it miscasts shareholders as creditors of out-of-pocket spending rather than as owners receiving surplus cash.

Buybacks and special dividends are classic return-of-capital tools, so the sentence needs "return capital to shareholders through buybacks and a special dividend."

**C) A rights issue was floated to plug the hole left by the failed overseas expansion.**

A company floats when it lists, and a flotation is an IPO; a rights issue is launched, announced or underwritten when existing shareholders are offered new stock. "Float" therefore imports the wrong capital-markets ceremony, even though "plug the hole" is an acceptable informal description of repairing a funding gap.

**Trap:** Float the company; launch the rights issue.

The group is raising emergency equity from existing holders, so the natural line is "a rights issue was launched to plug the hole."

**D) The stock re-rated sharply once the new margin targets looked credible to the market.**

A stock re-rates when investors assign it a higher or lower multiple, and the verb is standard in research notes for a lasting change in valuation rather than a one-day move. Credibility of margin targets is exactly the kind of narrative shift that produces a re-rating.

The technical verb and the catalyst both belong to equity commentary, so this line holds.

**E) Analysts warned that a further profit warning could wipe the floor with the rating.**

"Wipe the floor with" means defeat someone comprehensively in a contest, and its home is sport and argument rather than valuation. A rating is hit, cut, or left looking stretched; research English also says a warning would "weigh on the rating" or "put the rating under pressure."

A profit warning is a valuation event, not a contest, so the sober wording is "could weigh heavily on the rating."
tasks.solution_overview: Equity writing has fixed ways of talking about relative valuation, cash returned to owners, emergency equity raises and changes in how the market prices a stock. Ask which preposition a premium takes, what a company does with surplus cash, and which verbs belong to listing ceremonies rather than to cash calls. One trap imports a sporting idiom into a ratings discussion, so discard anything that could not appear in a sober research note.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five lines from a governance briefing on boards, pay and shareholder votes. Decide whether each phrase matches corporate-governance English.
statements: Proxy advisers urged investors to vote down the remuneration report at the annual meeting.
The chair refused to rubber-stamp a related-party deal without an independent fairness opinion.
Succession planning had been deferred for so long that the board risked a leadership vacuum.
Activist funds built a stake large enough to force a seat at the table in strategy talks.
Directors were reminded of their fiduciary duty to act in the company's best interests.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Proxy advisers urged investors to vote down the remuneration report at the annual meeting.**

A resolution is voted down when shareholders reject it, and the remuneration report is the classic target of that protest in markets with an advisory say-on-pay vote. Proxy advisers are precisely the intermediaries who issue that recommendation ahead of the AGM.

The verb, the report and the meeting all belong to one settled AGM frame, so the sentence is idiomatic as written.

**B) The chair refused to rubber-stamp a related-party deal without an independent fairness opinion.**

Rubber-stamping is the settled metaphor for approving something without real scrutiny, and refusing to do it is how serious boards describe their oversight role. Related-party deals are the textbook case that demand independent review, and a fairness opinion is the document that review often produces.

The sceptical metaphor and the transaction type fit together as governance writing joins them, so this line stands.

**C) Succession planning had been deferred for so long that the board risked a leadership vacuum.**

A leadership vacuum is the standard label for the gap that opens when a chief executive leaves without a ready successor. Linking that risk to deferred succession planning is the warning governance reports issue when boards have failed to groom a replacement.

The metaphor and the cause are the ones this failure routinely attracts, so the wording holds.

**D) Activist funds built a stake large enough to force a seat at the table in strategy talks.**

Activists build stakes, amass positions or accumulate shares, and "a seat at the table" is the usual prize they then demand in board or strategy discussions. "Force" correctly marks that the invitation is extracted rather than offered.

Both the stake-building verb and the access metaphor are fixtures of activist coverage, so the sentence reads as a briefing would.

**E) Directors were reminded of their fiduciary duty to act in the company's best interests.**

Fiduciary duty is the legal term for the obligation of loyalty and care directors owe the company, and "act in the company's best interests" is the plain-English restatement that accompanies it. The reminder is a stock move in governance training and in board minutes when conflicts loom.

The legal label and its gloss appear here in their normal pairing, so the line is exact.
highlights: force a seat at the table
tasks.solution_overview: Governance writing mixes AGM procedure, board oversight metaphors and a few legal terms of art. Test each line against the wording used for pay votes, related-party scrutiny, succession risk and activist pressure. Where a phrase is already a fixture of governance commentary, the only question is whether the sentence has used it in its ordinary sense.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five lines from a banking and credit-risk briefing. Decide whether each phrase is the combination credit writing uses.
