statements: Rising defaults forced the bank to take larger provisions against its corporate book.
The syndicate was oversubscribed within hours of the order book opening.
Covenant-lite loans left lenders with little room to pull the plug at the first sign of stress.
Stress tests asked whether capital buffers could withstand a severe downturn.
The regulator ordered the lender to set aside more capital to cover concentration risk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Rising defaults forced the bank to take larger provisions against its corporate book.**

Banks make, book or raise provisions for expected losses, and "provision against" is the pattern that names the exposure being covered. "Take" does not govern provisions in credit English, even though speakers take a charge or take a hit; the accounting act itself is making or booking the provision.

**Tip:** Make a provision; take a charge.

Defaults are exactly what drive higher expected-loss numbers, so the line should read "make larger provisions against its corporate book."

**B) The syndicate was oversubscribed within hours of the order book opening.**

An issue or an order book is oversubscribed when demand exceeds the amount on offer; the syndicate is the group of banks arranging the deal, not the thing investors subscribe for. Saying the syndicate was oversubscribed confuses the arrangers with the paper they are selling.

**Trap:** Oversubscribe the issue or the book, not the syndicate that runs it.

What filled too fast was demand for the loan, so the natural wording is "the issue was oversubscribed" or "the order book was oversubscribed."

**C) Covenant-lite loans left lenders with little room to pull the plug at the first sign of stress.**

"Pull the plug" is accepted credit slang for cutting a facility or forcing a default once protections are breached, and covenant-lite structures are defined by how little of that power they leave. The colourful verb is therefore doing exact technical work here rather than drifting into journalism.

The contrast between thin covenants and limited enforcement power is the standard critique of these loans, so the sentence stands.

**D) Stress tests asked whether capital buffers could withstand a severe downturn.**

Buffers withstand, absorb or weather a shock, and stress tests are built to ask exactly that question under a severe scenario. "Severe downturn" is the usual label for the adverse case those tests apply.

The verb, the buffer and the scenario form one settled supervisory frame, so this line is sound.

**E) The regulator ordered the lender to set aside more capital to cover concentration risk.**

Banks hold or maintain capital against risks, and supervisors require them to hold additional capital for concentrations; "set aside … to cover" is closer to provisioning language than to the capital stack. Capital is not an expense put on one side for a bill, but a permanent cushion measured against risk-weighted assets.

The order is about the capital requirement, so the phrasing a rulebook would use is "hold more capital against concentration risk."
highlights: set aside more capital to cover
tasks.solution_overview: Credit and banking English distinguishes provisions, syndication demand, covenant strength and capital held against risk, and each idea has a preferred verb. Ask what a bank does when it expects losses, what happens when a loan is popular with lenders, and how capital relates to the risks it is meant to absorb. One colourful phrase is accepted market slang; another only looks technical, so test each line against what a credit memo would actually print.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five lines from strategy notes on diversification, scale and competitive advantage. Decide whether each phrase matches strategy writing.
statements: The conglomerate vowed to stick to its knitting after two ill-judged foreign acquisitions.
Scale advantages allowed the platform to undercut rivals on price without sacrificing service.
Managers hoped the new brand would cannibalise sales from the group's older products overnight.
A first-mover advantage proved short-lived once imitators flooded the niche.
The board approved a bolt-on acquisition to deepen the firm's presence in diagnostics.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The conglomerate vowed to stick to its knitting after two ill-judged foreign acquisitions.**

The established strategy idiom is "stick to the knitting," not "stick to its knitting": the definite article is part of the fixed phrase, which means concentrate on the core business. Swapping in a possessive looks only slightly off, but it breaks the idiom that management commentary actually prints.

**Trap:** Stick to the knitting is fossilised with the.

After failed diversification the promise is a return to the core, so the line needs "stick to the knitting."

**B) Scale advantages allowed the platform to undercut rivals on price without sacrificing service.**

Rivals are undercut on price when a firm can charge less, and scale is the classic source of that ability. The pairing is so standard that "undercut on price" barely needs glossing in a strategy note.

Cost advantage and the pricing verb match exactly here, so the wording holds.

**C) Managers hoped the new brand would cannibalise sales from the group's older products overnight.**

Cannibalisation is usually a risk to be managed, not a hope to be celebrated: firms worry that a new product will cannibalise existing sales. Treating overnight cannibalisation as the desired outcome reverses the evaluation the verb carries in strategy English.

**Tip:** Cannibalise names damage to your own franchise, not a target to aim at.

If the goal is migration, writers speak of switching customers or replacing the old line; they do not hope to cannibalise it overnight, so this line fails.

**D) A first-mover advantage proved short-lived once imitators flooded the niche.**

First-mover advantage is the textbook label for the head start an early entrant enjoys, and saying it proved short-lived is the standard follow-up when copycats arrive. Flooding a niche is the usual image for that rush of imitators.

The technical term and the way it erodes appear here in their normal pairing, so the sentence is sound.

**E) The board approved a bolt-on acquisition to deepen the firm's presence in diagnostics.**

A bolt-on acquisition is a small, complementary deal added to an existing platform, as opposed to a transformative merger. Deepening presence in a known segment is precisely the purpose that label describes.

Deal-size jargon and strategic intent line up as M&A commentary expects, so this line stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Strategy commentary leans on a handful of metaphors for focus, pricing power, product overlap and deal size. Ask which phrases praise discipline, which describe deliberate self-competition, and which label a small deal meant to deepen a franchise. One trap is a folk idiom that sounds businesslike but is not the settled strategy phrase, and another treats a harmful side-effect as if it were the aim.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five lines from a supply-chain and trade-finance digest. Decide whether each phrase is the fixed combination logistics and trade credit use.
statements: Port congestion began to seal off shipments of intermediate goods into the assembly hubs.
Importers arranged a letter of credit to secure payment against shipping documents.
The manufacturer dual-sourced critical chips to hedge against a single-supplier failure.
Retailers' lean inventories left no buffer when the upstream shock hit.
Freight rates spiked as carriers blanked sailings to ration scarce vessel space.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Port congestion began to seal off shipments of intermediate goods into the assembly hubs.**

Areas, streets and crime scenes are sealed off; cargo flows are choked, disrupted or held up. "Seal off" pictures a cordon that people cannot cross, which is the wrong physical image for containers waiting outside a clogged harbour.

**Trap:** Seal off a zone; choke or disrupt a flow of goods.

Congestion is strangling movement rather than cordoning a place, so logistics writing would say "choke the flow of shipments into the assembly hubs."

**B) Importers arranged a letter of credit to secure payment against shipping documents.**

A letter of credit is the standard trade-finance instrument that promises payment when stipulated documents are presented, and "against shipping documents" is the classic formulation of that condition. Importers are the party that typically arranges it in favour of the exporter.

The instrument, the purpose and the documentary trigger are exactly as trade finance words them, so this line holds.

**C) The manufacturer dual-sourced critical chips to hedge against a single-supplier failure.**

Dual-sourcing is the settled term for splitting orders across two suppliers, and hedging against single-supplier failure is the textbook reason for doing it. Critical components such as chips are the usual example in resilience notes.

The sourcing verb and the risk it addresses match as strategy for supply risk expects, so the sentence is sound.

**D) Retailers' lean inventories left no buffer when the upstream shock hit.**

Inventories are lean when stock is kept deliberately thin, and the whole point of that model is the missing buffer the sentence names. An upstream shock is the standard event that then exposes the fragility.

The lean-inventory label and its consequence appear here in their ordinary coupling, so the wording holds.

**E) Freight rates spiked as carriers blanked sailings to ration scarce vessel space.**

Carriers blank sailings when they cancel scheduled voyages to tighten capacity, and the verb is now standard in shipping reports. Rationing scarce vessel space is precisely the effect those blankings produce when demand still exceeds supply.

The technical shipping verb and the capacity logic belong together, so this line is exact.
tasks.solution_overview: Supply-chain English mixes physical metaphors for blockage with the technical vocabulary of trade finance, sourcing and shipping schedules. Ask what congestion does to flows, how payment is secured against documents, and what carriers do to vessel capacity when rates are rising. One trap borrows a security verb that seals areas rather than choking cargo flows, so check whether the metaphor still matches a logistics scene.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five lines from a restructuring and insolvency memo. Decide whether each phrase matches distress and turnaround English.
statements: Creditors agreed to a debt-for-equity swap that left the founders with a minority stake.
The company filed for creditor protection after talks on a standstill agreement collapsed.
Advisers warned that fire-sale disposals would crystallise losses across the portfolio.
A white knight emerged with a rescue bid pitched above the liquidation value.
Lenders threatened to accelerate the debt if the interest cover covenant was breached.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Creditors agreed to a debt-for-equity swap that left the founders with a minority stake.**

A debt-for-equity swap converts claims into shares, and leaving founders diluted to a minority is the usual political price of that rescue. The hyphenated label is the fixed name for the exchange rather than a loose description.

The instrument and the ownership outcome match as restructuring memos describe them, so the sentence stands.

**B) The company filed for creditor protection after talks on a standstill agreement collapsed.**

A standstill agreement freezes enforcement while a deal is negotiated, and filing for creditor protection is the court route taken when those talks fail. Both phrases are terms of art in insolvency practice, and the sequence — failed standstill, then filing — is the standard narrative.

The two technical moves appear in the order distress stories expect, so this line holds.

**C) Advisers warned that fire-sale disposals would crystallise losses across the portfolio.**

Losses are crystallised when a sale turns a paper decline into a realised one, and a fire sale is the forced disposal that does exactly that. Portfolio-wide crystallisation is the warning turnaround teams issue when hurried exits are proposed.

The accounting verb and the forced-sale noun belong to one familiar pair, so the wording is exact.

**D) A white knight emerged with a rescue bid pitched above the liquidation value.**

A white knight is the friendly rescuer in a contested or distressed situation, and pitching a bid above liquidation value is how such a bid is justified to creditors. The chess metaphor is fully lexicalised in M&A and restructuring English.

The label, the purpose and the valuation floor line up as deal reporting joins them, so the sentence is sound.

**E) Lenders threatened to accelerate the debt if the interest cover covenant was breached.**

Acceleration makes the whole loan immediately due after a default, and an interest-cover breach is a classic trigger. "Accelerate the debt" is the lenders' own wording for that contractual right.

The remedy and the covenant that unlocks it are exactly as a facility agreement arranges them, so this line holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Distress vocabulary is highly conventional: exchanges of paper for ownership, pauses in enforcement, forced sales, rescue bidders and the right to call loans early each have a name. Test whether each line has used the term of art in the situation that term was coined for. Where the label already encodes the legal or market move, little else in the sentence needs to carry the meaning.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five lines from FX and capital-flow commentary. Decide whether each phrase is the combination markets and macro writing use.
statements: Heavy intervention failed to put a floor under the currency once reserves looked thin.
Portfolio managers rotated into defensive sectors as risk appetite dried away.
A carry trade dismantled abruptly when the funding currency began to appreciate.
Officials denied they were speaking down the exchange rate to help exporters.
Hot money flooded towards the local bond market in search of yield.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Heavy intervention failed to put a floor under the currency once reserves looked thin.**

Central banks try to put a floor under a currency, or under asset prices, when they buy to stop a freefall; the metaphor treats the rate as something that needs a base. Thin reserves are exactly why that defence then fails.

The support metaphor and the constraint on it are the ones FX desks use, so this line is sound.

**B) Portfolio managers rotated into defensive sectors as risk appetite dried away.**

Risk appetite dries up, not away; "dry up" is the fixed phrasal verb for a source that fails, while "dry away" is not an English pattern at all. Rotation into defensive sectors is the right accompanying move, so only the particle is wrong.

**Trap:** Dry up for vanishing supply or appetite; there is no dry away.

The sentence needs "as risk appetite dried up."

**C) A carry trade dismantled abruptly when the funding currency began to appreciate.**

Carry trades unwind when positions are closed in a hurry, and unwind is the market's own verb for that reversal. "Dismantle" governs machines, barriers and organisations — dismantle a scaffold, dismantle a cartel — and it never takes a trade as its object.

Appreciation of the funding currency is the classic trigger, so the line should read "a carry trade unwound abruptly when the funding currency began to appreciate."

**D) Officials denied they were speaking down the exchange rate to help exporters.**

The fixed phrase is talk down the currency, or talk the currency down: officials use words rather than intervention to push a rate lower. "Speak down" is not a capital-markets pattern, even though speak and talk overlap in everyday English.

**Tip:** Talk down a currency; talk up a stock — the verb is talk, not speak.

The denial concerns jawboning for a weaker rate, so the wording markets expect is "talking down the exchange rate."

**E) Hot money flooded towards the local bond market in search of yield.**

Hot money floods into a market, pours into it or flows into it; the preposition marks entry across the border into the asset class. "Towards" only signals direction without arrival, which is too weak for the surge the sentence wants to describe.

Yield-seeking foreign inflows are the classic hot-money story, so the phrase needs "flooded into the local bond market."
tasks.solution_overview: FX commentary depends on a few metaphors for supporting a rate, for risk appetite, for leveraged currency bets and for volatile foreign inflows. Ask which verbs keep a currency from falling further, what appetite does when it disappears, and which phrases belong to official rhetoric about the exchange rate. Several traps are near-miss particles or support verbs, so listen for the exact companion word the metaphor requires.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five lines from labour-economics notes on bargaining, hours and participation. Decide whether each phrase is the one specialist labour writing supplies.
statements: Unions threatened to ballot members on industrial action after talks stalled.
A higher reservation wage kept some claimants out of low-paid vacancies.
Employers tried to buy out restrictive practices with a one-off productivity bonus.
The participation rate edged higher as childcare places expanded in cities.
Zero-hours contracts left many workers unable to smooth their weekly earnings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Unions threatened to ballot members on industrial action after talks stalled.**

Unions ballot members for industrial action, or hold a ballot on strike action; the preposition that introduces the action is for, not on, when ballot is the verb. "Ballot on" appears with the noun — a ballot on strike action — but the verb pattern is ballot someone for something.

**Trap:** A ballot on X; ballot members for X.

After stalled talks the threat is a strike vote, so the line should read "ballot members for industrial action."

**B) A higher reservation wage kept some claimants out of low-paid vacancies.**

The reservation wage is the technical name for the lowest pay a worker will accept, and a higher one is exactly what keeps people out of poorly paid jobs. Claimants and vacancies are the usual cast in that explanation.

The term of art and the mechanism it names appear here correctly, so the sentence holds.

**C) Employers tried to buy out restrictive practices with a one-off productivity bonus.**

Restrictive practices are bought off, or management buys the abandonment of them; "buy out" governs owners and partners — buy out a shareholder, a buyout — rather than work rules. The productivity bonus is the right sort of sweetener, so only the verb is wrong.

**Tip:** Buy out equity; buy off resistance to change.

The deal is payment for giving up old rules, so industrial-relations English prefers "buy off restrictive practices."

**D) The participation rate edged higher as childcare places expanded in cities.**

Participation rates rise, fall or edge higher, and "edge" correctly marks a small move. Expanded childcare is a classic supply-side reason given for higher female participation in particular.

The statistical verb of small change and the policy cause fit labour-force commentary, so this line is sound.

**E) Zero-hours contracts left many workers unable to smooth their weekly earnings.**

Households and workers smooth earnings or consumption when they keep spending steady despite lumpy income; the verb is standard in labour and macroeconomics. Zero-hours contracts are precisely the arrangement that makes that smoothing hard because hours jump from week to week.

The technical verb and the contract type that frustrates it belong together, so the wording holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Labour economics has a precise vocabulary for strike procedure, the lowest acceptable wage, outdated work rules and measured labour-force entry. Ask which verbs belong with a strike ballot, what a reservation wage actually is, and how participation is reported when it moves only a little. One trap looks like industrial-relations English but uses the wrong support verb for ending a practice.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five lines from a regulatory-compliance and conduct briefing. Decide whether each phrase matches supervision and enforcement English.
statements: The watchdog threatened to throw the book at firms that mis-sold complex products.
Compliance teams scrambled to close out gaps ahead of the new disclosure rule.
A deferred prosecution agreement let the bank escape a full criminal trial.
Supervisors required the firm to remediate weaknesses in its financial-crime controls.
Whistleblowers are protected when they escalate concerns through approved channels.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The watchdog threatened to throw the book at firms that mis-sold complex products.**

"Throw the book at" is tabloid and police-drama English for maximum punishment; regulators impose fines, take enforcement action or pursue the full range of sanctions. Mis-selling is a real conduct offence, but the colourful idiom is not how supervision writes its threats.

**Trap:** Register failure — if it could headline a crime show, it probably does not belong in a regulatory brief.

The watchdog is promising tough enforcement, so the sober line is "take the full range of enforcement action against firms that mis-sold complex products."

**B) Compliance teams scrambled to close out gaps ahead of the new disclosure rule.**

Gaps in controls are closed or remediated; "close out" is trading and derivatives English for terminating a position — close out a trade, close out a hedge. Importing that particle into compliance work produces a blend that neither desk would print.

**Tip:** Close out a position; close a control gap.

Teams preparing for a new rule need to "close gaps" or "remediate gaps" in their disclosures.

**C) A deferred prosecution agreement let the bank escape a full criminal trial.**

Deferred prosecution agreements are real tools, but they resolve or settle potential charges; they do not "let" a bank "escape" in the wording counsel would use, and more importantly the collocation under test is strained because DPAs are entered into or reached, not pictured as jailbreaks. The sensational verb escape belongs to crime reporting rather than to the settlement vocabulary of "enter into a DPA" or "resolve charges through a DPA."

The instrument is named correctly, yet the support verb around it is journalistic rather than legal, so the line fails as specialist collocation — prefer "the bank entered into a deferred prosecution agreement rather than face a full criminal trial."

**D) Supervisors required the firm to remediate weaknesses in its financial-crime controls.**

Weaknesses are remediated in supervisory English, and financial-crime controls are a standard object of that order. The verb is more formal than fix or repair and is the one examination letters actually use.

The supervisory verb and the control area match as a consent order would word them, so this line holds.

**E) Whistleblowers are protected when they escalate concerns through approved channels.**

Concerns are escalated through a chain of command or through approved channels, and whistleblower policies are built around that escalation path. Protection attached to proper escalation is the usual legal and corporate framing.

The verb, the object and the channel phrase are the ones compliance manuals print, so the sentence is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Conduct and compliance writing mixes enforcement colour with precise verbs for fixing controls and raising alarms. Ask which phrases a regulator's press notice would actually print, what firms do to gaps before a rule bites, and how weaknesses in controls are formally repaired. Two traps sound forceful but belong to tabloid crime reporting or to trading desks rather than to supervisory English.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five lines from project-finance and infrastructure notes. Decide whether each phrase is the combination that sector uses.
statements: Lenders refused to take out construction risk until the plant had passed acceptance tests.
The concession agreement locked in tariffs for the first fifteen years of operation.
Sponsors injected additional equity to cure a cash-flow shortfall during ramp-up.
A take-or-pay clause obliged the offtaker to pay even when volumes fell short.
Political-risk insurance was bought to cover expropriation and contract frustration.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Lenders refused to take out construction risk until the plant had passed acceptance tests.**

Parties take on risk, assume it or are left with it; "take out" belongs to insurance — take out a policy — and to removing something. Construction risk passes from sponsors to contractors or remains with sponsors until completion tests, but nobody takes it out.

**Trap:** Take out insurance; take on risk.

Lenders are refusing to bear unfinished-plant risk, so the term-sheet wording is "refused to take on construction risk until the plant had passed acceptance tests."

**B) The concession agreement locked in tariffs for the first fifteen years of operation.**

Tariffs, prices and rates are locked in when a contract fixes them against later change, and concession agreements are the usual place that fix appears for infrastructure. A fifteen-year window is a typical availability period for that protection.

The verb and the regulated price it freezes are standard project-finance English, so this line holds.

**C) Sponsors injected additional equity to cure a cash-flow shortfall during ramp-up.**

Equity is injected when sponsors put fresh capital in, and shortfalls are cured in facility-agreement English when a breach or gap is repaired. Ramp-up is the phase when volumes are still climbing and cash is often tight.

Both technical verbs sit in their normal slots here, so the sentence is sound.

**D) A take-or-pay clause obliged the offtaker to pay even when volumes fell short.**

Take-or-pay is the fixed name for an offtake obligation to pay for capacity whether or not it is used, and it exists precisely for the shortfall case the sentence describes. The offtaker is the party bound by that clause.

The contract label and its economic effect match exactly, so this wording stands.

**E) Political-risk insurance was bought to cover expropriation and contract frustration.**

Political-risk insurance is the product that covers expropriation, currency inconvertibility and related sovereign events, and buying cover for those perils is how sponsors describe the purchase. Contract frustration sits inside the same family of covered political events.

The product name and the perils listed are the ones underwriters catalogue, so the line is exact.
tasks.solution_overview: Project finance has a ritual vocabulary for who bears construction risk, how tariffs are fixed, how equity plugs holes and how offtake is guaranteed. Ask which verbs mean assuming a risk, which mean fixing a price, and which name the contract forms that keep lenders whole. One trap uses an insurance verb for a risk-allocation idea that term sheets express differently.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five lines from a monetary-transmission and yield-curve briefing. Decide whether each phrase matches advanced macro-finance English.
statements: A steeper yield curve usually signals that markets are pricing in firmer growth ahead.
Quantitative tightening began to drain excess reserves from the banking system.
Forward guidance was recalibrated to avoid a premature easing of financial conditions.
Mortgage spreads widened as lenders passed on higher wholesale funding costs.
The policy rate was held in restrictive territory to keep demand in check.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A steeper yield curve usually signals that markets are pricing in firmer growth ahead.**

Markets price in an outcome when its probability is already reflected in asset prices, and firmer growth is a classic thing a steepening curve is said to price in. The phrasal verb is indispensable in rates commentary.

The curve signal and the pricing-in verb belong to one standard reading of steepening, so this line holds.

**B) Quantitative tightening began to drain excess reserves from the banking system.**

Tightening drains reserves when the central bank shrinks its balance sheet, and excess reserves are the precise stock being reduced. The plumbing verb drain is the one operations notes use for that shrinkage.

The policy label and the reserve effect match as balance-sheet policy describes them, so the sentence is sound.

**C) Forward guidance was recalibrated to avoid a premature easing of financial conditions.**

Financial conditions ease or tighten, and guidance is recalibrated when the committee resets what it wants markets to infer. Avoiding premature easing is a standard hawkish reason for adjusting that language.

Both halves — the guidance verb and the conditions noun phrase — are fixtures of policy writing, so the wording stands.

**D) Mortgage spreads widened as lenders passed on higher wholesale funding costs.**

Costs are passed on to customers when lenders raise retail rates in step with wholesale ones, and spreads widen when that pass-through is incomplete or lagged. The two movements are the usual pairing in credit-channel notes.

The pass-on verb and the spread outcome are exactly how transmission into mortgages is narrated, so this line is exact.

**E) The policy rate was held in restrictive territory to keep demand in check.**

A rate sits in restrictive territory when it is judged above neutral and is cooling the economy, and keeping demand in check is the purpose of staying there. Both phrases are now stock central-bank English.

The locative metaphor for stance and the demand objective fit together as a policy explanation would, so the sentence holds.
highlights: passed on higher wholesale funding costs
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced macro-finance writing treats the curve, the balance sheet, guidance and credit spreads as parts of one transmission story. Ask how markets embed a growth view in prices, what tightening does to reserves, and where a policy rate sits when it is meant to cool demand. Each line here turns on a phrase that is already a term of art in central-bank and rates commentary.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced trade and industrial-policy analysis. Decide whether each phrase is the specialist combination the field uses.
statements: Critics argued that local-content rules would fragment global value chains beyond repair.
Export credits were deployed to level the playing field against subsidised rivals.
The ministry announced a strategic stockpile to ride out disruptions in critical minerals.
Dumping margins were calculated by comparing export prices against normal value.
Supporters claimed the tariff would raise infant industries until they reached scale.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Critics argued that local-content rules would fragment global value chains beyond repair.**

Value chains fragment, or production fragments across borders, and that verb is sound; the failure is the tacked-on "beyond repair," which belongs to relationships and damaged objects rather than to supply networks that can be reconfigured. Specialist critique stops at fragment, reshape or shorten global value chains.

**Trap:** Beyond repair intensifies emotion but is not part of the trade collocation.

The charge against local-content rules is fragmentation, so the line should end at "fragment global value chains" without the irreversible flourish.

**B) Export credits were deployed to level the playing field against subsidised rivals.**

A playing field is levelled, but the complement is between rivals or for domestic firms — not against them. "Against" turns the metaphor into a weapon pointed at competitors, whereas the idiom means restoring fairness among them.

**Tip:** Level the playing field for X / between X and Y — never against.

Export credits as a counter-subsidy need "level the playing field with subsidised rivals" or "for domestic exporters facing subsidised rivals."

**C) The ministry announced a strategic stockpile to ride out disruptions in critical minerals.**

Countries ride out disruptions, shocks and storms when buffers let them endure a temporary shortage, and a strategic stockpile is built for exactly that purpose in critical minerals. The phrasal verb is standard resilience English.

The stockpile and the disruptions it is meant to survive belong together, so this wording holds.

**D) Dumping margins were calculated by comparing export prices against normal value.**

Anti-dumping calculations compare the export price with normal value, or set the margin as the difference between those two; "compare against" is not the statutory or textbook preposition. "Against" belongs to benchmarks in other settings — performance against a target — and it jars in the dumping formula.

The arithmetic is right in spirit, so the repaired line is "comparing export prices with normal value."

**E) Supporters claimed the tariff would raise infant industries until they reached scale.**

Infant industries are protected, fostered or sheltered under the infant-industry argument; "raise" governs children, funds and objections — raise a child, raise capital, raise an objection — and it does not take an industry as the thing cultivated behind a tariff wall.

**Trap:** Raise capital for an industry; protect an infant industry.

The classic case for temporary tariffs needs "protect infant industries until they reached scale."
highlights: fragment global value chains beyond repair
tasks.solution_overview: Industrial-policy English mixes value-chain analysis, subsidy counter-measures, stockpiles and anti-dumping arithmetic. Ask which metaphors describe breaking up production networks, what export credits are said to do to competition, and which verbs belong with infant-industry protection. Several lines are almost right but tip into overstatement or the wrong preposition, so judge the whole phrase rather than the familiar noun alone.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced corporate-governance and capital-structure analysis. Decide whether each phrase is the specialist combination boards and bondholders use.
statements: Independent directors were asked to form a special committee to opine on the related-party offer.
Bondholders complained that asset stripping had hollowed out their recovery prospects.
The dual-class structure entrenched founders against a hostile change of control.
Covenant carve-outs let the issuer leak value to equity through permitted distributions.
A poison pill was adopted to dilute any bidder who crossed the trigger threshold.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Independent directors were asked to form a special committee to opine on the related-party offer.**

Special committees opine on conflicted transactions, and "opine on" is the slightly formal verb minutes and fairness opinions still use. Related-party offers are the classic trigger for that committee structure.

The committee, the verb and the conflicted deal type match Delaware-style governance English, so this line holds.

**B) Bondholders complained that asset stripping had hollowed out their recovery prospects.**

Asset stripping is a real charge, but the fixed creditor complaint is that it has hollowed out the company or the collateral, not the abstract "recovery prospects." Prospects are damaged, impaired or weakened; hollow out takes a structure that once had substance — a firm, a balance sheet, a franchise.

**Trap:** Hollow out the company; impair recovery prospects.

Bondholders fear empty collateral, so the natural line is "asset stripping had hollowed out the company" or "had impaired their recovery prospects."

**C) The dual-class structure entrenched founders against a hostile change of control.**

Dual-class shares entrench founders, and entrenchment is the standard critique, but the preposition is wrong: founders are entrenched in control, or the structure entrenches them; "against" belongs to protect against or insure against. The hostile change of control is what the structure resists, yet English does not entrench someone against an event.

The repaired governance line is "entrenched founders in the face of a hostile change of control" or simply "entrenched founder control."

**D) Covenant carve-outs let the issuer leak value to equity through permitted distributions.**

Value leaks to equity when loopholes allow cash or assets to leave the restricted group, and covenant carve-outs are exactly those loopholes. Distressed-debt analysts use "leak value" as a term of art for that transfer.

The carve-out mechanism and the leakage metaphor belong together in bondholder English, so the sentence stands.

**E) A poison pill was adopted to dilute any bidder who crossed the trigger threshold.**

A poison pill is adopted or implemented, and its mechanical effect is to dilute a bidder who crosses a ownership trigger. Both the adoption verb and the dilution purpose are the textbook description of a shareholder-rights plan.

The defence and its trigger logic appear here as takeover manuals state them, so this wording holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Governance and leveraged-structure English has fixed ways of describing special committees, tunnelling of value, dual-class control and takeover defences. Ask which verbs boards use for formal opinions, what asset stripping does to creditors, and how poison pills actually work. Two traps are near-miss prepositions or support verbs around otherwise genuine terms of art.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five lines from derivatives and risk-management notes. Decide whether each phrase matches specialist market-risk English.
statements: The desk rolled the hedge forward into the next quarter to keep duration matched.
Counterparties posted variation margin as mark-to-market losses mounted.
Managers tried to diversify away idiosyncratic risk by holding a single concentrated name.
A wrong-way risk arose because the guarantor's credit improved as the underlying deteriorated.
The fund was caught on a short squeeze as borrowed stock became scarce and expensive.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The desk rolled the hedge forward into the next quarter to keep duration matched.**

Hedges are rolled forward when an expiring contract is replaced with a later one, and keeping duration matched is the usual reason. The particle "forward" is part of the fixed dealing phrase.

The roll and the duration motive are exactly how rates desks narrate that maintenance, so this line holds.

**B) Counterparties posted variation margin as mark-to-market losses mounted.**

Variation margin is posted as mark-to-market moves against a party, and mounting losses are the trigger. "Post margin" is the operational verb clearing houses and CSAs use.

The collateral verb and the MTM cause match market practice, so the sentence is sound.

**C) Managers tried to diversify away idiosyncratic risk by holding a single concentrated name.**

Idiosyncratic risk is diversified away by holding many imperfectly correlated names; a single concentrated holding does the opposite and increases that risk. The collocation "diversify away" is itself genuine, but pairing it with concentration is a selection failure: the means contradict the verb.

**Trap:** If the portfolio action undoes the verb, the line is false even when the phrase is familiar.

Diversifying idiosyncratic risk requires breadth, so this strategy description does not hold.

**D) A wrong-way risk arose because the guarantor's credit improved as the underlying deteriorated.**

Wrong-way risk arises when exposure to a counterparty grows as that counterparty's creditworthiness declines. Here the guarantor's credit improves while the underlying deteriorates, which is right-way: the protection gets stronger as the need appears. Labelling that pattern wrong-way reverses the definition.

**Tip:** Wrong-way = exposure and credit quality move against you together.

The mechanism described is right-way risk, so calling it wrong-way does not hold.

**E) The fund was caught on a short squeeze as borrowed stock became scarce and expensive.**

Funds are caught in a short squeeze, not on one; the preposition matches trapped in a corner or caught in a squeeze. Scarce, expensive borrow is the correct accompanying detail, so only the particle fails.

The repaired markets line is "caught in a short squeeze as borrowed stock became scarce and expensive."
tasks.solution_overview: Derivatives English is exact about rolling hedges, posting margin, diversifying risk and the directionality of credit exposures. Ask what a desk does when a hedge expires, what counterparties deliver as prices move, and whether a described portfolio could possibly diversify anything. Two traps state a genuine term of art in a situation that contradicts its definition, and one uses the wrong particle with a squeeze.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five lines from sustainable-finance and climate-risk briefing notes. Decide whether each phrase is the combination that field uses.
statements: Asset managers pledged to steward portfolio companies toward credible transition plans.
Critics said the green bond merely window-dressed ordinary spending without ring-fenced proceeds.
Physical climate risk was mapped against acute flood and heatwave scenarios in the book.
Insurers began to load chronic heat risk into premiums across their property books.
The taxonomy aimed to channel capital into activities aligned with net-zero pathways.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Asset managers pledged to steward portfolio companies toward credible transition plans.**

Stewardship language has managers steward companies, or exercise stewardship over holdings, toward better practice; "toward credible transition plans" is the standard climate engagement objective. The verb is now institutional rather than pastoral.

Engagement purpose and the stewardship verb match as responsible-investment policies word them, so this line holds.

**B) Critics said the green bond merely window-dressed ordinary spending without ring-fenced proceeds.**

Window-dressing is what funds and banks do to portfolios or balance sheets at a reporting date; greenwashing critiques say issuers relabel, rebrand or refinance ordinary spending without ring-fenced proceeds. Applying window-dress to spending imports the wrong ceremony.

**Trap:** Window-dress a portfolio; relabel or rebrand spending as green.

The integrity attack needs "merely relabelled ordinary spending without ring-fenced proceeds."

**C) Physical climate risk was mapped against acute flood and heatwave scenarios in the book.**

Physical risk is assessed against acute hazards such as floods and heatwaves, as distinct from chronic risks such as sea-level rise; mapping exposures against those scenarios is standard climate-risk practice. The acute label correctly marks short-lived shocks rather than gradual change.

The risk type and the scenario family belong together, so this wording holds.

**D) Insurers began to load chronic heat risk into premiums across their property books.**

Underwriters load a peril into premiums when they rebuild rates so that the price of cover reflects that hazard, and chronic heat is a recognised physical risk for property books. The load-into-premiums pattern is standard insurance-pricing English rather than a markets "price in" metaphor.

The peril, the verb and the premium object match as climate-underwriting notes word them, so the sentence stands.

**E) The taxonomy aimed to channel capital into activities aligned with net-zero pathways.**

Capital is channelled into aligned activities, and taxonomies exist to guide that channelling toward net-zero pathways. Both halves of the phrase are stock sustainable-finance wording.

The policy tool and the capital-flow verb fit as taxonomy preambles state them, so this line is exact.
highlights: load chronic heat risk into premiums
tasks.solution_overview: Sustainable-finance English distinguishes stewardship, use-of-proceeds integrity, climate-scenario design and the channelling of capital. Ask what managers do when they engage holdings, what makes a green label hollow, and which scenario names belong with physical risk. One trap borrows a year-end portfolio idiom to attack a bond label, so check whether the verb still fits greenwashing critique.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced competition and platform-economics analysis. Decide whether each phrase matches specialist antitrust English for digital markets.
statements: Rivals alleged that self-preferencing on the marketplace foreclosed equally efficient competitors.
Network effects helped the platform tip the market once critical mass was reached.
The authority floated behavioural remedies before contemplating a structural break-up.
Multi-homing by users was expected to dilute the winner-takes-most dynamic.
Gatekeeper status triggered ex-ante obligations on interoperability and data access.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Rivals alleged that self-preferencing on the marketplace foreclosed equally efficient competitors.**

Self-preferencing is the established label for a platform favouring its own services, and foreclosure of equally efficient competitors is the standard theory of harm attached to it. Marketplace ranking and default placement are the usual scene for that allegation.

The conduct label and the foreclosure test appear together as competition decisions join them, so this line holds.

**B) Network effects helped the platform tip the market once critical mass was reached.**

Markets tip when network effects push users toward a single platform after critical mass, and both "tip" and "critical mass" are textbook in platform economics. The causal chain in the sentence is the classic one.

The tipping verb and the threshold that unlocks it match specialist usage, so the wording is sound.

**C) The authority floated behavioural remedies before contemplating a structural break-up.**

Remedies are behavioural or structural, and authorities often float or propose the lighter behavioural package before a break-up. "Float" here means canvass as an option, which is ordinary regulatory English.

The remedy spectrum and the sequencing are exactly as merger and antitrust toolkits describe them, so this line stands.

**D) Multi-homing by users was expected to dilute the winner-takes-most dynamic.**

Multi-homing is the term for using several platforms at once, and it is routinely said to dilute or weaken winner-takes-most tendencies. The pair is a staple of digital-competition argument.

User behaviour and the market-dynamic label fit as platform papers couple them, so the sentence holds.

**E) Gatekeeper status triggered ex-ante obligations on interoperability and data access.**

Gatekeeper is the regulatory status that triggers ex-ante duties, and interoperability plus data access are emblematic obligations in that regime. "Triggered" correctly marks automatic consequences of designation.

The status, the timing of the rules and the duty types match digital-markets legislation, so this wording is exact.
tasks.solution_overview: Digital-competition English has rapidly stabilised around self-preferencing, tipping, remedies, multi-homing and gatekeeper duties. Test whether each line uses those labels in the situations regulators and platform economists coined them for. Where a term already encodes the theory of harm or the remedy type, the sentence only needs to keep the surrounding verbs in the same register.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five lines from specialist macro notes on imbalances, credibility and regime shifts. Decide whether each phrase is the combination advanced policy writing uses.
statements: A sudden stop forced the treasury to burn through reserves defending the peg.
Policy credibility hinged on the bank's willingness to look through transitory shocks.
Fiscal dominance threatened to subordinate the inflation target under debt financing needs.
Hysteresis in the labour market meant that structural unemployment proved purely cyclical.
Officials denied any attempt to jawbone markets into pricing a shallower path.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A sudden stop forced the treasury to burn through reserves defending the peg.**

Sudden stops are real, and defending a peg does consume reserves, but the settled verb is run down reserves, deplete them or spend them; "burn through" is informal narrative English for cash and runway, not the balance-of-payments verb for reserve loss under a peg. Specialist notes keep to run down or deplete.

**Trap:** Burn through cash in a startup; run down reserves in a peg defence.

The crisis sequence needs "run down reserves defending the peg."

**B) Policy credibility hinged on the bank's willingness to look through transitory shocks.**

Central banks look through transitory shocks when they refuse to react to noise that will fade, and credibility is often said to hinge on that discipline. Both "look through" and "transitory shocks" are stock policy phrases.

The conditional credibility story and the looking-through verb match as inflation reports word them, so this line holds.

**C) Fiscal dominance threatened to subordinate the inflation target under debt financing needs.**

Fiscal dominance subordinates the inflation target to debt-financing needs, and that to-preposition is fixed: one goal is placed under another in the sense of hierarchy only through "subordinate X to Y." "Under" belongs to live under, under pressure, under a regime — not to the object pattern of subordinate.

**Tip:** Subordinate X to Y; never subordinate X under Y.

The regime risk needs "subordinate the inflation target to debt financing needs."

**D) Hysteresis in the labour market meant that structural unemployment proved purely cyclical.**

Hysteresis is the claim that cyclical damage hardens into structural unemployment; saying structural unemployment proved purely cyclical reverses that claim and empties the term. The collocation is intact only when scars become lasting, not when lasting joblessness is reclassified as temporary.

The definition points the other way, so this line does not hold — hysteresis means cyclical scars become structural.

**E) Officials denied any attempt to jawbone markets into pricing a shallower path.**

Jawboning is the established label for using words to move markets, and "jawbone markets into" pricing an outcome is how policy writers describe that pressure. A shallower rate path is a classic thing officials are accused of talking markets toward.

The persuasion verb and the pricing outcome belong to one familiar policy frame, so the wording stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced macro writing leans on sudden stops, looking through shocks, fiscal dominance, hysteresis and jawboning. Ask which verbs belong with reserve loss in a peg defence, what a credible bank does with noise in the data, and which terms name lasting labour-market damage. Two traps attach a genuine term of art to the wrong support verb, the wrong preposition, or a reversed definition.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five lines from specialist banking notes on resolution, liquidity and wholesale funding. Decide whether each phrase matches crisis-management English.
statements: Resolution plans assumed the group could bail in eligible liabilities without taxpayer support.
A ring-fenced retail bank was meant to insulate depositors from trading-book losses.
Wholesale funding evaporated once counterparties began to smell distress on the name.
Liquidity coverage assumed high-quality liquid assets could be mortgaged under stress.
Supervisors demanded a living will that mapped how critical functions would be preserved.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Resolution plans assumed the group could bail in eligible liabilities without taxpayer support.**

Eligible liabilities are bailed in when losses are written onto creditors rather than taxpayers, and that assumption is the core of modern resolution planning. "Without taxpayer support" restates the point of the tool.

The bail-in verb and the eligible-liability object are exactly as resolution regimes word them, so this line holds.

**B) A ring-fenced retail bank was meant to insulate depositors from trading-book losses.**

Ring-fencing insulates retail depositors from investment-banking and trading losses, and that purpose clause is how the structural reform is always explained. The from-preposition correctly marks the risk kept outside the fence.

The structural label and the insulation purpose match as the statute's own rhetoric, so the sentence stands.

**C) Wholesale funding evaporated once counterparties began to smell distress on the name.**

Wholesale funding can evaporate, but "smell distress on the name" is dealing-floor slang rather than the collocation crisis notes use; specialists say counterparties sniffed trouble, pulled lines, or lost confidence in the name. "Smell distress on" is not a fixed funding phrase.

**Trap:** Evaporate is fine; the olfactory slang around the name is not.

A resolution-ready version is "once counterparties began to pull lines on the name" or "lost confidence in the name."

**D) Liquidity coverage assumed high-quality liquid assets could be mortgaged under stress.**

The liquidity coverage ratio assumes high-quality liquid assets can be monetised under stress — sold or repo'd for cash — not mortgaged. Mortgaging names a secured borrowing against property or specific collateral in a different legal sense, and it is not the LCR verb for turning the buffer into liquidity.

**Tip:** Monetise HQLA under stress; mortgage a property.

The stress assumption needs "could be monetised under stress."

**E) Supervisors demanded a living will that mapped how critical functions would be preserved.**

A living will, or resolution plan, maps how critical functions continue through failure, and supervisors demand exactly that mapping. The colloquial label is now settled in regulatory English beside the formal resolution-plan title.

The document name and the preservation purpose appear as rulebooks join them, so this wording holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Resolution and liquidity English is deliberately technical: bail-in, ring-fencing, HQLA monetisation and living wills each have approved wording. Ask which verbs belong with loss absorption, what ring-fencing is meant to do for depositors, and how stress assumes assets can be turned into cash. One trap slips into trader slang; another mortgages assets that should be monetised.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced financial-reporting notes on OCI, impairment and tax. Decide whether each phrase matches specialist accounting English.
statements: The group recycled gains from OCI into profit on disposal of the debt instruments.
An impairment charge was levied on goodwill after the cash-generating unit failed its recoverability test.
Hedge effectiveness was demonstrated solely by matching notionals without further testing.
Fair-value hierarchy disclosures ranked the Level 1 inputs as the most judgmental.
Deferred tax was recognised on a permanent difference arising from non-deductible fines.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The group recycled gains from OCI into profit on disposal of the debt instruments.**

Amounts in other comprehensive income are recycled into profit or loss on disposal when the standard requires it, and debt instruments accounted through OCI are a classic case. "Recycle … from OCI into profit" is the fixed reporting phrase.

The movement and the trigger match as financial-instrument notes describe them, so this line holds.

**B) An impairment charge was levied on goodwill after the cash-generating unit failed its recoverability test.**

Impairment charges are recognised, recorded or taken against carrying amounts; "levy" belongs to taxes, duties and fines imposed by an authority. Goodwill impairments after a failed recoverability test are real, but the support verb is wrong.

**Trap:** Levy a tax; recognise an impairment.

The CGU failure needs "an impairment charge was recognised on goodwill."

**C) Hedge effectiveness was demonstrated solely by matching notionals without further testing.**

Matching notionals alone does not demonstrate effectiveness under modern hedge accounting; qualitative or quantitative testing of the economic relationship is required. Presenting notional matching as sufficient is a selection failure against the rules the collocation lives in.

Effectiveness must be evidenced properly, so this shortcut description does not hold.

**D) Fair-value hierarchy disclosures ranked the Level 1 inputs as the most judgmental.**

Level 1 inputs are quoted prices in active markets and are the least judgmental; Level 3 inputs are the most judgmental. Ranking Level 1 as most judgmental reverses the hierarchy the disclosure is built to show.

**Tip:** Level 1 least judgment; Level 3 most.

The hierarchy label is used upside down here, so the line fails.

**E) Deferred tax was recognised on a permanent difference arising from non-deductible fines.**

Permanent differences, such as non-deductible fines, never reverse and therefore never create deferred tax; deferred tax arises on temporary differences. Recognising deferred tax on a permanent difference contradicts the definition that governs the collocation.

Non-deductible fines affect the effective tax rate, not the deferred-tax balance, so this accounting line does not hold.
highlights: recycled gains from OCI into profit
Level 1 inputs as the most judgmental
Deferred tax was recognised on a permanent difference
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced IFRS English is unforgiving about recycling, impairment verbs, hedge tests, fair-value levels and permanent differences. Ask what happens to OCI on disposal, which verbs take an impairment charge, and which hierarchy level is most judgmental. Three traps reverse a definition or borrow a tax verb for an accounting charge.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five lines from private-equity portfolio notes on capital extraction, incentives and exits. Decide whether each phrase matches specialist buyout English.
statements: The sponsor extracted a dividend recap once leverage covenants allowed.
Management rolled equity into the newco to keep skin in the game.
A performance ratchet favoured management if exit multiples compressed below plan.
Portco reporting was standardised to a monthly flash for the investment committee.
The exit was timed to ride a seller's market in the specialty-chemicals niche.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The sponsor extracted a dividend recap once leverage covenants allowed.**

A dividend recapitalisation is extracted or taken when sponsors pay themselves a debt-funded dividend, and covenant headroom is the usual gate. "Extract a dividend recap" is established PE shorthand.

The extraction verb and the covenant condition match as deal notes word them, so this line holds.

**B) Management rolled equity into the newco to keep skin in the game.**

Managers roll equity into the newco when they reinvest proceeds or retain shares across the buyout, and "skin in the game" is the stock justification. Both halves are PE fixtures.

The roll and the incentive metaphor belong together, so the sentence stands.

**C) A performance ratchet favoured management if exit multiples compressed below plan.**

Ratchets adjust management's equity share when performance beats a hurdle; compression of exit multiples below plan is underperformance and would dilute or leave management worse off, not favour them. Pairing favour with a downside miss reverses how the ratchet is meant to work.

**Trap:** Ratchets reward outperformance, not multiple compression.

A coherent line would favour management if exit multiples expanded above plan, so this wording fails.

**D) Portco reporting was standardised to a monthly flash for the investment committee.**

Portfolio companies file a monthly flash — a short KPI pack — to the investment committee, and standardising that pack across the portco set is ordinary PE operating practice. "Flash" is the settled informal label.

The report type and its audience match buyout operations English, so this line holds.

**E) The exit was timed to ride a seller's market in the specialty-chemicals niche.**

Exits ride a seller's market when timing exploits strong buyer demand, and niche specialty chemicals are a typical place that phrase appears. "Ride" is the usual verb for catching that window.

The timing metaphor and the market label fit as exit memos write them, so the wording is exact.
highlights: ratchet favoured management if exit multiples compressed
monthly flash for the investment committee
tasks.solution_overview: Buyout English has fixed labels for dividend recaps, rolled equity, ratchets, portfolio-company flashes and exit timing. Ask what sponsors extract when covenants allow, how managers keep exposure after a deal, and which way a ratchet pays when performance disappoints. One trap states a genuine incentive term with the wrong performance trigger.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced open-economy macro and sovereign-debt analysis. Decide whether each phrase is the specialist combination the literature uses.
statements: Original sin left the sovereign unable to borrow abroad in its own currency.
A debt overhang discouraged private investment even after primary balances improved.
Contingent liabilities crystallised when the state guaranteed a failing utility's bonds.
Real exchange-rate misalignment was estimated against a fundamentals-based equilibrium.
Official creditors granted a reprofiling that pushed maturities beyond the election cycle.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Original sin left the sovereign unable to borrow abroad in its own currency.**

Original sin is Eichengreen's label for the inability of many sovereigns to borrow abroad in local currency, and "left the sovereign unable" correctly states that constraint. The term is not a moral metaphor here but a market-structure one.

The research label and the borrowing limit it names appear together as the literature joins them, so this line holds.

**B) A debt overhang discouraged private investment even after primary balances improved.**

A debt overhang discourages investment when future creditors are expected to claim the returns, and the phrase survives even when the primary balance improves. Discouraged private investment is the classic symptom.

The overhang label and the investment channel match as debt-theory English states them, so the sentence stands.

**C) Contingent liabilities crystallised when the state guaranteed a failing utility's bonds.**

Contingent liabilities crystallise when a guarantee or similar commitment becomes an actual claim on the budget, and guaranteeing a failing utility is a textbook trigger. "Crystallise" is the public-finance verb for that moment.

The contingent label and the crystallisation event belong together, so this wording holds.

**D) Real exchange-rate misalignment was estimated against a fundamentals-based equilibrium.**

Misalignment is measured against an estimated equilibrium rate grounded in fundamentals, and that comparison language is standard in open-economy empirics. The fundamentals-based equilibrium is the usual benchmark named in such studies.

The misalignment noun and the equilibrium benchmark fit as research notes couple them, so the line is sound.

**E) Official creditors granted a reprofiling that pushed maturities beyond the election cycle.**

Reprofiling extends maturities without necessarily cutting face value, and official creditors grant or agree that reprofiling. Pushing maturities past an election cycle is a frequently cited political motive.

The instrument name and the maturity extension match as sovereign-workout English uses them, so this line is exact.
tasks.solution_overview: Sovereign-debt and open-economy English uses a compact set of research terms — original sin, debt overhang, contingent liabilities, misalignment and reprofiling — each with a preferred verb. Test whether each line keeps the term in the situation the literature defined it for. When the label already carries the theory, the surrounding wording only has to stay in the same register.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: Five lines from specialist notes on market microstructure, clearing and settlement. Decide whether each phrase matches that technical register.
statements: Market makers widened spreads to harvest adverse selection when informed flow arrived.
Netting at the CCP evaporated exposures before members posted default-fund contributions.
A failed trade was resolved through buy-in procedures after the settlement fail persisted.
Dark-pool prints were said to reveal only the tip of the iceberg of block-size institutional demand.
Herstatt risk was cited whenever payment legs cleared in non-overlapping time zones.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Market makers widened spreads to harvest adverse selection when informed flow arrived.**

Market makers widen spreads to protect against adverse selection, or to compensate for it; they do not harvest adverse selection, which is the loss they suffer when better-informed traders hit their quotes. Harvesting would celebrate the very cost the wider spread is meant to offset.

**Trap:** Compensate for / protect against adverse selection; never harvest it.

Informed flow correctly triggers wider spreads, so the line should read "to protect against adverse selection when informed flow arrived."

**B) Netting at the CCP evaporated exposures before members posted default-fund contributions.**

Netting compresses, reduces or nets exposures; evaporate belongs to liquidity and funding that vanishes in a run — wholesale funding evaporates — not to the multilateral offsetting a CCP performs. Default-fund contributions are a separate membership resource, so the funding metaphor is doubly out of place.

**Tip:** Funding evaporates; exposures are netted or compressed.

The post-trade fact needs "netting at the CCP compressed exposures."

**C) A failed trade was resolved through buy-in procedures after the settlement fail persisted.**

Persistent settlement fails are cured through buy-in procedures, in which the failing party is bought in at market to complete delivery. The collocation is standard in CSDR-style settlement discipline.

The fail, the persistence and the buy-in remedy match as operations manuals join them, so this line holds.

**D) Dark-pool prints were said to reveal only the tip of the iceberg of block-size institutional demand.**

"Tip of the iceberg" is the fixed metaphor for the visible fraction of a much larger mass, and dark-pool prints are routinely described that way relative to unseen block demand. The of-phrase correctly names what lies beneath.

The iceberg metaphor and the block-size context are exactly how microstructure commentary reads sparse dark prints, so the wording stands.

**E) Herstatt risk was cited whenever payment legs cleared in non-overlapping time zones.**

Herstatt risk names principal risk in foreign-exchange settlement when payment legs fall in different time zones, after the Herstatt Bank failure. Citing it for non-overlapping clearing hours is the textbook modern use of the historical label.

The risk name and the time-zone mechanism belong together as settlement literature keeps them, so this line is exact.
tasks.solution_overview: Microstructure and post-trade English is precise about spreads, CCP netting, buy-ins, dark pools and Herstatt risk. Ask what market makers do when informed flow arrives, what netting does to exposures, and which historic risk name still labels cross-currency settlement gaps. Two traps misuse a metaphor that belongs to funding stress or celebrate the very cost a wider spread is meant to offset.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five claims about the verbs scholars use when they bring evidence forward, confirm it or call it into question. Decide whether each description of the verb is accurate.
statements: A historian who announces that she will "adduce" three unpublished letters is saying that she will set that material aside as irrelevant.
A laboratory report needs "substantiate" when a claimed effect has to be backed with measurements rather than merely asserted.
A second excavation that "corroborates" the dating of a burial site has shown that dating to be mistaken.
A conservator who "impugns" the provenance of a painting is confirming that its ownership history is sound.
Witnesses asked to "attest" to a signature are being asked to deny that they ever saw it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A historian who announces that she will "adduce" three unpublished letters is saying that she will set that material aside as irrelevant.**

"Adduce" means to bring forward evidence or an example in support of an argument, so it is the verb of citing rather than discarding. A historian who adduces unpublished letters is putting them on the table for the reader to weigh. Setting material aside as irrelevant would be discounting or dismissing it, which is the opposite movement.

Bringing material into the argument is the whole force of the verb, so the description reverses it: the letters are being produced as support, not shelved.

**B) A laboratory report needs "substantiate" when a claimed effect has to be backed with measurements rather than merely asserted.**

"Substantiate" means to support a claim with evidence, which is exactly the obligation a report takes on when it says a treatment shifted an outcome. Restating the claim in more confident language is assertion, not substantiation, and scientific prose keeps the two apart. The verb belongs where evidence is expected to be produced rather than promised.

Evidence-backing is precisely the work this verb names, so the sentence places it where it belongs.

**C) A second excavation that "corroborates" the dating of a burial site has shown that dating to be mistaken.**

To corroborate is to confirm: independent work corroborates an earlier result when its findings point the same way and add weight to it. Showing the dating to be mistaken is the contrary move, and archaeologists reach for "contradict" or "overturn" there. The distinction matters because corroboration builds a case while contradiction dismantles one.

**Trap:** The word sounds severe, but it always supports rather than attacks.

Confirmation and refutation pull in opposite directions, so the definition sends the verb the wrong way; a corroborating excavation strengthens the date it tests.

**D) A conservator who "impugns" the provenance of a painting is confirming that its ownership history is sound.**

"Impugn" means to call into question the honesty or validity of something, so impugning a provenance casts doubt over the chain of ownership. Vouching for a history that is sound would be to authenticate or endorse it. The verb carries an adversarial charge that catalogue entries use deliberately when they signal suspicion.

Doubt rather than endorsement is what the verb delivers, so the claim inverts it; a conservator who impugns a provenance is attacking the very history described here as settled.

**E) Witnesses asked to "attest" to a signature are being asked to deny that they ever saw it.**

"Attest" means to bear witness to something or certify that it is genuine, which is why the word sits on wills and affidavits. Witnesses who attest a signature formally affirm that they saw it made. Denying knowledge of it would be to disclaim or repudiate the document, a different act altogether.

Affirmation is built into the verb, so the description cannot hold: attesting witnesses put their names behind the signature instead of distancing themselves from it.
tasks.solution_overview: These five turn on the direction a formal verb points: towards evidence or away from it, towards confirmation or towards attack. Paraphrase each verb in plain words and ask whether the sentence still describes the same act. Where the paraphrase reverses the picture, the definition on offer has been turned around.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Five judgements about formal words that recur in statutes, clinical guidance and research summaries. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: In a research summary, a "caveat" is a guarantee that the finding will hold in every population studied.
A tribunal that "deems" a notice served on the day it was posted is treating it as having that status whether or not it arrived then.
A vaccination schedule that "obviates" the need for a booster makes that booster more urgently required.
"Provisional" magnitudes released in the hours after an earthquake are expected to change once more stations have reported.
A court that hears "extenuating" circumstances is hearing facts that make the offence look more serious than it first appeared.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a research summary, a "caveat" is a guarantee that the finding will hold in every population studied.**

A "caveat" is a warning or qualification attached to a claim, telling the reader where it may not apply. Summaries add caveats about sample size or setting precisely because the finding is not universal. A guarantee of general validity would be the opposite gesture and would need very different wording.

The word exists to narrow a claim rather than underwrite it, so the sentence mistakes a hedge for a promise.

**B) A tribunal that "deems" a notice served on the day it was posted is treating it as having that status whether or not it arrived then.**

"Deem" is the formal verb for treating something as having a particular status by decision rather than by observation. Deeming provisions are common in procedural rules because they fix a date that everyone can work from. The point of the verb is that the legal status holds even where the facts are untidy.

**Tip:** Where "deem" appears, look for a rule assigning a status rather than a report of what actually happened.

Assigning a status by decision is what the verb does, so the tribunal's deeming provision works just as the sentence describes.

**C) A vaccination schedule that "obviates" the need for a booster makes that booster more urgently required.**

"Obviate" means to remove a difficulty or make something unnecessary, so a schedule that obviates a booster has done away with the need for one. Making the booster more urgent would be to necessitate it. The verb is a favourite of formal writing precisely because it compresses "removes the need for" into one word.

Removing a requirement and intensifying it cannot be the same event, so the claim fails; a schedule that obviates a booster is one that leaves no call for it.

**D) "Provisional" magnitudes released in the hours after an earthquake are expected to change once more stations have reported.**

"Provisional" marks a figure issued for the time being and open to revision as better data arrives. Seismology publishes provisional magnitudes exactly because early estimates rest on a thin network of readings. A number no longer open to revision would be called final or definitive.

Openness to revision is the sense the adjective carries, so the description matches the practice it names.

**E) A court that hears "extenuating" circumstances is hearing facts that make the offence look more serious than it first appeared.**

"Extenuating" circumstances reduce the blame attaching to an act without excusing it altogether, which is why they belong to mitigation rather than to proof of guilt. Facts that deepen fault are aggravating, and the two terms sit on opposite sides of a sentencing decision. The root sense of thinning or weakening points the same way.

The adjective lightens culpability rather than adding to it, so this description swaps it for its counterpart: facts that worsen an offence are the aggravating ones.
tasks.solution_overview: Each item pairs a formal noun, verb or adjective with a paraphrase, and only some of the paraphrases keep the original force. Watch in particular for words that limit or qualify a claim, since these are the ones a careless reading turns into guarantees. Read the whole sentence before judging, because the surrounding facts often contradict the paraphrase outright.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Five statements about formal words used in engineering reports, statutes and environmental science. Decide whether each statement describes the word correctly.
statements: A drainage scheme that "ameliorates" waterlogging on upland farmland has made the flooding worse for the fields it serves.
A fault described as "latent" in a bridge deck is one that is plainly visible on a routine inspection.
Calling reliable cold storage a "sine qua non" of a rural vaccination campaign presents it as the condition without which the campaign cannot work.
When a statute leaves a sentencing decision to the judge's "discretion," the judge may weigh each case on its own facts within the limits the statute sets.
Describing a run of Arctic winter temperatures as "anomalous" claims that it departs markedly from the established pattern for that season.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A drainage scheme that "ameliorates" waterlogging on upland farmland has made the flooding worse for the fields it serves.**

"Ameliorate" means to make a bad situation better, and it belongs to the same family as improvement rather than aggravation. A scheme that ameliorates waterlogging leaves the ground drier than it found it. Worsening the flooding would be to aggravate or exacerbate the problem.

Improvement is the only direction this verb travels in, so the sentence describes an outcome the word cannot cover.

**B) A fault described as "latent" in a bridge deck is one that is plainly visible on a routine inspection.**

"Latent" describes something present but not yet apparent, which is why engineers use it for defects that surveys miss until they develop. A crack that anyone can see on a walk-over is patent or manifest instead. The whole reason latent defects attract special clauses is that they escape ordinary examination.

**Trap:** Latent means hidden, not merely serious; visibility rather than severity is what the word settles.

Concealment is the condition the adjective reports, so a defect anyone can see on a walk-over is the one thing it cannot describe.

**C) Calling reliable cold storage a "sine qua non" of a rural vaccination campaign presents it as the condition without which the campaign cannot work.**

The Latin phrase names an indispensable condition, literally something without which the thing in question does not stand. Applied to a vaccination campaign, it says that no amount of staffing or funding compensates for a broken cold chain. A merely helpful factor would be described as an advantage or a contributory element.

Indispensability is exactly what the phrase asserts, so the reading offered here is the right one.

**D) When a statute leaves a sentencing decision to the judge's "discretion," the judge may weigh each case on its own facts within the limits the statute sets.**

"Discretion" in legal drafting is the authority to choose among lawful options rather than freedom from the law altogether.
