A discretionary power is bounded by the purposes and limits of the statute that grants it. The contrast is with a mandatory provision, which leaves the decision-maker no room to weigh anything.

Bounded judgement of the individual case is what the term confers, so the description states the position accurately.

**E) Describing a run of Arctic winter temperatures as "anomalous" claims that it departs markedly from the established pattern for that season.**

"Anomalous" marks a departure from what the record leads one to expect, which is why the word attaches to readings that sit far from the seasonal norm. It reports a deviation without yet explaining it, so it is a description rather than a diagnosis. A run that matched the long-term pattern would be unremarkable or typical.

Departure from the established pattern is the whole content of the adjective, so this use of it is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: The contrasts here are between improvement and harm, hidden and visible, necessary and optional. Test each item by asking what the writer would have to observe for the word to be justified. If the sentence describes the opposite observation, the label has been misapplied.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five short definitions of formal terms drawn from legislation, treaties and grant conditions. Decide whether each definition matches the word.
statements: A protocol that "abrogates" an earlier convention leaves that convention fully in force.
A grant agreement that "stipulates" annual ethics review sets that review down as a binding condition of the award.
When a public health law "mandates" the fortification of salt with iodine, it makes that fortification compulsory rather than advisory.
A conservation statute that "proscribes" trade in wild-caught parrots forbids that trade outright.
A clause that "indemnifies" a volunteer organisation against claims promises to cover the losses it may have to meet.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A protocol that "abrogates" an earlier convention leaves that convention fully in force.**

"Abrogate" means to repeal or abolish a rule or agreement by formal act, so an abrogating protocol puts an end to the instrument it names. Leaving the earlier text in force would be to preserve or reaffirm it. Treaty drafters keep the verb for outright repeal rather than for amendment, which only alters what remains.

Repeal and preservation cannot describe the same act, so the definition collapses; a convention that has been abrogated no longer binds anyone.

**B) A grant agreement that "stipulates" annual ethics review sets that review down as a binding condition of the award.**

"Stipulate" means to specify something as an essential term of an agreement, which is stronger than merely recommending it. A stipulated condition can be enforced, and failing it puts the award itself at risk. Funders reach for the verb when they want an expectation to be read as a requirement.

Setting a term down as a condition is exactly what the verb does, so the definition holds good.

**C) When a public health law "mandates" the fortification of salt with iodine, it makes that fortification compulsory rather than advisory.**

"Mandate" as a verb imposes a requirement backed by the authority of the instrument that contains it. Fortification that is merely advisable would be encouraged, recommended or promoted instead. The choice between those verbs is the difference between a duty and a suggestion, and drafters make it deliberately.

Compulsion is the force the verb carries, so the account of the law is accurate.

**D) A conservation statute that "proscribes" trade in wild-caught parrots forbids that trade outright.**

"Proscribe" means to prohibit by authority, and it should not be confused with "prescribe," which lays down what must be done. A proscribed trade is banned rather than regulated, so no licence brings it back within the law. The near-identical shapes of the two verbs are what makes the pair worth pausing over.

**Tip:** Proscribe forbids; prescribe directs. One closes the door, the other says which door to use.

An outright ban is what the verb imposes, so the statute is described correctly here.

**E) A clause that "indemnifies" a volunteer organisation against claims promises to cover the losses it may have to meet.**

To indemnify is to undertake to make good another party's loss, so an indemnity shifts the financial consequences of a claim to the party giving it. It does not stop claims being brought; it decides who ultimately pays. That is why insurers and public bodies alike draft indemnity clauses with such care.

Assumption of loss is precisely what the clause promises, so the definition matches the term.
tasks.solution_overview: These items test verbs that create, remove or enforce obligations, and the differences between them are differences of legal effect. Ask in each case who is bound afterwards and to what. A definition that leaves the parties in the same position as before has usually mistaken the verb.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal verbs used when a harm is reduced, worsened, brought on or headed off. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Mitigate" is the verb for making a harm less severe, as when replanted mangroves mitigate storm damage along a delta coast.
Antibiotic overuse that "exacerbates" resistance on a hospital ward makes an already serious problem worse.
A dam failure that "precipitates" the evacuation of a valley has brought that evacuation on suddenly.
Lead shielding that "attenuates" a beam reduces its intensity rather than removing it altogether.
A product recall that "forestalls" a wider outbreak has headed that outbreak off before it could develop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Mitigate" is the verb for making a harm less severe, as when replanted mangroves mitigate storm damage along a delta coast.**

"Mitigate" softens an impact without necessarily preventing it, which is exactly what a mangrove belt does to a storm surge. The verb takes harms and penalties as its objects rather than benefits, so one mitigates damage but does not mitigate a recovery. That selectional restriction is part of knowing the word.

Reduction in severity is the sense on offer, and the mangrove example fits it neatly, so the account stands.

**B) Antibiotic overuse that "exacerbates" resistance on a hospital ward makes an already serious problem worse.**

"Exacerbate" intensifies something that is already bad, so it needs a pre-existing problem to work on. Resistance on a ward is such a problem, and heavy prescribing deepens it. Writing that a measure exacerbates an improvement would misuse the verb, since its object must be negative.

The verb needs an existing harm and then deepens it, which is just what the sentence describes.

**C) A dam failure that "precipitates" the evacuation of a valley has brought that evacuation on suddenly.**

To precipitate an event is to cause it to happen abruptly or earlier than expected, and the abruptness is part of the meaning. A slow, planned withdrawal would be organised or staged rather than precipitated. The verb suits emergencies because it carries the sense of being pitched headlong into them.

Sudden onset is what separates this verb from ordinary causing, and a dam failure supplies it, so the reading is right.

**D) Lead shielding that "attenuates" a beam reduces its intensity rather than removing it altogether.**

"Attenuate" means to weaken or thin something down, and in physics it names a measurable reduction in intensity. Complete removal would be absorption or blocking, and the calculations treat the two differently. The verb is equally at home in argument, where an objection can be attenuated rather than answered.

Weakening short of elimination is exactly the technical sense, so the sentence uses the verb correctly.

**E) A product recall that "forestalls" a wider outbreak has headed that outbreak off before it could develop.**

"Forestall" means to act in advance so as to prevent something, and the timing is essential to it. A response that arrives after the outbreak has spread would be containing or managing it instead. The prefix does the work: to fore-stall is to stop the thing before it starts.

Anticipatory prevention is the heart of the verb, and the recall arrives in time to supply it, so the account is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: All five verbs describe an effect on a harm, and the strategy is to fix the direction and the timing of that effect. Ask whether the harm becomes smaller or larger, and whether it arrives sooner or is avoided altogether. Naming both features usually settles the item without recourse to a dictionary.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Five descriptions of formal verbs and adjectives used when writers assign causes, support an argument or attach conditions. Decide whether each description is right.
statements: "Ascribe" is the verb a historian needs when assigning a change to a particular cause, as in ascribing a fall in child mortality to cleaner water.
To say that fresh fieldwork "buttresses" a disputed theory is to say that it undermines the theory's support.
An interview question designed to "elicit" candid recollections is intended to suppress them.
Saying that an anomaly in the data "warrants" further investigation means the anomaly rules such investigation out.
Funding described as "contingent" on ethical clearance will be released only if that clearance is granted.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Ascribe" is the verb a historian needs when assigning a change to a particular cause, as in ascribing a fall in child mortality to cleaner water.**

"Ascribe" attributes an effect, quality or work to a source, and it is the standard verb for causal attribution in careful prose. The historian is not claiming to have proved the link, only stating where the credit is being placed. That is why ascriptions are so often qualified with hedges about the strength of the evidence.

Assigning an outcome to a cause is the verb's core function, so the description fits it exactly.

**B) To say that fresh fieldwork "buttresses" a disputed theory is to say that it undermines the theory's support.**

"Buttress" borrows from architecture, where a buttress is built against a wall to hold it up, and in argument it means to reinforce a position. Fieldwork that buttresses a theory adds weight to it. Undermining is the excavating metaphor that runs the other way, removing support from beneath a claim.

The two metaphors work in opposite directions, so the description swaps them: buttressing shores a theory up rather than eating away at it.

**C) An interview question designed to "elicit" candid recollections is intended to suppress them.**

"Elicit" means to draw out a response that would not otherwise be volunteered, which is why the verb belongs to interviewing and testimony. A question designed to suppress answers would be described as leading, closed or deterrent. The whole design effort in oral history goes into eliciting rather than shutting down.

Drawing out and shutting down are contrary purposes, so the sentence cannot stand; a question that elicits recollections invites them into the open.

**D) Saying that an anomaly in the data "warrants" further investigation means the anomaly rules such investigation out.**

To warrant something is to justify it or provide sufficient grounds for it, so an anomaly that warrants investigation makes that investigation reasonable. Ruling the inquiry out would require language such as "does not justify" or "excludes." The noun behind the verb is the same one that names an authorisation to act.

Justification is what the verb supplies, so the gloss reverses it; an anomaly that warrants a closer look is the reason for taking one.

**E) Funding described as "contingent" on ethical clearance will be released only if that clearance is granted.**

"Contingent" makes one thing depend on another, so contingent funding is promised subject to a condition rather than unconditionally. Until the condition is met, the money is committed but not payable. Grant letters use the adjective to keep the commitment alive while withholding the release.

Dependence on a stated condition is the sense of the adjective, so the paraphrase captures it well.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these items test whether a verb strengthens or weakens what it takes as its object, and the fifth turns on a condition. Substituting a plain paraphrase such as "supports," "draws out" or "only if" exposes the mismatches quickly. Where the paraphrase contradicts the rest of the sentence, the description has gone wrong.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five statements about hedging and evidential marking in academic register. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: In a briefing note, the "salient" risks of a new reactor design are the ones that stand out as most significant for the decision at hand.
Calling a rival account of the collapse "plausible" asserts that it has been proved correct.
A "putative" common ancestor on a phylogenetic tree is one supposed to occupy that position on current evidence rather than one established beyond dispute.
Writing that a decree was "ostensibly" issued to protect public order commits the writer to accepting that stated reason as the whole truth.
Prefacing a casualty figure with "reportedly" marks it as coming from another source and not yet verified by the writer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a briefing note, the "salient" risks of a new reactor design are the ones that stand out as most significant for the decision at hand.**

"Salient" marks what projects above the rest of the detail, so salient risks are the prominent ones a reader must not miss. The adjective is relative to a purpose: what is salient for a licensing decision may be marginal for a maintenance schedule. It says nothing about how numerous or how technical the risks are.

Prominence relative to the decision is precisely what the adjective picks out, so the sentence describes it well.

**B) Calling a rival account of the collapse "plausible" asserts that it has been proved correct.**

"Plausible" says that an account is credible on its face and worth taking seriously, which stops well short of establishing it. Proof would be signalled by "demonstrated," "established" or "confirmed." Careful writers reach for plausible exactly when they want to concede reasonableness without conceding truth.

The adjective grants credibility while withholding proof, so reading it as a verdict of correctness overstates it badly.

**C) A "putative" common ancestor on a phylogenetic tree is one supposed to occupy that position on current evidence rather than one established beyond dispute.**

"Putative" flags a status that is assumed or reputed rather than confirmed, which is why taxonomy uses it for placements still under revision. The word leaves the door open to reclassification without abandoning the working hypothesis. An ancestor whose position was settled would simply be named as such.

Supposition held provisionally is the whole content of the adjective, so this use of it is exact.

**D) Writing that a decree was "ostensibly" issued to protect public order commits the writer to accepting that stated reason as the whole truth.**

"Ostensibly" reports the reason given in public while quietly reserving the possibility of another motive beneath it. Historians use it to record an official justification they are not prepared to endorse. A writer who accepted the stated reason outright would drop the adverb or replace it with "indeed" or "duly."

The adverb marks distance from the official account rather than agreement with it, so the sentence turns a hedge into an endorsement.

**E) Prefacing a casualty figure with "reportedly" marks it as coming from another source and not yet verified by the writer.**

"Reportedly" is an evidential marker: it attributes the information to someone else and suspends the writer's own guarantee. It is weaker than "documented" and stronger than "rumoured," which is why despatches and later histories lean on it. The figure may well turn out to be right, but the adverb declines to vouch for it.

Attributed but unverified is exactly the standing the adverb signals, so the account of it holds.
tasks.solution_overview: The words here tell the reader how much weight a claim can bear and where it came from. Ask of each one whether it asserts, supposes or merely relays, and check that the sentence around it matches that strength. Overstating a hedge is the commonest error these items are built to catch.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal verbs from treaty practice, committee procedure and university regulation. Decide whether each account matches the way the verb is used.
statements: A state that "accedes to" a treaty already in force becomes a party to it by joining later rather than by signing at the outset.
A researcher who "forgoes" an offer of commercial funding has accepted that funding in full.
A committee that "adjourns" a hearing until the expert report arrives has broken off the proceedings with the intention of resuming them.
A university that "waives" a residency requirement has chosen not to insist on a rule it could have enforced.
A parliament that "ratifies" a climate accord gives it the formal approval it needs to bind the state.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A state that "accedes to" a treaty already in force becomes a party to it by joining later rather than by signing at the outset.**

Accession is the formal route by which a state joins an instrument it did not negotiate, and it produces the same obligations as ratification by an original signatory. The distinction is one of timing and procedure, not of standing. That is why treaty texts set out accession clauses alongside the signature provisions.

Late entry with full effect is exactly what accession achieves, so the description is accurate.

**B) A researcher who "forgoes" an offer of commercial funding has accepted that funding in full.**

"Forgo" means to give up or do without something one could have had, so forgoing an offer is declining it. Acceptance would be described with "takes up," "secures" or "draws on." The verb often carries a note of deliberate sacrifice, which is why it suits a decision made to protect independence.

Declining and accepting are opposite responses to the same offer, so the account fails; a researcher who forgoes the money walks away from it.

**C) A committee that "adjourns" a hearing until the expert report arrives has broken off the proceedings with the intention of resuming them.**

To adjourn is to suspend proceedings to a later time, leaving the matter alive on the list. Ending the case altogether would be to dismiss or discontinue it. The verb carries the expectation of a resumption, which is why an adjournment is usually granted to a date.

Suspension with resumption in view is the force of the verb, so the sentence reports the step correctly.

**D) A university that "waives" a residency requirement has chosen not to insist on a rule it could have enforced.**

To waive is to relinquish a right or requirement voluntarily, and the power to enforce it must exist for the waiver to mean anything. Abolishing the rule for everyone would be to repeal it; a waiver operates in the individual case. The homophone "waves" has nothing to do with it, which is worth remembering in formal writing.

Voluntary non-insistence on an enforceable rule is what a waiver is, so the description matches the practice.

**E) A parliament that "ratifies" a climate accord gives it the formal approval it needs to bind the state.**

Ratification is the act of confirming an agreement so that it takes legal effect for the party concerned. Signature alone often expresses intent without creating binding obligations, which is why the two steps are reported separately. The verb belongs to the moment when consent becomes commitment.

Formal confirmation that brings an instrument into force is precisely the act named, so the account stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Each verb marks a formal step: joining, declining, pausing, relaxing or approving. Ask what changes the moment the step is taken and who is bound afterwards. A paraphrase that leaves the position unchanged, or reverses it, is the signal that the account has slipped.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Five claims about verbs of compliance, delegation, criticism and argument in official and scholarly writing. Decide whether each claim describes the verb correctly.
statements: A laboratory that "contravenes" its containment protocol has been found to be following that protocol to the letter.
A ministry that "devolves" licensing powers to regional authorities has drawn those powers back to the centre.
To "interrogate" a source in historical writing is to accept its account without examination.
A philosopher who "espouses" a theory of distributive justice has adopted it and argues for it in public.
In careful academic usage, to "refute" an argument is merely to deny it forcefully, with no evidence required.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A laboratory that "contravenes" its containment protocol has been found to be following that protocol to the letter.**

"Contravene" means to act contrary to a rule or provision, so a contravening laboratory is in breach. Faultless compliance would be reported with "adheres to," "observes" or "complies with." Inspection reports keep the vocabulary sharp because the two findings carry entirely different consequences.

Breach and exemplary compliance are opposite findings, so the claim inverts the verb; a laboratory that contravenes its protocol has departed from it.

**B) A ministry that "devolves" licensing powers to regional authorities has drawn those powers back to the centre.**

"Devolve" transfers powers downwards from a central body to a subordinate or regional one. Pulling authority back to the centre is centralisation or recentralisation, sometimes described as clawing powers back. The direction of travel is the whole point of the word in constitutional writing.

Downward transfer is what the verb encodes, so a ministry that devolves licensing has given the power away rather than gathered it in.

**C) To "interrogate" a source in historical writing is to accept its account without examination.**

In academic register, to interrogate a source is to question it closely, testing its origin, purpose and silences. Accepting an account at face value would be to take it uncritically. The word has migrated from the police cell to the seminar room, but the pressing quality of the questioning has come with it.

Close questioning is exactly what the academic sense demands, so the definition offered here describes the opposite habit of mind.

**D) A philosopher who "espouses" a theory of distributive justice has adopted it and argues for it in public.**

"Espouse" means to take up and support a cause or doctrine, usually with some commitment behind it. It is stronger than entertaining or considering a view and weaker than proving it. The marital metaphor buried in the word captures the sense of binding oneself to a position.

Adoption together with public advocacy is what the verb conveys, so the description is a fair account of it.

**E) In careful academic usage, to "refute" an argument is merely to deny it forcefully, with no evidence required.**

To refute is to disprove: it requires showing that a claim is false, not simply saying so with conviction. Denial without evidence is rejection, repudiation or dismissal, and careful writers keep those verbs for the weaker act. The distinction matters because refutation is a result, while denial is only a stance.

**Trap:** Loose journalism treats refute as a synonym for deny, but in scholarly prose the evidence has to come with it.

Disproof rather than emphatic denial is what the verb commits a writer to, so the claim strips the word of the very burden it carries.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these verbs concern whether a rule or power has been kept or passed on, and three concern how an argument is handled. In each case name the plain equivalent before judging: breaks, hands down, questions, champions, disproves. The plain equivalent usually exposes the item at once.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five statements about the formal vocabulary of reasoning, concession and assumption. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: An author who "concedes" that her sample came from a single clinic is admitting a point that tells against her own argument.
A reader who "infers" a conclusion from a table of results is drawing it out of the evidence rather than being told it directly.
A report that "implies" a link between overcrowding and infection has suggested that link through its wording without stating it outright.
An argument that "presupposes" a stable climate baseline takes that baseline for granted before the reasoning begins.
An inspector who "ascertains" the true occupancy of a building has established it by checking rather than by estimating.
tactical_explanations:
**A) An author who "concedes" that her sample came from a single clinic is admitting a point that tells against her own argument.**

"Concede" is the verb for granting a point one would rather not grant, and it presupposes some cost to the speaker. Conceding a narrow sample acknowledges a limit on how far the findings travel. Simply reporting the sampling method without that acknowledgement would be description rather than concession.

Yielding ground against one's own interest is what the verb marks, and a confessed limitation supplies exactly that, so the reading holds.

**B) A reader who "infers" a conclusion from a table of results is drawing it out of the evidence rather than being told it directly.**

Inference is the reader's work: it moves from what is shown to what follows. The writer's counterpart is implication, where the text suggests something without stating it. Keeping the pair straight is a matter of who is doing what, and formal prose depends on that division of labour.

The reader draws, the writer hints, and this sentence puts the drawing where it belongs, so the statement is sound.

**C) A report that "implies" a link between overcrowding and infection has suggested that link through its wording without stating it outright.**

To imply is to convey something indirectly, leaving the reader to complete the thought. The report has not committed itself, which is why implication is so often a matter of careful phrasing and telling juxtaposition. If the link were asserted in terms, the verb would be "states" or "claims."

Suggestion carried by wording rather than open assertion is the mark of implication, so the sentence describes it accurately.

**D) An argument that "presupposes" a stable climate baseline takes that baseline for granted before the reasoning begins.**

A presupposition is an assumption built into an argument rather than defended within it, and it operates whether or not the writer notices it. Criticism often works by exposing presuppositions instead of attacking conclusions. The prefix marks the timing: the assumption is in place before the case is made.

An assumption taken as settled in advance is precisely what the verb identifies, so the account is correct.

**E) An inspector who "ascertains" the true occupancy of a building has established it by checking rather than by estimating.**

"Ascertain" means to find something out with certainty, and the verb implies a method: counting, measuring, inspecting. An estimate reached from floor area would be a calculation or an approximation. Formal reports use the word to signal that a figure has been verified at source.

Verification through checking is the sense the verb carries, so the description of the inspector's work is right.
tasks.solution_overview: These verbs describe what a writer or reader does with evidence: yields a point, draws a conclusion, hints at one, takes something for granted or checks it. Locate the person doing the act in each sentence, since several of these verbs are distinguished by who performs them. Once the agent is fixed, the meaning usually follows.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five descriptions of formal verbs that report growth, decline, composition and necessity. Decide whether each description is correct.
statements: Coastal erosion that has "abated" since the groynes were installed is advancing faster than it did before.
A "burgeoning" literature on microplastics is one that has stopped growing.
To say that three upland parishes "constitute" the study area is to say that they were excluded from it.
Saying that a dam scheme "entails" the resettlement of two villages presents that resettlement as a necessary consequence of the scheme.
A licence condition that "precludes" resale of the specimens prevents that resale from lawfully taking place.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Coastal erosion that has "abated" since the groynes were installed is advancing faster than it did before.**

"Abate" means to lessen in force or intensity, and it is the standard verb for storms, nuisances and rates of loss. Erosion that has abated is eating into the shore more slowly. Acceleration would be reported with "intensified" or "quickened," which is the reading the sentence actually gives.

Slackening is the only movement the verb allows, so a description of faster advance contradicts the very word it is explaining.

**B) A "burgeoning" literature on microplastics is one that has stopped growing.**

"Burgeoning" describes rapid expansion, borrowed from the budding of plants, and reviewers use it for fields that are hard to keep up with. A literature that has stopped growing would be mature, stable or moribund. The word also carries a faint suggestion of untidiness, since fast growth outruns organisation.

Vigorous expansion is what the participle reports, so calling a burgeoning literature static empties the word of its meaning.

**C) To say that three upland parishes "constitute" the study area is to say that they were excluded from it.**

"Constitute" means to make up or form something, so the parishes named are the study area rather than a set left outside it. Exclusion would be signalled by "fall outside" or "were omitted from." The verb points from parts to whole, which is why it appears in definitions of scope.

Composition is the relation the verb states, so the parishes it names are precisely the ones inside the study area.

**D) Saying that a dam scheme "entails" the resettlement of two villages presents that resettlement as a necessary consequence of the scheme.**

"Entail" marks a consequence that follows of necessity from what has gone before, not one that merely tends to accompany it. An incidental effect would be described as an associated or possible outcome. The logical use of the word is the same: one proposition entails another when it cannot be true without it.

Necessity rather than mere accompaniment is what the verb asserts, so the sentence reads it correctly.

**E) A licence condition that "precludes" resale of the specimens prevents that resale from lawfully taking place.**

"Preclude" rules something out in advance, closing off a possibility rather than merely discouraging it. A condition that only discouraged resale would restrict or regulate it. The verb takes actions and possibilities as objects, which is why one precludes resale but not the reseller.

Ruling out in advance is the work the verb does, so the account of the licence condition holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these verbs describe a quantity moving and two describe a relation between parts and wholes or causes and consequences. Fix the direction of movement first, then ask whether the relation described is one of inclusion or exclusion. Both checks can be made without any specialist knowledge of the subject matter.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five judgements about verbs of speeding up, obstructing and ending, including one question of register in a formal report. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: A digital filing system that "expedites" asylum decisions makes those decisions come through more quickly.
Silt that "encumbers" a river channel is clearing that channel for navigation.
A notice reporting that a permit "lapsed" in March states that it expired then without being renewed.
In a formal archaeological report, "the excavation kicked off in April" is more appropriate than "the excavation commenced in April."
Saying that a new statute "renders" an earlier permit invalid uses "render" in its formal sense of causing something to become a particular way.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A digital filing system that "expedites" asylum decisions makes those decisions come through more quickly.**

"Expedite" means to hasten a process by removing friction from it, and it takes procedures rather than people as its object. Slowing the process would be to delay or retard it. The verb is at home in administrative prose because it describes an improvement in speed without promising a change in outcome.

Acceleration of a procedure is exactly what the verb reports, so the judgement is correct.

**B) Silt that "encumbers" a river channel is clearing that channel for navigation.**

"Encumber" means to burden or obstruct, leaving something harder to use or move. Silt that encumbers a channel is what dredging is meant to remove. Clearing would be described with "scours," "opens" or "frees," and the legal sense of the verb, burdening property with a charge, points the same way.

Obstruction rather than relief is what the verb describes, so the sentence has the silt doing the opposite of what the word allows.

**C) A notice reporting that a permit "lapsed" in March states that it expired then without being renewed.**

"Lapse" describes a right or permission falling out of force because a fixed period has run, rather than through any positive act. A permit withdrawn by decision would be revoked or cancelled, and the difference matters when someone asks who ended it. Nothing need have gone wrong for a lapse to occur.

Expiry through inaction is the sense of the verb, so the notice is being read correctly.

**D) In a formal archaeological report, "the excavation kicked off in April" is more appropriate than "the excavation commenced in April."**

"Kick off" is a sporting idiom that has spread into speech and informal email, and it sits badly in a document written for the record. "Commence" is the neutral formal verb for the same event, which is why permits and reports use it. Register is a matter of fit rather than of correctness, but the fit here is poor.

A phrasal idiom from the touchline cannot carry the weight of a formal report, so the preference stated here is the wrong way round: "the excavation commenced in April" is the register-appropriate version.

**E) Saying that a new statute "renders" an earlier permit invalid uses "render" in its formal sense of causing something to become a particular way.**

"Render" followed by an object and an adjective means to cause that object to be in the stated condition, as in rendering a clause unenforceable. The pattern is fixed: the adjective must follow the object, which is why "renders invalid the permit" reads awkwardly. Other senses of the verb, such as rendering assistance or rendering an account, are distinct.

The object-plus-adjective pattern is the formal use being described, and the statute example fits it, so the judgement holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Four items test what a verb does to a process, and one tests whether a phrase belongs in formal writing at all. For the register item, read both versions aloud and ask which would look out of place in a document meant for the record. Tone is as much part of word choice at this level as meaning.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five statements about words that fix what a term stands for, what generally holds, and how far a claim has been proved. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: In technical writing, a symbol that "denotes" acidity stands for it explicitly, whereas a term that connotes decay merely carries an association.
A wind direction that "prevails" over a valley is the one generally in force there.
Tremors that "presage" an eruption are taken as signs of what is coming.
A statement that a clinic "allegedly" falsified consent forms reports an accusation that has not been proved.
A manuscript that "purports" to be a fifteenth-century original is thereby confirmed as genuine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In technical writing, a symbol that "denotes" acidity stands for it explicitly, whereas a term that connotes decay merely carries an association.**

Denotation is the direct relation between a sign and what it stands for, fixed by convention and stated in the key to a diagram. Connotation is the freight a word carries alongside its literal sense, which is why the same reading can be neutral in a table and loaded in a caption. Technical prose leans on denotation because it needs the relation to be stipulated rather than felt.

Explicit standing-for against mere association is the distinction the sentence draws, and it draws it the right way round.

**B) A wind direction that "prevails" over a valley is the one generally in force there.**

"Prevail" means to be predominant or to hold sway, so a prevailing wind is the direction recorded most of the time rather than the strongest gust ever measured. The verb also carries a sense of winning out, which fits a pattern that dominates its rivals across a season. Nothing in it implies constancy, only predominance.

General predominance rather than invariable occurrence is the sense at work, so the description of the term is sound.

**C) Tremors that "presage" an eruption are taken as signs of what is coming.**

To presage is to foreshadow or give warning of a future event, and the subject of the verb is the sign rather than the observer. Volcanologists treat swarms of small tremors as presaging an eruption because the pattern has preceded eruptions before. A verb such as "cause" would make a very different and much stronger claim.

Foreshadowing rather than causing is what the verb contributes, and the tremors are cast as signs, so the statement is accurate.

**D) A statement that a clinic "allegedly" falsified consent forms reports an accusation that has not been proved.**

"Allegedly" attributes a claim to an accuser and withholds the writer's own endorsement, which is why it survives in legal and journalistic prose under threat of defamation. It signals that proceedings or findings may follow but have not yet concluded. Dropping the adverb would convert a report of an accusation into an assertion of fact.

Unproved accusation is exactly the standing the adverb preserves, so the sentence describes its function correctly.

**E) A manuscript that "purports" to be a fifteenth-century original is thereby confirmed as genuine.**

"Purport" reports what something claims about itself while leaving the claim open, and cataloguers use it for precisely that reason. A manuscript that purports to be early may be authentic, a copy or a forgery. Confirmation would call for "has been authenticated" or "is established as," which commits the writer in a way the original verb refuses to.

The verb voices the document's own claim rather than the cataloguer's verdict, so it can never amount to confirmation of what the manuscript says it is.
tasks.solution_overview: This set moves between semantics, prevalence and the marking of unproven claims. For the evidential items, ask what the writer would still have to show for the sentence to become an assertion of fact. For the semantic ones, ask whether the word names a meaning outright or only an association.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five accounts of high-register connectors and adverbs found in academic prose and legal drafting. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Notwithstanding the loss of two field seasons, the survey was completed on schedule" uses a formal connector meaning "despite."
"Albeit" introduces a concessive qualification, as in "the glacier is retreating, albeit more slowly than in the 1990s."
"Whereby" introduces the means or arrangement by which something happens, as in "a scheme whereby hospitals share rare blood stocks."
An annual report stating that the company refinanced its debt, "thereby" lowering its interest costs, uses the adverb to link an action to the result it produces.
In a deed, writing "the National Archive, hereinafter the Depositor," fixes a short name to be used for that party throughout the rest of the document.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Notwithstanding the loss of two field seasons, the survey was completed on schedule" uses a formal connector meaning "despite."**

"Notwithstanding" introduces a circumstance that might have been expected to prevent the outcome but did not, which is the work "despite" and "in spite of" also do. It can stand before its noun phrase or, in older legal drafting, after it. The formality is the reason it survives in statutes long after speech abandoned it.

Concession in the face of an obstacle is exactly the relation set up here, so the paraphrase is a fair one.

**B) "Albeit" introduces a concessive qualification, as in "the glacier is retreating, albeit more slowly than in the 1990s."**

"Albeit" attaches a qualifying phrase to a claim already made, conceding something without withdrawing the main point. It takes a phrase rather than a full clause with its own subject and verb, so "albeit it was slow" reads awkwardly. The glacier example keeps to that pattern with a comparative phrase.

A conceded qualification riding on the main claim is what the connector supplies, so the account matches the example.

**C) "Whereby" introduces the means or arrangement by which something happens, as in "a scheme whereby hospitals share rare blood stocks."**

"Whereby" is a relative adverb standing for "by which," and it needs a preceding noun such as scheme, mechanism or arrangement to attach to. Using it as a loose substitute for "where" or "in which" is the commonest slip. The blood-stock example gives it the arrangement it requires.

**Tip:** If "by which" cannot be substituted, "whereby" is the wrong connector.

Naming the means by which an arrangement operates is the connector's function, and the sharing scheme supplies just such an arrangement, so the account is sound.

**D) An annual report stating that the company refinanced its debt, "thereby" lowering its interest costs, uses the adverb to link an action to the result it produces.**

"Thereby" means "by that means" and normally introduces a participle clause naming the consequence of the action just described. It is tighter than "and so," because it ties the result to the specific means rather than to the situation at large. Corporate reporting favours it for exactly that economy.

Means and consequence bound into one clause is what the adverb achieves here, so the account of it is right.

**E) In a deed, writing "the National Archive, hereinafter the Depositor," fixes a short name to be used for that party throughout the rest of the document.**

"Hereinafter" points forward within the document itself, introducing the label that will be used from that point on. It belongs to the family of legal adverbs built on here- and there-, each anchored to the text rather than to the world outside it. Defining a party this way saves the drafter from repeating the full name at every mention.

Forward reference inside the instrument is precisely what the adverb performs, so the description of the drafting device holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Connectors of this kind do grammatical work as well as carrying meaning, so it helps to name the relation each one sets up: concession, means, result or naming. Test a suggested paraphrase by putting it into the example and seeing whether the sentence still holds together. Where the paraphrase fits, the account is usually sound.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five claims about adjectives used to judge whether something survives, can be solved or holds up under pressure. Decide whether each claim describes the adjective correctly.
statements: A modelling problem described as "tractable" has been judged impossible to solve with the methods available.
A species described as "extant" in the fossil record survey is one that has died out.
A statistical finding described as "robust" collapses as soon as the model specification is changed.
Negotiations described as "protracted" were concluded within a single afternoon.
An effect described as "negligible" is too small to matter for the conclusion being drawn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A modelling problem described as "tractable" has been judged impossible to solve with the methods available.**

"Tractable" means manageable or amenable to treatment, so a tractable problem is one the available methods can handle. A problem beyond them would be intractable or refractory. The adjective is a judgement about workability rather than about how interesting the problem is.

Workability is what the adjective certifies, so a problem declared insoluble is the very case it excludes.

**B) A species described as "extant" in the fossil record survey is one that has died out.**

"Extant" means still in existence, and it is the standard contrast with "extinct" in biology and with "lost" in manuscript studies. A survey that lists extant species is listing those still living today. Describing a vanished species that way would collapse the distinction the survey exists to draw.

Continued existence is the whole point of the adjective, so applying it to a species that has died out reverses it; the word wanted there is extinct.

**C) A statistical finding described as "robust" collapses as soon as the model specification is changed.**

In quantitative work, "robust" means that a result survives reasonable changes to assumptions, samples or specifications. That resilience is what robustness checks are designed to demonstrate. A finding that vanishes under a different specification is fragile or specification-dependent.

Survival under altered assumptions is the technical content of the term, so a result that collapses at the first change cannot claim it.

**D) Negotiations described as "protracted" were concluded within a single afternoon.**

"Protracted" means drawn out over an unusually long period, often with a hint of weariness at the delay. Talks finished in an afternoon would be brief, swift or expeditious. The participle comes from a verb meaning to draw forward, and the sense of stretching remains audible in it.

Extended duration is what the adjective asserts, so a settlement reached in one afternoon contradicts the very word chosen to describe it.

**E) An effect described as "negligible" is too small to matter for the conclusion being drawn.**

"Negligible" marks a quantity that can safely be neglected, which is a claim about relevance rather than about the measuring instrument. A detectable effect can still be negligible if it makes no difference to the argument. Writers who mean undetectable should say so instead.

Smallness measured against what the argument needs is precisely the test the adjective sets, so the description is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Every item pairs an adjective with a situation that either fits it or plainly contradicts it. Decide first what the adjective demands of the world, then read the rest of the sentence to see whether that demand is met. Four of these adjectives set a positive test, and the last sets a threshold of importance.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five claims about the vocabulary of relevance, method and error in research writing. Decide whether each claim is correct.
statements: Testimony described as "germane" to an inquiry is testimony that has no bearing on it.
"Confounding" variables in a trial are factors outside the one under study that can distort the apparent effect.
A qualifying threshold described as "arbitrary" was fixed without a principled reason for that exact figure.
Measurement error described as "systematic" is random noise that cancels out across a large sample.
A search of the archive described as "exhaustive" left no relevant holding unexamined.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Testimony described as "germane" to an inquiry is testimony that has no bearing on it.**

"Germane" means closely relevant to the matter in hand, and it is a shade more formal than "relevant" itself. Testimony with no bearing would be immaterial, extraneous or beside the point. Tribunals use the word when deciding what evidence to admit, so the direction of the judgement matters.

Close relevance is what the adjective certifies, so material with no bearing on the inquiry is exactly what it rules out.

**B) "Confounding" variables in a trial are factors outside the one under study that can distort the apparent effect.**

A confounder is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, so it can manufacture or mask an apparent relationship between them. Trials randomise and studies adjust precisely to keep confounders from doing that work unseen. The word names a threat to inference rather than a mistake in measurement.

Outside factors distorting an apparent effect is the definition itself, so this account of confounding is correct.

**C) A qualifying threshold described as "arbitrary" was fixed without a principled reason for that exact figure.**

"Arbitrary" means settled by choice rather than by reason, so an arbitrary threshold could have been set a little higher or lower without any argument being violated. It does not follow that the threshold is unfair or useless; lines often have to be drawn somewhere. The criticism is about justification, not about motive.

Absence of a principled ground for the particular figure is the charge the adjective makes, so the claim describes it well.

**D) Measurement error described as "systematic" is random noise that cancels out across a large sample.**

Systematic error is bias: it pushes readings consistently in one direction and survives however many observations are collected. Random error is the kind that cancels as the sample grows. Averaging therefore helps with one and entrenches the other, which is why the labels must be kept apart.

Consistent bias is what the term names, so treating it as noise that averages away describes random error under the wrong label.

**E) A search of the archive described as "exhaustive" left no relevant holding unexamined.**

"Exhaustive" means complete in its coverage, exhausting the material rather than the searcher. It is a strong claim, which is why cautious writers prefer "extensive" when they cannot vouch for completeness. The related word "exhausting" says something quite different about the same afternoon.

Complete coverage of the relevant material is what the adjective promises, so the description is a fair use of it.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these words classify how something relates to an inquiry and two describe the quality of a procedure or its errors. For the methodological items, ask whether the fault is patterned or random, and whether the coverage is complete or partial. Relevance items turn on whether the material bears on the question at all.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five statements about formal words for agreeing, objecting, denouncing and permitting, including one word that faces both ways. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: Two peer reviewers who "concur" on a manuscript have arrived at the same judgement about it.
A judge who records a "dissent" is confirming full agreement with the majority.
An epidemiologist who "inveighs against" a screening programme is arguing warmly in its favour.
A trustee board that will not "countenance" a change to the deed is content to approve that change.
"Sanction" can mean both to authorise and to penalise, so a formal sentence has to supply enough context to show which sense is intended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Two peer reviewers who "concur" on a manuscript have arrived at the same judgement about it.**

"Concur" means to agree, usually about a conclusion reached independently, which is why editors report it with relief. It is more formal than "agree" and carries a suggestion of separate paths meeting at one point. Judges concur for the same reason: they reach the same result and say so.

Independent arrival at a shared judgement is what the verb reports, so the statement describes it accurately.

**B) A judge who records a "dissent" is confirming full agreement with the majority.**

A dissent is a formally recorded disagreement with the decision of the majority, and it is published so that the reasoning survives for later courts. Agreement would be expressed in a concurring opinion instead. The whole institutional value of dissent lies in preserving the road not taken.

Recorded disagreement is what the noun means, so a dissenting judge stands apart from the majority rather than joining it.

**C) An epidemiologist who "inveighs against" a screening programme is arguing warmly in its favour.**

To inveigh against something is to attack it in strong, often indignant language, and the preposition fixes the target of the attack. Speaking in favour would be to advocate, commend or champion the programme. The verb is rarely neutral; it reports heat as well as direction.

Vehement attack is the sense the phrase carries, so an epidemiologist inveighing against a programme is opposing it, not commending it.

**D) A trustee board that will not "countenance" a change to the deed is content to approve that change.**

To countenance something is to tolerate or give approval to it, so refusing to countenance a change is refusing to allow it. The noun behind the verb means face, and the metaphor is one of looking favourably on a proposal. A board content to approve the change would simply countenance it.

Refusal to tolerate is the position the sentence actually describes, so it cannot also be a willingness to approve.

**E) "Sanction" can mean both to authorise and to penalise, so a formal sentence has to supply enough context to show which sense is intended.**

The verb descends from a root concerned with making something binding, and it developed in two directions: giving official approval and imposing a penalty for breach. A regulator that sanctions a trial has approved it; a state sanctioned by its neighbours has been punished. Only the surrounding words settle which reading applies.

Two established and opposite senses do live in the one word, so the warning about context is well founded.
tasks.solution_overview: Four items test whether a verb or noun expresses support or opposition, so the reliable move is to ask which side of the argument the speaker ends up on. The fifth turns on a word with two established and opposed senses. Where a term is genuinely double-edged, the surrounding sentence has to do the disambiguating.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five accounts of terms describing how openly something is stated and what kind of evidence lies behind it. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: A "tacit" understanding between neighbouring states is one acted on without ever being set down in words.
To call a premise "axiomatic" within a proof is to treat it as accepted without further argument in that system.
A fee described as "nominal" is set so low that it amounts to little more than a token.
"Empirical" evidence is reasoning conducted purely from first principles, without observation or measurement.
"Anecdotal" evidence rests on individual reports rather than on systematically collected data.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "tacit" understanding between neighbouring states is one acted on without ever being set down in words.**

"Tacit" describes what is understood and relied on without being expressed, which is why diplomacy values it: nothing has to be conceded on paper. A written arrangement would be express or formal. Tacit consent works the same way, taking silence in circumstances that invited objection as agreement.

Unspoken but operative is exactly the condition the adjective names, so the account of it is right.

**B) To call a premise "axiomatic" within a proof is to treat it as accepted without further argument in that system.**

An axiom is a starting point taken as given, and calling a premise axiomatic locates it at the foundation rather than in the body of the reasoning. It is a claim about the role of the statement, not about how obvious it feels. In looser usage the word has drifted towards "self-evident," but the technical sense stays with the system.

Foundational acceptance within a system is the status the term confers, so the description matches its technical use.

**C) A fee described as "nominal" is set so low that it amounts to little more than a token.**

A nominal charge exists in name rather than in substance, which is why archives and registries levy one to deter idle requests without creating a barrier. The word has a separate life in economics, where nominal figures are those unadjusted for inflation. Context decides which sense is running, and a fee of a few pence plainly signals the first.

A charge that is a formality rather than a real cost is what the adjective conveys here, so the account holds.

**D) "Empirical" evidence is reasoning conducted purely from first principles, without observation or measurement.**

Empirical evidence comes from observation or experiment, so it is precisely what reasoning from first principles lacks. Argument conducted without recourse to data is a priori or theoretical. The contrast is one of source, and the word points firmly at experience.

Observation is the defining source of empirical evidence, so a description that removes it has swapped the term for its opposite.

**E) "Anecdotal" evidence rests on individual reports rather than on systematically collected data.**

Anecdotal evidence consists of particular cases gathered without a sampling frame, so it can suggest a hypothesis but cannot establish a rate. The label is not a synonym for false: the individual reports may each be accurate. What they lack is the structure that would let a general claim be drawn from them.

Individual reports outside a systematic design is exactly what the label picks out, so the account is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: The first pair concerns whether something is spelled out or left understood, and the last pair concerns where evidence comes from. Ask in each case what a reader would have to find in the text or the data for the label to be justified. A word that hedges the size of a fee behaves quite differently from the same word in an economic table.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five judgements about choosing the right level of formality in reports, deeds and scholarly writing. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: In a formal report, "the authority will endeavour to reduce waiting times" is register-appropriate where "the authority will have a go at cutting them" would not be.
A company's annual report uses "remuneration" rather than "pay packet" when it sets out what its directors received, because the formal noun suits the document.
"The requisite permissions were obtained before excavation" is the register a formal report expects, where "the permissions we needed" would read as conversational.
A treaty stating that a state will "cede" jurisdiction over an enclave reports a formal giving-up of that authority, and the verb suits the register better than "hand over."
Dating a mosaic to "circa 320 CE" is the register-appropriate way to hedge a date in scholarly writing, where "round about 320" would read as conversational.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a formal report, "the authority will endeavour to reduce waiting times" is register-appropriate where "the authority will have a go at cutting them" would not be.**

"Endeavour" is the formal verb for making a serious attempt, and it commits the body to effort rather than to a result. "Have a go" belongs to speech and would sit oddly in a document that may be quoted back at the authority. The choice also affects how binding the sentence sounds when it is read years later.

A published undertaking calls for the formal verb, so the preference described here is the right one for the document.

**B) A company's annual report uses "remuneration" rather than "pay packet" when it sets out what its directors received, because the formal noun suits the document.**

"Remuneration" covers salary, bonuses, pensions and benefits in a single formal term, which is why disclosure rules are drafted around it. "Pay packet" is colloquial and, worse, too narrow to catch the whole of what has to be reported. Register and coverage happen to pull the same way here.

A disclosure written for shareholders and regulators needs the inclusive formal noun, so the judgement about register stands.

**C) "The requisite permissions were obtained before excavation" is the register a formal report expects, where "the permissions we needed" would read as conversational.**

"Requisite" is the formal adjective for what is required by a rule or procedure, and it points at an external standard rather than at the writer's convenience. "The permissions we needed" personalises the requirement and loosens the tone. Formal reports prefer the impersonal version because it can be checked against the regulations.

An impersonal appeal to what the rules demand is what the setting calls for, so the register judgement is well made.

**D) A treaty stating that a state will "cede" jurisdiction over an enclave reports a formal giving-up of that authority, and the verb suits the register better than "hand over."**

"Cede" means to yield or surrender something, typically territory or rights, under a formal instrument. "Hand over" describes the same movement in everyday terms and lacks the sense of a right being relinquished in law. Treaty language keeps the Latin-derived verb because it carries that legal weight.

Formal surrender of a right is exactly what the verb encodes, so it fits the instrument better than its everyday counterpart.

**E) Dating a mosaic to "circa 320 CE" is the register-appropriate way to hedge a date in scholarly writing, where "round about 320" would read as conversational.**

"Circa" marks an approximate date and is understood across the scholarly literature wherever it appears, most often in its abbreviated form. "Round about" carries the same approximation in a wholly informal voice. Using the conventional form also signals that the hedge is deliberate rather than careless.

A conventional scholarly hedge is what the catalogue entry needs, so the preference described here holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Register is the whole subject here: each item sets a formal item against a conversational one and asks which the document calls for. Consider who reads the text and what it has to survive, whether that is an audit, a court or a century in a library. The formal choice is not always the longer word, but it is always the one that fits the setting.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five descriptions of adjectives that grade strictness, care and stability. Decide whether each description matches the adjective.
statements: Emission limits described as "stringent" are loosely drafted and easy for an incinerator operator to satisfy.
An inspection described as "perfunctory" was carried out with unusual care and thoroughness.
A "circumspect" statement about a new therapy stakes everything on the strongest claim the data could conceivably support.
A volcano described as "quiescent" is erupting steadily from one month to the next.
A coral reef described as "resilient" can absorb a bleaching event and recover its function.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Emission limits described as "stringent" are loosely drafted and easy for an incinerator operator to satisfy.**

"Stringent" means strict and demanding, allowing little latitude to those who must comply. Limits that are easy to satisfy would be lax, permissive or undemanding. The word implies a binding tightness, and regulators use it when they want to advertise severity.

Strictness is the pole the adjective occupies, so limits described as easy to meet are the opposite of stringent ones.

**B) An inspection described as "perfunctory" was carried out with unusual care and thoroughness.**

"Perfunctory" describes something done as a mere formality, with minimal attention and no real engagement. A careful inspection would be thorough, searching or diligent. The word carries a note of criticism, which is why it appears in reports on failures of oversight.

Going through the motions is what the adjective reports, so an inspection praised for unusual care cannot be described that way.

**C) A "circumspect" statement about a new therapy stakes everything on the strongest claim the data could conceivably support.**

"Circumspect" means cautious and alert to consequences, looking around before speaking or acting. A statement that reaches for the strongest available claim is bold, incautious or overreaching. Clinical communication prizes circumspection because early results so often shrink on replication.

Caution is the disposition the adjective names, so a statement pitched at the maximum defensible claim is precisely what it excludes.

**D) A volcano described as "quiescent" is erupting steadily from one month to the next.**

"Quiescent" means inactive or at rest for the time being, without any promise that the rest is permanent. A volcano in steady eruption is active, and one that will never erupt again is extinct. The three labels do different work in monitoring reports and cannot be exchanged.

Temporary inactivity is what the adjective records, so a mountain in continuous eruption falls under a different label altogether.

**E) A coral reef described as "resilient" can absorb a bleaching event and recover its function.**

Resilience in ecology is the capacity to absorb a disturbance and return to something like the previous state, which is not the same as never being disturbed. A reef that simply avoided bleaching would be sheltered or fortunate rather than resilient. The concept therefore depends on recovery as much as on resistance.

Absorbing a shock and coming back is the very capacity the term names, so this use of it is exact.
tasks.solution_overview: Each adjective sits on a scale, and the sentence either places it correctly or slides it to the far end. Fix the pole the adjective belongs to before reading the rest of the sentence. Four of these have been pushed to the opposite pole, and the reasoning is the same in every case.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five statements about formal adjectives drawn from treaty practice, sentencing and public administration. Decide whether each statement describes the adjective correctly.
statements: A "reciprocal" arrangement on recognising professional qualifications is one in which each state accepts the other's on the same terms.
A "unilateral" declaration of a marine reserve is made by one state acting on its own, without the agreement of its neighbours.
A "punitive" sentence is one set deliberately light in order to reward cooperation with the investigation.
"Remedial" works are those intended to correct a defect that has already been identified.
Spending described as "statutory" can be varied at will by the department that administers it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "reciprocal" arrangement on recognising professional qualifications is one in which each state accepts the other's on the same terms.**

"Reciprocal" describes an exchange in which each side gives what it receives, so the obligations mirror one another. An arrangement in which only one state opened its register would be unilateral concession. The adjective says nothing about whether the two professions are of equal size, only that the terms match.

Mutual and matching obligations are what the adjective requires, and the recognition scheme supplies them, so the statement is accurate.

**B) A "unilateral" declaration of a marine reserve is made by one state acting on its own, without the agreement of its neighbours.**

"Unilateral" marks action taken by one party alone, in contrast with bilateral action by two and multilateral action by several. The prefix carries the whole meaning, and international lawyers use the word without any implication that the act is improper. Whether it binds others is a separate question from how it was made.

Action by a single party is exactly what the prefix and the adjective assert, so the description holds.

**C) A "punitive" sentence is one set deliberately light in order to reward cooperation with the investigation.**

"Punitive" means intended to punish, so a punitive element in a sentence is there to impose a penalty rather than to soften one. A reduction for cooperation is a discount or a mitigation of sentence. Courts distinguish the punitive purpose from the deterrent and rehabilitative ones, but none of them is served by leniency as such.

Punishment is the purpose written into the adjective, so a sentence lightened as a reward is the very opposite of a punitive one.

**D) "Remedial" works are those intended to correct a defect that has already been identified.**

"Remedial" points backwards at a fault and forwards at its repair, which is why the word covers strengthening a cracked abutment or reworking a failed joint. Measures taken before any defect appears are preventive or precautionary. The distinction decides who pays under most construction contracts.

Correction of an identified defect is precisely the work the adjective describes, so the statement is correct.

**E) Spending described as "statutory" can be varied at will by the department that administers it.**

"Statutory" means required or governed by an Act, so statutory spending is fixed by law rather than by administrative choice. Money a department may adjust within its allocation is discretionary. The contrast shapes every budget debate, since only one of the two categories is genuinely available for cuts.

Being set by legislation is what the adjective means, so spending a department may vary at will belongs in the discretionary column instead.
tasks.solution_overview: The first two turn on how many parties act, the middle two on the purpose of a measure, and the last on where a power comes from. Ask who is doing what to whom, and whether the aim is to punish, to repair or simply to comply with a rule. Those questions settle every item in the set.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal terms for obligation, charges and amounts building up over time. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: A rural clinic "exempt" from the reporting requirement is the one most tightly bound by it.
A landowner "liable" for the cost of remediation has been released from any obligation to pay it.
A borrower who "incurs" default charges on a business overdraft has become subject to them.
Annual leave that "accrues" month by month for hospital staff disappears from the entitlement as fast as it is earned.
An authority that "remits" a penalty has cancelled the obligation to pay it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A rural clinic "exempt" from the reporting requirement is the one most tightly bound by it.**

"Exempt" means released from an obligation that applies to others, so exemption is a form of relief rather than a heightened duty. A body held to the strictest version of the rule would be subject to it or specially designated. Exemptions are usually granted by name or by threshold, and they are read narrowly.

Release from a duty is what exemption confers, so the clinic described here is the one that does not have to report at all.

**B) A landowner "liable" for the cost of remediation has been released from any obligation to pay it.**

"Liable" means legally responsible, so liability is the condition of being answerable for a cost or a wrong. Release would be described as being discharged, indemnified or exonerated. Contaminated land regimes turn on exactly this word, since it decides who funds the clean-up.

Legal responsibility is what the adjective fastens on the landowner, so being liable is the opposite of being let off the bill.

**C) A borrower who "incurs" default charges on a business overdraft has become subject to them.**

"Incur" means to bring something on oneself, and it takes costs, penalties and liabilities as its objects rather than benefits. The borrower has not chosen the charges directly, but conduct has triggered them. One incurs a debt or a fine; one does not incur a rebate.

Bringing a liability on oneself through one's own conduct is exactly what the verb reports, so the account is right.

**D) Annual leave that "accrues" month by month for hospital staff disappears from the entitlement as fast as it is earned.**

"Accrue" means to accumulate over time, adding to a balance rather than draining it. Leave that accrues monthly builds up until it is taken or paid out. Entitlement that vanished as it arose would be described as lapsing or expiring, which is a different provision altogether.

Accumulation is the direction the verb sets, so leave that accrues each month is piling up rather than melting away.

**E) An authority that "remits" a penalty has cancelled the obligation to pay it.**

In this sense "remit" means to cancel or refrain from exacting a debt or punishment, which is why the noun remission covers both fines and sentences. The same verb elsewhere means to send back or to refer a matter to another body, so context has to select the reading. Here the object is a penalty, and cancellation is the natural sense.

Cancellation of what was owed is the reading the object forces, so the account of the authority's decision is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Each item names a party and then says what that party owes, has been released from, or has built up. Ask whether the term places a burden on someone or lifts one, and whether the amount involved is growing or disappearing. Two of these turn on the direction of accumulation.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five statements about how findings, rulings and figures are labelled according to how settled they are. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: A "preliminary" excavation report sets out early findings released before the full analysis is complete.
A "definitive" edition of a poet's letters is one intended to settle the text and not to be superseded.
Timings described as "indicative" in a research infrastructure plan are offered as a guide rather than as a commitment.
Evidence described as "inconclusive" has settled the matter beyond further dispute.
A "counterfactual" scenario in a policy evaluation describes what would have happened without the intervention rather than what actually occurred.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "preliminary" excavation report sets out early findings released before the full analysis is complete.**

"Preliminary" marks work issued at an early stage so that others can respond while the detailed study continues. Such a report is expected to be superseded, and its figures are usually hedged accordingly. A document intended to close the matter would be described as final.

Early publication ahead of the full analysis is exactly the status the adjective claims, so the statement holds.

**B) A "definitive" edition of a poet's letters is one intended to settle the text and not to be superseded.**

"Definitive" means authoritative and conclusive, putting an end to the question it addresses. Editors reach for it when the manuscripts have been collated and the readings resolved as far as the evidence allows. It is a claim about standing rather than about length or luxury of production.

Settling the matter for future readers is the ambition the adjective declares, so the description is a fair one.

**C) Timings described as "indicative" in a research infrastructure plan are offered as a guide rather than as a commitment.**

"Indicative" figures show the general shape of what is expected without binding anyone to them. Planners use the label to share a schedule while the funding and permissions are still moving. A date that had been committed to would be described as firm or contractual.

Guidance without commitment is precisely what the label reserves, so the account of the plan is correct.

**D) Evidence described as "inconclusive" has settled the matter beyond further dispute.**

"Inconclusive" means that the evidence does not permit a firm conclusion either way, which is a statement about what can be inferred rather than about the quality of the work. Evidence that closed the question would be conclusive or decisive. Trials often report inconclusive results simply because they were too small to detect the effect they sought.

Failure to settle the question is the whole content of the word, so evidence said to be inconclusive is exactly what leaves the dispute open.

**E) A "counterfactual" scenario in a policy evaluation describes what would have happened without the intervention rather than what actually occurred.**

The counterfactual is the comparison case an evaluation has to construct, since the effect of a programme is the difference between the world with it and the world without it. It is built from evidence but never observed directly, which is why so much method goes into estimating it. Describing what did happen is the factual half of the comparison.

An unobserved comparison case standing against the facts is what the term denotes, so the statement describes it accurately.
tasks.solution_overview: These labels tell a reader how much may still change, so the strategy is to place each one on a line running from provisional to final. Ask what would have to happen for the label to be withdrawn. One item also asks about a scenario constructed for analysis rather than observed.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five accounts of the formal vocabulary used to describe how quantities move in relation to one another. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: Estimates produced by independent dating methods that "converge" are moving towards the same value.
Climate projections that "diverge" give increasingly different answers as the horizon lengthens.
To report that two series "correlate" is to say that they move together, without by itself showing that one causes the other.
Groundwater levels that "oscillate" through the year move up and down rather than following one steady path.
A retailer reporting that sales have "plateaued" says that they have levelled off after a period of growth rather than fallen away.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Estimates produced by independent dating methods that "converge" are moving towards the same value.**

"Converge" describes lines or values approaching one another, and in dating work convergence between independent methods is treated as a mark of reliability. The verb concerns direction rather than arrival: values may converge without ever meeting. Agreement reached by adjusting one method to match another would not count.

Movement towards a common value is exactly what the verb reports, so the account is sound.

**B) Climate projections that "diverge" give increasingly different answers as the horizon lengthens.**
