**Tip:** Sovereignty is about who rules; jurisdiction is about which body may decide this particular case.

Authority over territory and competence over a case are answered by different tests, so the situation the sentence describes is entirely ordinary.
tasks.solution_overview: Constitutional vocabulary is graded by scope and by permanence, so ask how far each word reaches and how long it is meant to last. Self-rule inside a state and statehood itself differ in kind, a pause differs from a prohibition, and ultimate authority over land differs from a court's competence over one case. Two lines involve labels that carry legal consequences, so check whether the word merely describes conduct or actually triggers a test.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five statements about words that mark the register of a document or the agency behind an event. Judge whether each account of the pair is accurate.
statements: "Peruse" is the formal word for glancing quickly over a document, so a reviewer who perused the appendix spent very little time on it.
"Dwelling" is the administrative term for a unit of accommodation, so a housing census counts dwellings while a charity's fundraising letter speaks of homes.
"Ascertain" is a formal way of saying "estimate", so an investigator who has ascertained the cause of the warehouse fire is offering an approximation.
In a lender's records an account described as "in arrears" has by that fact been placed "in default", since the two terms mark the same point in a credit agreement.

"Expire" happens when a fixed term simply runs out, while "terminate" is an act someone performs, so a discharge permit expires on its own date but is terminated only when the regulator ends it early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Peruse" is the formal word for glancing quickly over a document, so a reviewer who perused the appendix spent very little time on it.**

In its established sense peruse means to read closely and in detail, which is why it appears in phrases such as perusing the accounts before a meeting. The verb for a quick pass is skim or scan, and the two describe opposite depths of attention. The mistaken sense is common enough to appear in job adverts, but careful editors still treat it as an error.

**Trap:** The formal ring of the word tempts readers to assume it means something loftier than plain reading, when it actually means more of it.

Close attention rather than a rapid glance is what the verb reports, so the conclusion fails — a reviewer who perused the appendix went through it thoroughly.

**B) "Dwelling" is the administrative term for a unit of accommodation, so a housing census counts dwellings while a charity's fundraising letter speaks of homes.**

Dwelling is defined for statistical purposes as a self-contained set of rooms intended for occupation, which lets an agency count structures consistently whether or not anyone lives in them. Home carries the emotional freight of belonging and cannot be counted, since one family can have a home in a caravan and another can own a dwelling it has never slept in. Each word suits the document that uses it.

Countable units and felt attachment are different things to write about, so the split between the statistical return and the appeal letter is exactly the split the two words maintain.

**C) "Ascertain" is a formal way of saying "estimate", so an investigator who has ascertained the cause of the warehouse fire is offering an approximation.**

Ascertain means to establish something as certain, usually by inquiry: the fact has been pinned down and can be reported without hedging. Estimate does the opposite work, offering an approximate value while acknowledging that the true one is unknown. Fire investigators use the first only when the evidence supports a definite finding, and reach for probable cause when it does not.

Certainty and approximation are opposite commitments, so the sentence reverses the force of the verb — an ascertained cause is one the investigator says has been settled.

**D) In a lender's records an account described as "in arrears" has by that fact been placed "in default", since the two terms mark the same point in a credit agreement.**

Arrears simply means that scheduled payments have been missed and an overdue balance has built up; a borrower one payment behind is in arrears and may clear it next month. Default is a contractual status triggered when the agreement's own conditions are met, commonly after a set period or a formal notice, and it unlocks remedies such as acceleration of the whole balance or enforcement. Lenders keep the terms distinct because the second changes what they are entitled to do.

A missed payment and a triggered contractual status are different stages, so the equation fails — arrears can accumulate for some time before the agreement treats the account as in default.

**E) "Expire" happens when a fixed term simply runs out, while "terminate" is an act someone performs, so a discharge permit expires on its own date but is terminated only when the regulator ends it early.**

Expire is intransitive and agentless: nobody does it, the calendar simply arrives at the end date written into the instrument. Terminate takes an agent and a decision, and it usually requires grounds, notice and a right of appeal. The distinction matters in regulation because an expired permit lapses quietly while a terminated one is an enforcement event with consequences on the record.

A date arriving and an authority acting are different causes of the same outcome, and the sentence assigns each verb to its own cause, so the description holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Formality is not the only thing a heavier word signals, so ask what each one commits its writer to: how much attention was paid, how certain a finding is, or who performed the act. Two lines here assume that a formal-sounding verb must mean something vaguer or quicker than its plain partner, when in fact it claims more. The remaining lines reward asking whether an event happened by itself or was brought about, and whether a stage in a process has really been reached.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five statements about terms that quantitative writing uses precisely and everyday speech uses loosely. Decide whether each distinction is drawn correctly.
statements: "Exponential" is an emphatic way of saying "rapid", so any steeply rising curve of measles cases can properly be described as exponential.

An earthquake's "magnitude" measures the energy released and is a single figure for the event, while its "intensity" measures the shaking experienced at a given place, so one quake has one magnitude but many intensities.
"Accuracy" says how close readings sit to the true value while "precision" says how close they sit to one another, so a badly calibrated balance can be precise to the milligram and still be wrong.

In a results section "significant" reports that an effect is unlikely to be an accident of sampling while "substantial" claims that it is large, so a significant difference in reaction times may amount to a few milliseconds.
"Mean" and "median" name the same central value, so a sharply skewed distribution of examination marks yields the same figure whichever is reported.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Exponential" is an emphatic way of saying "rapid", so any steeply rising curve of measles cases can properly be described as exponential.**

Exponential growth has a specific shape: each increment is proportional to the current total, so the quantity doubles over a constant interval however large it becomes. A curve can climb steeply and yet be linear, or be slowing towards a ceiling, and outbreak curves usually bend once susceptible contacts run short. Epidemiologists therefore test for a constant doubling time before using the word.

**Tip:** Ask whether the doubling time stays the same; steepness alone never settles the question.

Steepness and proportional growth are different properties, so the word cannot be applied on the strength of a dramatic slope — many sharply rising outbreaks are not exponential at all.

**B) An earthquake's "magnitude" measures the energy released and is a single figure for the event, while its "intensity" measures the shaking experienced at a given place, so one quake has one magnitude but many intensities.**

Magnitude is derived from the seismic waves themselves and characterises the source, which is why a single number is quoted worldwide. Intensity is assessed from effects on people, buildings and ground at each location, so it falls away with distance and varies with soil and construction. That is how a moderate event on soft sediment can produce higher intensities than a larger one on rock.

One figure for the source and many for the places affected is exactly how seismic reporting is organised, so the sentence describes the pair correctly.

**C) "Accuracy" says how close readings sit to the true value while "precision" says how close they sit to one another, so a badly calibrated balance can be precise to the milligram and still be wrong.**

Accuracy is a comparison against a reference or accepted value and is degraded by systematic offsets. Precision describes the spread of repeated measurements and is degraded by random scatter, which is why it can be improved by better technique while the calibration error remains untouched. An instrument reading consistently five milligrams high is the standard illustration.

Closeness to truth and closeness to each other are independent, so a tightly repeatable but miscalibrated balance is a real possibility rather than a contradiction, and the sentence names it correctly.

**D) In a results section "significant" reports that an effect is unlikely to be an accident of sampling while "substantial" claims that it is large, so a significant difference in reaction times may amount to a few milliseconds.**

Statistical significance is a statement about compatibility with chance, and it depends heavily on sample size: with enough participants, a tiny difference clears the threshold. Substantial, important and meaningful are claims about magnitude and are argued with effect sizes and practical consequences. Journals ask for both because the first alone tells a reader nothing about whether the finding matters.

Detectability and size answer separate questions, and the sentence keeps the technical sense clear of the everyday one, so the account is right.

**E) "Mean" and "median" name the same central value, so a sharply skewed distribution of examination marks yields the same figure whichever is reported.**

The mean adds every value and divides by the count, so a handful of extreme marks pulls it towards the tail. The median takes the middle observation once the marks are ordered and is barely moved by those extremes. On a symmetric distribution the two coincide, which is exactly why the skewed case in the sentence is the one that separates them.

Skew is the condition under which the two measures diverge, so the claim fails — a long tail of very low marks drags the mean below the median while the middle mark stays put.
tasks.solution_overview: Quantitative vocabulary describes a shape, a source or a spread, so ask what each term is actually computed from before accepting the comparison. Two of these lines separate a property of the event from a property of the place or the reading, and one separates whether an effect is detectable from whether it is large. Where a word has drifted into everyday use as a general intensifier, check whether the technical condition behind it is being met.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five statements about clinical near-synonyms that separate laboratory conditions from ordinary practice, and partial improvement from resolution. Judge whether each is accurate.
statements: "Efficacy" reports how a treatment performs under trial conditions while "effectiveness" reports how it performs in ordinary practice, so a vaccine with high efficacy can show lower effectiveness once storage failures and missed appointments are in play.
"Remission" says a disease is undetectable for the moment while "recovery" claims a return to health, so a patient can be in remission and still be counted among those who have not recovered.
Every "contagious" disease is "infectious", though not every infectious one is contagious, since tetanus is acquired from the environment rather than from another person.
An "analgesic" removes sensation and awareness altogether, while an "anaesthetic" merely dulls pain that the patient can still feel.

A "screening" test is offered to people without symptoms in order to decide who needs further investigation, while a "diagnostic" test answers the question for one patient, so a positive screen is not yet a diagnosis.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Efficacy" reports how a treatment performs under trial conditions while "effectiveness" reports how it performs in ordinary practice, so a vaccine with high efficacy can show lower effectiveness once storage failures and missed appointments are in play.**

Efficacy is measured in a controlled setting with selected participants, monitored adherence and standardised handling, which is designed to isolate the treatment's own contribution. Effectiveness is measured in the population as it is, complete with cold chains that break, doses given late and people who never return for the second appointment. The gap between the two numbers is a health-system finding rather than a failure of the trial.

**Tip:** Efficacy answers whether it can work, effectiveness whether it does work where it is used.

Controlled conditions and everyday conditions are measured separately for good reason, so the drop the sentence describes is the expected pattern rather than a contradiction.

**B) "Remission" says a disease is undetectable for the moment while "recovery" claims a return to health, so a patient can be in remission and still be counted among those who have not recovered.**

Remission is a statement about current disease activity: signs and symptoms have receded, and in some conditions no cells or lesions can be found, but the possibility of relapse is built into the word. Recovery is a broader judgement covering function, strength and the resumption of ordinary life, which often lags months behind the disappearance of the disease. Oncology and rheumatology both need the narrower word for exactly that reason.

Absent disease activity and restored health are separate milestones, so the sentence is right that reaching the first leaves the second still to come.

**C) Every "contagious" disease is "infectious", though not every infectious one is contagious, since tetanus is acquired from the environment rather than from another person.**

Infectious is the wider term, covering any illness caused by a pathogen entering the body, whatever the route. Contagious narrows that to transmission between hosts, whether by direct contact, droplets or contaminated hands. Tetanus, legionellosis and many fungal infections are caught from soil, water or air without any infected person being involved, which places them inside the wider circle and outside the narrower one.

The nesting runs in one direction only, and the sentence states it in that direction with an example that sits precisely in the gap, so it holds.

**D) An "analgesic" removes sensation and awareness altogether, while an "anaesthetic" merely dulls pain that the patient can still feel.**

An analgesic relieves pain while leaving other sensation and consciousness intact, which is why a patient on one can still feel pressure and movement. An anaesthetic abolishes sensation in a region, or consciousness entirely, and is the reason surgery is tolerable at all. The functions have been handed to the wrong words.

**Trap:** Both words come from the vocabulary of pain relief, which makes the swap easy to read past.

The definitions belong to the opposite terms, so the line does not stand — the analgesic dulls pain while the anaesthetic removes sensation.

**E) A "screening" test is offered to people without symptoms in order to decide who needs further investigation, while a "diagnostic" test answers the question for one patient, so a positive screen is not yet a diagnosis.**

Screening is a population activity, tuned to miss as few cases as possible and therefore accepting a high number of false alarms. Diagnostic testing is tuned for confirmation in someone already suspected of having the condition, and it carries the accuracy needed to justify treatment. The two are designed with different trade-offs, which is why a screening programme always has a follow-up pathway attached.

Sorting a population and confirming one case are different jobs, so the caution the sentence attaches to a positive screen follows directly from how the test was designed.
tasks.solution_overview: Clinical vocabulary separates ideal conditions from messy ones and partial improvement from full resolution, so ask what each word is measured under and how much it claims. Two lines nest a narrow term inside a wider one, and the direction of that nesting is what makes the inference work or fail. One pair has simply been handed each other's definitions, which becomes obvious once you ask what a patient would still be able to feel.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five statements about pairs that look like restatements of one another but describe different stages, bases or standards. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Weathering" breaks rock down where it stands while "erosion" carries the loosened material away, so a sandstone facade can be deeply weathered without a grain of it having been eroded from the site.
A retailer's "markup" is calculated on what the goods cost while its "margin" is calculated on what they sell for, so the same twenty pounds of difference represents a larger markup than margin.

A "projection" states what follows if a stated scenario holds while a "prediction" asserts what will actually happen, so a modelling group can publish several projections without contradicting itself.

"Calibrating" an instrument adjusts its readings against a known standard while "validating" a model asks whether its outputs match independent observations, so a perfectly calibrated sensor can still be feeding an invalid model.
"Reproducing" an analysis re-runs it on the original data while "replicating" a study repeats it with newly collected data, so a finding can be reproducible and still fail to replicate.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Weathering" breaks rock down where it stands while "erosion" carries the loosened material away, so a sandstone facade can be deeply weathered without a grain of it having been eroded from the site.**

Weathering is disintegration in place, driven by frost, salt crystallisation, acid rain and biological action, and it leaves the debris where it forms. Erosion requires transport, by water, wind, ice or gravity, and it removes the products of weathering to somewhere else. On a sheltered stone facade the chemistry proceeds while nothing is carried off, which is why conservators find crumbling surfaces with the powder still sitting on them.

Breakdown and removal are separate processes that often occur together, and the facade example holds one without the other, so the distinction is drawn correctly.

**B) A retailer's "markup" is calculated on what the goods cost while its "margin" is calculated on what they sell for, so the same twenty pounds of difference represents a larger markup than margin.**

Markup expresses the difference between cost and price as a percentage of cost, so it answers how much has been added to what the buyer paid the supplier. Margin expresses the same difference as a percentage of the selling price, which is the figure that appears in accounts and comparisons between firms. Because the selling price is the larger denominator, the same cash difference always produces the smaller percentage when reported as margin.

Different denominators produce different percentages from identical cash, so the ranking the sentence gives follows arithmetically and the description is sound.

**C) A "projection" states what follows if a stated scenario holds while a "prediction" asserts what will actually happen, so a modelling group can publish several projections without contradicting itself.**

A projection is conditional by construction: given these assumptions about emissions, migration or fertility, the model produces this path. A prediction drops the condition and commits to an outcome, which is why forecasting agencies are careful about which word appears in a headline. Publishing a family of scenarios is a way of showing how sensitive the result is to assumptions rather than a display of indecision.

Conditional output and unconditional claim are different products, so a set of divergent projections is internally consistent in exactly the way the sentence describes.

**D) "Calibrating" an instrument adjusts its readings against a known standard while "validating" a model asks whether its outputs match independent observations, so a perfectly calibrated sensor can still be feeding an invalid model.**

Calibration is a comparison against a reference with a traceable value, and it corrects the instrument rather than the reasoning built on top of it. Validation tests whether a representation of the world behaves like the world, using data that were not used to build it. Good inputs into a poorly specified model produce confident nonsense, which is why environmental agencies require both steps.

The instrument and the model are checked against different references, so the failure mode the sentence describes is a real and familiar one rather than a contradiction in terms.

**E) "Reproducing" an analysis re-runs it on the original data while "replicating" a study repeats it with newly collected data, so a finding can be reproducible and still fail to replicate.**

Reproducibility tests the computational trail: given the same dataset and code, does the same table come out. Replication tests the finding itself: does a fresh sample, gathered independently, produce the same effect. A result can pass the first because the arithmetic is sound and fail the second because the original sample was unusual or the effect was a chance one.

**Tip:** Same data and same code is reproduction; new data and the same question is replication.

The two checks interrogate different things, so the combination the sentence describes is common enough to be a standing concern in research methods.
tasks.solution_overview: Each pair here divides a process into two stages or measures the same quantity against two different bases, so identify the base or the step before judging the claim. Breaking down and carrying away, adjusting an instrument and testing a model, re-running code and gathering fresh data all describe adjacent but distinct operations. Where percentages are involved, the decisive question is what sits in the denominator, and where models are involved it is whether a condition has been attached to the output.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five statements about pairs that describe the same behaviour while passing opposite judgements on it. Decide whether each account of the connotation is accurate.
statements: "Notorious" and "renowned" both report wide fame, but only the first assumes the fame is for something discreditable, so a prison notorious for overcrowding is not being complimented.
"Childish" is the appreciative term, describing an adult's unspoilt sense of wonder, while "childlike" condemns behaviour as immature.
"Miserly" is the neutral word for careful spending while "frugal" is the insult, so calling a scholarship fund's administrator frugal is a complaint about meanness.
"Propaganda" is a neutral synonym for "publicity", so a health ministry would ordinarily describe its own vaccination campaign as propaganda.
"Stubborn" is the admiring word and "tenacious" the critical one, so a researcher who keeps working on an unfashionable question for twenty years is being praised as stubborn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Notorious" and "renowned" both report wide fame, but only the first assumes the fame is for something discreditable, so a prison notorious for overcrowding is not being complimented.**

Both adjectives measure how widely something is known, and neither says anything about scale on its own. Renowned attaches that fame to achievement and invites admiration, while notorious attaches it to a fault, a scandal or a danger, and the noun that follows almost always names the trouble. Overcrowding is a failing, so the adjective is doing evaluative work rather than merely reporting reputation.

The shared meaning is reach and the difference is verdict, and the sentence keeps that verdict attached to the right word, so the account is accurate.

**B) "Childish" is the appreciative term, describing an adult's unspoilt sense of wonder, while "childlike" condemns behaviour as immature.**

Childlike is the sympathetic form, reserved for qualities of childhood that adults are glad to keep: curiosity, delight, directness, trust. Childish is dismissive and marks behaviour as beneath the age of the person showing it, which is why it collocates with sulking, squabbling and refusing to cooperate. The morphology gives no clue, so the pair has to be learnt as a matter of usage.

**Trap:** Two adjectives from one root can carry opposite evaluations, and nothing in the suffix warns you which is which.

The compliment and the rebuke have been assigned to the wrong forms, so the line fails — wonder is childlike, while a tantrum is childish.

**C) "Miserly" is the neutral word for careful spending while "frugal" is the insult, so calling a scholarship fund's administrator frugal is a complaint about meanness.**

Frugal describes restraint that is chosen and admired: spending little, wasting nothing, and often doing so on principle. Miserly describes hoarding at the expense of others and carries the figure of the miser behind it, so it implies withholding rather than economy. An administrator praised for frugal management is being credited with stewardship of somebody else's money.

Approval and disapproval sit on the opposite words here, so the sentence misreads the compliment — frugal is the praise and miserly the accusation.

**D) "Propaganda" is a neutral synonym for "publicity", so a health ministry would ordinarily describe its own vaccination campaign as propaganda.**

Publicity is the neutral term for making something widely known, and organisations apply it to their own work without embarrassment. Propaganda now carries a strong charge of manipulation and one-sided persuasion, which is why it is almost always applied to somebody else's messaging. The word had a more technical past in the vocabulary of information campaigns, but current usage keeps the pejorative sense firmly attached.

A label nobody applies to their own materials cannot be the neutral option, so the claim fails — a ministry publicises its campaign and leaves propaganda for its opponents to allege.

**E) "Stubborn" is the admiring word and "tenacious" the critical one, so a researcher who keeps working on an unfashionable question for twenty years is being praised as stubborn.**

Tenacious frames persistence as a virtue, implying purpose, resilience and a grip that will not be shaken loose. Stubborn frames the same behaviour as a fault, implying resistance to reason and an unwillingness to revise, which is why it pairs with refusal rather than with pursuit. The behaviour described can be identical; the judgement passed on it is not.

The praise belongs to the other adjective, so the sentence inverts the evaluation — twenty years on a neglected question is tenacity, and only a critic would call it stubbornness.
tasks.solution_overview: These pairs agree about the facts and disagree about the verdict, so ask which member you would use of your own conduct and which you would reserve for someone else's. Fame, thrift, persistence and persuasion all come with an approving word and a disapproving one, and the morphology offers no reliable guide to which is which. Testing each adjective in a sentence of praise and then in a complaint usually makes the mismatch audible at once.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five statements about verbs that differ over who acted, whether permission existed, and whether a duty was owed. Judge whether each account holds.
statements: "Delay" and "postpone" both require somebody to take a decision, so a rocket launch held up by fog has been postponed.
"Disclose" presents the release of a document as authorised while "leak" implies it went out without permission, so an inspectorate that discloses its own report has not leaked it.
"Omit" reports only that something was left out while "neglect" adds that it ought to have been done, so an editor who omits a footnote has not necessarily neglected a duty.
"Abandon" presupposes a formal act of giving up a right, while "relinquish" suggests simply walking away and leaving something behind.
"Concede" reports giving ground to an opponent's case while "admit" needs no opponent at all, so a glaciologist who admits an uncertainty in her measurements is not conceding an argument.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Delay" and "postpone" both require somebody to take a decision, so a rocket launch held up by fog has been postponed.**

Delay can happen to a schedule without anyone choosing it: weather, traffic and equipment faults all delay events by themselves, and the verb works happily in the passive with no agent in sight. Postpone needs an agent and a new time, since it means moving something deliberately to a later slot. A launch stopped by fog is delayed at the moment the fog arrives; it becomes postponed only when the flight director sets another date.

**Tip:** If you can ask who decided, the verb is postpone; if the cause is a condition rather than a person, it is delay.

Only one of these verbs carries a decision-maker inside it, so the sentence overreaches — fog delays a launch, and a controller postpones it.

**B) "Disclose" presents the release of a document as authorised while "leak" implies it went out without permission, so an inspectorate that discloses its own report has not leaked it.**

Disclose describes a release made by someone entitled to make it, often under a statutory duty or a transparency policy, and it carries no suggestion of wrongdoing. Leak describes an unauthorised passage of information out of an organisation, usually to journalists, and it invites questions about who was responsible. The same document reaching the same readers can be described either way depending on whether permission stood behind it.

Authorisation is the whole of the difference, and the sentence attaches the neutral verb to the body publishing its own findings, so the wording is right.

**C) "Omit" reports only that something was left out while "neglect" adds that it ought to have been done, so an editor who omits a footnote has not necessarily neglected a duty.**

Omit is descriptive and can be entirely deliberate: material is left out for length, relevance or style, and no criticism follows. Neglect is evaluative and presupposes an obligation that went unmet, which is why it appears in findings of professional misconduct rather than in editorial notes. An omission becomes neglect only once someone shows the item was required.

A missing element and a breached duty are separate claims, so the sentence is right to let the first stand without the second following from it.

**D) "Abandon" presupposes a formal act of giving up a right, while "relinquish" suggests simply walking away and leaving something behind.**

Relinquish is the formal, deliberate verb: a right, a title or a claim is given up by someone entitled to hold it, usually in writing and often in exchange for something. Abandon suggests desertion, leaving property, a project or a post without arrangements and often without warning, which is why it carries a note of reproach. Legal drafting uses the first and incident reports the second.

Deliberate surrender and desertion have been attached to the wrong verbs, so the sentence does not hold — a right is relinquished, while an unattended site is abandoned.

**E) "Concede" reports giving ground to an opponent's case while "admit" needs no opponent at all, so a glaciologist who admits an uncertainty in her measurements is not conceding an argument.**

Concede is a dialectical verb: it presupposes a dispute and reports that one side has yielded a point to the other, which is why it appears in debates, negotiations and courtrooms. Admit reports an acknowledgement of fact and can be made to a notebook, a reader or nobody in particular. Stating the error bars on a measurement is ordinary scientific candour rather than a retreat under pressure.

One verb needs an adversary and the other does not, so the sentence draws the right line between honest reporting and losing an argument.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line hangs on something the verb quietly assumes: an agent who decided, a permission that existed, a duty that was owed, or an opponent who had to be answered. Test every claim by asking whether the sentence supplies that ingredient, since a fog bank is not a decision-maker and a footnote is not necessarily an obligation. Where two verbs seem to differ only in formality, check whether one of them is actually the deliberate act and the other the desertion.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five statements about the verbs and labels that official documents select where ordinary speech would choose a plainer word. Decide whether each is accurate.
statements: "Contract" is the clinical partner of "catch", so a case note records that the child contracted measles where a parent would say she caught it.
In a museum catalogue "the collection is comprised of four bequests" is the form careful editors prefer, since "comprise" takes "of" while "compose" does not.
"Insolvency" and "bankruptcy" name the same event, so a company that cannot pay its debts as they fall due has by that fact been declared bankrupt.
"Administer" is the verb that pairs with oaths, doses and examinations in official records, so a court transcript notes that the oath was administered rather than given.
"Deceased" is the warmer and more personal choice while "the late" is the clinical one, which is why a coroner's report refers to "the late Mr Harun" rather than to the deceased.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Contract" is the clinical partner of "catch", so a case note records that the child contracted measles where a parent would say she caught it.**

Both verbs describe acquiring an infection, and neither adds anything to the medical facts. Contract belongs to clinical and epidemiological registers and takes named diseases as its object, which is why it appears in notes, notifications and journal abstracts. Catch is the everyday equivalent and would look out of place in a discharge summary.

**Tip:** Where two verbs share a meaning exactly, the choice between them is a choice of document rather than of content.

Register is the only variable at work, and each verb has been matched to the setting where it belongs, so the line reads correctly.

**B) In a museum catalogue "the collection is comprised of four bequests" is the form careful editors prefer, since "comprise" takes "of" while "compose" does not.**

Comprise means to consist of and already contains the sense of the preposition, so the whole comprises its parts: the collection comprises four bequests. Compose runs the other way, from parts to whole, and it is the verb that takes the passive with of, as in the collection is composed of four bequests. Style guides treat is comprised of as the construction to avoid, precisely because it welds one verb's preposition onto the other.

The prepositional pattern has been assigned to the wrong verb, so the recommendation fails — the sound catalogue wording is "the collection comprises four bequests."

**C) "Insolvency" and "bankruptcy" name the same event, so a company that cannot pay its debts as they fall due has by that fact been declared bankrupt.**

Insolvency is a financial condition: liabilities exceed assets, or debts cannot be met as they fall due, and a business can be in that state for months while trading on and negotiating with creditors. Bankruptcy, and its corporate equivalents, is a formal legal process opened by a court or an appointed officeholder, with consequences for control of the assets and for the directors. One is a description of the balance sheet, the other a change of legal status.

A condition does not become a proceeding without somebody commencing it, so the inference fails — insolvency is the state that may lead to a formal process rather than the process itself.

**D) "Administer" is the verb that pairs with oaths, doses and examinations in official records, so a court transcript notes that the oath was administered rather than given.**

Administer carries the sense of dispensing something under authority and in a prescribed form, which is why it collocates with oaths, medication, aid, tests and justice. Give would convey the same event but with none of that procedural weight, and it is the verb used in conversation about the same moment. The pairing is a matter of settled collocation rather than of meaning.

Official records reach for the verb that marks a formal procedure, and the transcript in the sentence does exactly that, so the account is accurate.

**E) "Deceased" is the warmer and more personal choice while "the late" is the clinical one, which is why a coroner's report refers to "the late Mr Harun" rather than to the deceased.**

The deceased is the impersonal administrative term, used across coroners' findings, insurance files and probate to name the person as a party to a process. The late before a name is the respectful and slightly softer form, appearing in obituaries, dedications and letters of condolence. The registers are the reverse of what the sentence claims.

**Trap:** Both expressions avoid the blunt word dead, which can make them feel equally formal until you notice which one keeps the person's name.

The administrative term is the colder one, so the line does not stand — a coroner writes about the deceased and a memorial notice about the late Mr Harun.
tasks.solution_overview: Official registers select particular verbs and labels by convention, so ask which document each wording belongs in and what procedure it signals. Two lines here are decided by collocation alone, one by the grammatical pattern a verb actually takes, and one by the gap between a financial condition and the legal process that may follow it. Reading each sentence aloud as a case note, a catalogue entry or a condolence letter usually exposes the wording that has been placed in the wrong file.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five statements about terms used in publishing, archives and textual scholarship, where each word names a different operation on a text or a collection. Judge whether each is accurate.
statements: A new "impression" reprints the same setting of a text while a new "edition" involves substantive changes to it, so a monograph can run to five impressions and remain a first edition.
An "abridged" text has been shortened for length while a "redacted" one has had passages withheld from the reader, so a field diary cut down for publication is not a redacted document.

A "gloss" explains a single word or phrase where it stands while an "annotation" may comment on anything from a date to an argument, so a glossary at the back does narrower work than a critical apparatus.
A "facsimile" edition reinterprets the original's layout for modern readers, while a plain "reproduction" copies it page for page.
"Collecting" accumulates objects while "curating" selects and interprets them for an audience, so an archive can hold a large collection that has never been curated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A new "impression" reprints the same setting of a text while a new "edition" involves substantive changes to it, so a monograph can run to five impressions and remain a first edition.**

An impression is a print run from unchanged type or unchanged files, correcting at most a few obvious slips, and it exists because copies ran out rather than because the book changed. An edition marks a new state of the text: revised chapters, new apparatus, a fresh preface, or a resetting substantial enough to alter pagination. Cataloguers and citation styles depend on the distinction, since page references survive an impression but not always an edition.

Reprinting and revising are different events in a book's life, and the sentence lets the copies multiply without the text changing, which is exactly what the terms allow.

**B) An "abridged" text has been shortened for length while a "redacted" one has had passages withheld from the reader, so a field diary cut down for publication is not a redacted document.**

Abridgement is an editorial decision about scale, made openly and usually announced on the title page, and its purpose is to keep the work readable at a manageable length. Redaction is a decision about disclosure, obscuring names, locations or findings that someone has judged must not be released, and its marks are deliberately visible so readers know material is missing. One asks what a reader needs, the other what a reader may not have.

Length and permission are separate grounds for removing text, so the shortened diary belongs under the first, exactly as the sentence has it.

**C) A "gloss" explains a single word or phrase where it stands while an "annotation" may comment on anything from a date to an argument, so a glossary at the back does narrower work than a critical apparatus.**

A gloss is lexical and local: it renders a difficult word into a plainer one, often in the margin or between the lines it serves. An annotation is open-ended, taking in sources, variants, historical background and editorial judgement, and it can run to several hundred words. Every gloss is a kind of annotation, but the reverse relationship does not hold.

The narrower term sits inside the wider one, and the sentence keeps the vocabulary list beneath the full apparatus, so the comparison is sound.

**D) A "facsimile" edition reinterprets the original's layout for modern readers, while a plain "reproduction" copies it page for page.**

A facsimile aims at visual fidelity: the page opening, the line breaks, the marginalia and often the paper size are preserved so that the reader confronts something as close to the original object as printing allows. Reproduction is the looser and more general word, covering any copy of an image or text in any format, including one that has been resized, cropped or reset. Reinterpretation for modern readers describes a modernised or critical edition instead.

**Trap:** Both words mean copy in ordinary speech, which conceals that only one of them promises the original's appearance.

The definitions have been exchanged, so the line fails — a facsimile is the page-for-page copy, while reproduction is the general term that permits changes.

**E) "Collecting" accumulates objects while "curating" selects and interprets them for an audience, so an archive can hold a large collection that has never been curated.**

Collecting is acquisition: material arrives by donation, purchase or transfer and is accessioned into the holdings. Curating adds judgement and framing, choosing what to show, arranging it, and writing the interpretation that lets a visitor make sense of it. Vast backlogs of uncatalogued material in national archives are the ordinary proof that the first can run far ahead of the second.

Acquiring and interpreting are separate professional tasks with separate resources behind them, so the uncurated collection the sentence describes is a familiar reality rather than a contradiction.
tasks.solution_overview: Textual scholarship names operations rather than objects, so ask what was actually done and why: reprinted or revised, shortened or withheld, explained locally or discussed at length, copied faithfully or reset. Where one term nests inside another, check that the sentence keeps the narrower one underneath. The two lines about copying reward a closer look at which word actually promises fidelity to the original page.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five statements about words whose laboratory senses are narrower than their everyday ones. Decide whether each account of the technical use is accurate.
statements: In a reaction write-up a "catalyst" is recovered unchanged while a "reagent" is consumed, so the everyday use of catalyst for anything that starts a change is looser than the chemical sense.
"Organic" in a chemistry paper classifies carbon-based compounds and says nothing about farming methods, so an organic solvent may be manufactured by wholly synthetic means.
"Power" is the rate at which energy is transferred, so a battery's capacity is quoted in energy units while a kettle's demand is quoted in power units, and the two figures cannot be swapped.
"Sterilising" removes every viable organism including spores while "disinfecting" reduces them to a level judged safe, so a wipe that disinfects a laboratory bench has not sterilised it.
"Toxic" says a substance poisons living tissue while "hazardous" covers any material capable of causing harm, including things that merely corrode or ignite, so a hazardous cargo need not be toxic.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a reaction write-up a "catalyst" is recovered unchanged while a "reagent" is consumed, so the everyday use of catalyst for anything that starts a change is looser than the chemical sense.**

A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction and emerges from it in its original form, which is why small quantities can process large amounts of material. A reagent is a participant that is used up as the reaction proceeds and must be replenished for the next run. The metaphorical sense, in which a person or an event catalyses change, keeps the idea of triggering but drops the crucial condition of surviving untouched.

Surviving the process is what the technical term insists on, and the sentence names that condition as the thing the everyday use quietly abandons, so it holds.

**B) "Organic" in a chemistry paper classifies carbon-based compounds and says nothing about farming methods, so an organic solvent may be manufactured by wholly synthetic means.**

In chemistry the label is a taxonomic one: organic compounds are built on carbon skeletons, and toluene from a refinery qualifies as readily as a molecule from a leaf. In food labelling the same word is a certification about how a crop or animal was raised, with rules on inputs and inspection behind it. Nothing connects the two beyond a shared history in the study of living matter.

A structural class and a production standard are entirely separate claims, so the sentence is right that a synthetic solvent can be organic in the only sense the paper means.

**C) "Power" is the rate at which energy is transferred, so a battery's capacity is quoted in energy units while a kettle's demand is quoted in power units, and the two figures cannot be swapped.**

Energy is a quantity that can be stored and counted, which is why storage is measured in joules or kilowatt hours. Power is that quantity per unit of time, measured in watts, and it describes how fast a device draws or delivers energy rather than how much is available. Multiplying a power by a duration returns an energy, which is the only legitimate bridge between the two.

**Tip:** If a figure needs a time attached before it means anything, it is already a rate and belongs to power.

A stock and a flow answer different questions about the same system, and the sentence keeps each measurement with the quantity it belongs to, so the account is right.

**D) "Sterilising" removes every viable organism including spores while "disinfecting" reduces them to a level judged safe, so a wipe that disinfects a laboratory bench has not sterilised it.**

Sterilisation is an absolute standard, achieved by autoclave, irradiation or filtration, and it is validated because instruments entering sterile tissue must carry nothing at all. Disinfection is a graded reduction on surfaces where a defined level of residual organisms is acceptable, and most disinfectants leave bacterial spores untouched. Choosing between them is a choice about what the item will be used for.

An absolute requirement and a graded one are met by different procedures, so a surface wipe cannot reach the higher standard, and the sentence marks that limit correctly.

**E) "Toxic" says a substance poisons living tissue while "hazardous" covers any material capable of causing harm, including things that merely corrode or ignite, so a hazardous cargo need not be toxic.**

Toxicity is a specific mode of harm involving a biological mechanism and a dose, and it is assessed in the laboratory against organisms. Hazardous is the umbrella classification used in transport and storage rules, admitting flammability, corrosivity, reactivity, pressure and radioactivity alongside toxicity. A tanker of concentrated acid is dangerous through corrosion rather than through poisoning, and it is labelled accordingly.

One term names a mechanism and the other collects every mechanism that can cause harm, so the sentence draws the containment relationship in the direction the regulations use.
tasks.solution_overview: Laboratory language narrows familiar words with a condition attached, so hunt for that condition in each line: surviving the reaction, resting on a carbon skeleton, carrying a time in the units, admitting no survivors, or naming one specific route to harm. Everyday usage keeps the vivid part of the meaning and drops the condition, which is where the loose sense parts company from the strict one. Asking what would have to be measured to justify each word keeps the two senses apart.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five statements about words that are widely used in a sense their careful definitions do not support. Decide whether each account of the established meaning is accurate.
statements: "Fortuitous" means lucky in the sense of welcome, which is why a chance power cut that destroyed a season's samples cannot be described as fortuitous.
"Enormity" is the standard neutral noun for great size, so the enormity of a new telescope's mirror is the ordinary way to praise its scale.
A "dilemma" is any difficult problem, so a shortage of ventilators with no alternative supply available is precisely a dilemma.
"Disinterested" reports a lack of curiosity, so an arbitrator described as disinterested in the outcome is being criticised for inattention.
"Decimate" now commonly reports heavy loss short of destruction while "devastate" claims something close to ruin, so a fungal disease can decimate a bat colony that a later fire devastates.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Fortuitous" means lucky in the sense of welcome, which is why a chance power cut that destroyed a season's samples cannot be described as fortuitous.**

Fortuitous reports that something happened by chance, and the chance may be good, bad or indifferent; a fortuitous meeting is simply an unplanned one. Fortunate is the word that carries the good luck, and the two have converged in casual use because happy accidents are the ones people mention. The strict sense is worth keeping in scientific writing, where accidental and lucky need to stay distinct.

**Tip:** Fortuitous answers how it came about; fortunate answers how it turned out.

Chance rather than good fortune is what the adjective reports, so the exclusion fails — the unplanned power cut is fortuitous and decidedly unfortunate.

**B) "Enormity" is the standard neutral noun for great size, so the enormity of a new telescope's mirror is the ordinary way to praise its scale.**

In careful use enormity means extreme wickedness or the moral gravity of an act, which is why it collocates with crimes, atrocities and betrayals. The neutral nouns for sheer size are enormousness, immensity, magnitude and scale, and one of those is what an engineering description of a mirror would take. The size sense of enormity is common, but it remains contested in edited prose and jars badly where admiration is intended.

Moral weight rather than physical bulk is the settled sense, so the recommendation fails — praise for the instrument would speak of "the immensity of the mirror."

**C) A "dilemma" is any difficult problem, so a shortage of ventilators with no alternative supply available is precisely a dilemma.**

A dilemma is a forced choice between options, classically two, each of which carries a real cost, and the difficulty lies in having to pick rather than in the situation being hard. A shortage with no alternative offers no choice at all, so it is a predicament, a crisis or simply a problem. Where clinicians must decide which of two patients receives the last machine, the word becomes exact.

The defining ingredient is a choice between unwelcome courses, and the sentence describes a situation with none, so the label misses — an absence of options is a predicament rather than a dilemma.

**D) "Disinterested" reports a lack of curiosity, so an arbitrator described as disinterested in the outcome is being criticised for inattention.**

Disinterested means having no stake in the result: no financial interest, no personal connection, nothing to gain whichever way the decision falls. Uninterested is the word for indifference or boredom. The distinction is worth defending precisely because impartiality is a professional requirement, and calling an arbitrator disinterested is the highest praise available.

Having no stake and having no interest are different states, so the reading fails — the arbitrator is being commended for impartiality rather than reproached for boredom.

**E) "Decimate" now commonly reports heavy loss short of destruction while "devastate" claims something close to ruin, so a fungal disease can decimate a bat colony that a later fire devastates.**

The Roman sense of executing one soldier in ten survives only as a historical footnote, and modern usage has settled on severe but partial loss, which is why the verb takes populations, workforces and colonies as objects. Devastate claims comprehensive damage and applies to the place as much as to the population within it. Using the pair in sequence therefore describes an escalation rather than a repetition.

Partial loss and near-total ruin sit at different points on the same scale, and the sentence puts the disease below the fire, so the ordering is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Each of these words is regularly used in a sense its careful definition does not license, so recover the strict meaning before testing the example. Ask whether the word reports chance or good luck, moral weight or physical size, a forced choice or simply a hard situation, and a missing stake or a missing interest. Where a line offers a plausible modern reading, check whether the situation described actually contains the ingredient the strict sense demands.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five statements about the graded vocabulary of crisis reporting, where each label carries a threshold or a legal status behind it. Judge whether each account is accurate.
statements: In macroeconomic writing a "recession" is a contraction meeting a conventional threshold while a "depression" is a far deeper and longer collapse, so describing two negative quarters of output as a depression overstates what the data show.

"Famine" is a technical classification requiring measured thresholds of hunger, malnutrition and mortality while "food insecurity" covers a much wider range of shortage, so a region can be severely food-insecure without a famine being declared.

"Refugee" is a legal status held by someone unable to return home for fear of persecution while "migrant" describes movement without saying anything about status, so every refugee is a migrant though most migrants are not refugees.
"Displaced" households have been moved under an organised instruction from an authority, while "evacuated" ones have left of their own accord ahead of the danger.
In an incident report "casualties" counts only those who died, while "fatalities" is the wider figure taking in the injured as well.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In macroeconomic writing a "recession" is a contraction meeting a conventional threshold while a "depression" is a far deeper and longer collapse, so describing two negative quarters of output as a depression overstates what the data show.**

Recession is the routine label for a downturn that satisfies an agreed test, most commonly two consecutive quarters of falling output or a dating committee's broader judgement. Depression has no equally settled definition but is reserved in practice for contractions of extraordinary depth and duration, with double-digit falls in output and years rather than months of unemployment. Because the second word invokes the interwar comparison, reaching for it changes what readers expect of the figures.

The severity gap between the two terms is very wide, so applying the graver word to a threshold-level contraction inflates the claim rather than sharpening it.

**B) "Famine" is a technical classification requiring measured thresholds of hunger, malnutrition and mortality while "food insecurity" covers a much wider range of shortage, so a region can be severely food-insecure without a famine being declared.**

Famine declarations rest on measured criteria: proportions of households facing extreme food gaps, rates of acute malnutrition in children, and deaths per ten thousand people per day. Food insecurity is a graded concept running from anxiety about the next meal to emergency conditions, and most of that range never approaches the declaration threshold. Agencies keep the stronger word rare so that it retains its power to mobilise a response.

A measured threshold sits above a broad continuum, and the sentence places the region below that threshold while acknowledging real hardship, which is how the classification is meant to be used.

**C) "Refugee" is a legal status held by someone unable to return home for fear of persecution while "migrant" describes movement without saying anything about status, so every refugee is a migrant though most migrants are not refugees.**

Migrant is the neutral umbrella term for anyone who moves across a border, whatever the reason and whatever their standing. Refugee is defined in international law by a well-founded fear of persecution and the impossibility of returning, and it brings protections and obligations that attach to no other traveller. The narrower category therefore sits inside the wider one and cannot be assigned by description alone.

A legal status nests inside a descriptive term, and the sentence runs the implication in the only direction that nesting permits, so it stands.

**D) "Displaced" households have been moved under an organised instruction from an authority, while "evacuated" ones have left of their own accord ahead of the danger.**

Evacuation is organised: an authority orders or arranges the movement, usually with transport, destinations and a return plan attached. Displacement describes people forced from their homes by conflict, disaster or persecution, whether or not anyone directed the movement, and it says nothing about assistance. Relief agencies count the displaced precisely because so many of them left without any authority to guide them.

The organised movement and the forced one have been attached to the wrong words, so the account fails — an authority evacuates residents, while conflict and flooding displace them.

**E) In an incident report "casualties" counts only those who died, while "fatalities" is the wider figure taking in the injured as well.**

Casualties is the inclusive count, covering everyone killed, injured or otherwise incapacitated in an event, which is why the figure is often broken down in the next line of a report. Fatalities is the narrow subset of deaths and is quoted separately when precision matters. Emergency services keep the two apart because triage, hospital capacity and investigation all depend on knowing how many survivors need care.

**Trap:** Headline coverage often reports casualties in a way that sounds like a death toll, which is exactly the confusion the sentence repeats.

The wider figure has been named as the narrower one, so the line does not hold — casualties include the injured, and fatalities count only the dead.
tasks.solution_overview: Crisis vocabulary is built on thresholds and legal definitions, so ask what test has to be met before each label can be used and how much of the situation the word actually covers. Several lines nest a narrow category inside a broad one, and the inference only runs upwards, from the specific status to the general description. Two lines reward attention to who organised the movement and to which count includes survivors.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five statements about the reporting verbs that signal how far a writer stands behind a claim or presses for a response. Decide whether each comparison is accurate.
statements: A journal that writes an author "claims" to have observed the effect is endorsing the observation, since "claim" and "report" are neutral equivalents in academic prose.

"Urge" presses for action with a note of insistence while "recommend" merely puts an option forward, so a safety committee that urges an immediate grounding of the fleet is doing more than recommending one.
"Caution" is the stronger of the two verbs, so a seismologist who cautions against building on the fault line is issuing a graver alert than one who warns against it.
"Acknowledge" concedes that a point exists without accepting it while "agree" signs up to it, so a paper can acknowledge an objection that it goes on to reject.
"Speculate" is the term for a formally testable proposal in a methods section, while "hypothesise" marks guesswork offered without supporting evidence.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A journal that writes an author "claims" to have observed the effect is endorsing the observation, since "claim" and "report" are neutral equivalents in academic prose.**

Report is the neutral verb: it passes on what was found and leaves the writer's own stance out of it. Claim distances the writer from the assertion, hinting that the evidence may not carry it, which is why editors query the verb when no scepticism is intended. The same sentence can therefore read as summary or as scepticism depending on which verb is chosen.

The distancing verb withholds exactly the endorsement the sentence attributes to it, so the line fails — writing that an author claims the observation signals reserve rather than agreement.

**B) "Urge" presses for action with a note of insistence while "recommend" merely puts an option forward, so a safety committee that urges an immediate grounding of the fleet is doing more than recommending one.**

Recommend offers a course of action for consideration and leaves the recipient comfortable in declining it. Urge adds pressure and usually urgency, implying that the writer regards inaction as unacceptable, which is why it appears in safety findings where lives are at stake. Regulators read the difference as a signal about how quickly they are expected to move.

Insistence is the extra ingredient the stronger verb supplies, and the grounding recommendation carries exactly that weight, so the comparison is sound.

**C) "Caution" is the stronger of the two verbs, so a seismologist who cautions against building on the fault line is issuing a graver alert than one who warns against it.**

Warn names a danger and asks for it to be avoided, and it is the verb used when the risk is definite and serious. Caution is the softer, more advisory choice, urging care rather than announcing a threat, which is why it pairs with restraint and with provisional findings. Hazard communication guidance ranks the two in that order for exactly this reason.

The intensities have been reversed, so the sentence does not hold — warning against building on the fault is the graver statement, and cautioning the milder one.

**D) "Acknowledge" concedes that a point exists without accepting it while "agree" signs up to it, so a paper can acknowledge an objection that it goes on to reject.**

Acknowledge registers something as present and worth addressing: an objection, a limitation, a competing result. Agree commits the writer to its truth and closes off the possibility of arguing against it a few lines later. Peer reviewers look for the first because a paper that never registers rival explanations reads as though it has not seen them.

Recognising a point and endorsing it are separate moves, and the sentence keeps the door open for the rebuttal that follows, which is standard practice in a discussion section.

**E) "Speculate" is the term for a formally testable proposal in a methods section, while "hypothesise" marks guesswork offered without supporting evidence.**

Hypothesise is the disciplined verb: it introduces a statement framed so that data could contradict it, and it belongs in the section where the study's predictions are set out. Speculate signals that the writer has moved beyond the evidence, which is why it appears late in a discussion, hedged and clearly flagged as going further than the results allow. Reviewers accept speculation in its proper place and object when it wears the other verb's clothes.

**Trap:** Both verbs introduce something unproven, which hides the fact that only one of them promises testability.

The roles have been exchanged, so the claim collapses — a methods section hypothesises, while a closing discussion speculates.
tasks.solution_overview: Reporting verbs carry a stance as well as a meaning, so ask how much distance or pressure each one adds to the same content. Two lines here concern the strength of an appeal or an alarm, and reversing the order of intensity is the easiest error to miss. The others reward asking whether a verb endorses a finding, keeps it at arm's length, or merely registers a point the writer intends to answer.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five statements about terms of art in contract and procedure, where a small difference in wording changes what a party may do. Decide whether each distinction is correctly drawn.
statements: A contract that is "void" never had legal effect while one that is "voidable" stands until the party entitled to set it aside actually does so, so a voidable agreement can be performed for years without difficulty.
"Rescinding" an instrument cancels it altogether while "varying" it leaves it in force on altered terms, so a regulator that varies a discharge licence has not rescinded it.
"Testimony" is the broader term covering documents, objects and expert reports, while "evidence" names only what a witness says aloud in the hearing.
A judgment cited as "persuasive" authority may be followed while a "binding" precedent must be, so a court can admire a decision from another jurisdiction and still decline to apply it.
"Compensate" pays for a loss that has already occurred while "indemnify" promises in advance to cover a loss if it arises, so an indemnity in a museum's loan agreement may never be called on at all.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A contract that is "void" never had legal effect while one that is "voidable" stands until the party entitled to set it aside actually does so, so a voidable agreement can be performed for years without difficulty.**

A void agreement is a nullity from the outset: no obligations ever arose, and no act by the parties can breathe life into it. A voidable agreement is valid and enforceable unless and until the protected party elects to avoid it, which is the position where consent was obtained by misrepresentation or where a party lacked capacity. That election can be delayed, and it can be lost by affirmation.

Existing from the start and lasting until someone objects are quite different legal states, so the sentence is right that a voidable bargain can run its course untroubled.

**B) "Rescinding" an instrument cancels it altogether while "varying" it leaves it in force on altered terms, so a regulator that varies a discharge licence has not rescinded it.**

Rescission ends the instrument, and the holder is left with no permission at all, which is why the power usually attracts notice requirements and a right of appeal. Variation adjusts what the instrument permits, tightening a limit or changing a monitoring condition while the permission itself survives. Environmental regulators rely on variation as the ordinary tool of enforcement, keeping rescission for serious or repeated breach.

Amending a permission and withdrawing it are different exercises of power with different consequences for the holder, so the sentence separates them correctly.

**C) "Testimony" is the broader term covering documents, objects and expert reports, while "evidence" names only what a witness says aloud in the hearing.**

Evidence is the general category: anything a tribunal may receive to prove a fact, including documents, physical exhibits, recordings, admissions and the accounts of witnesses. Testimony is the narrow species consisting of what a witness states, whether orally or in a sworn statement adopted at the hearing. The nesting runs from the general to the particular, not the other way round.

The categories have been inverted, so the line does not hold — testimony is one form of evidence, and evidence takes in every exhibit besides.

**D) A judgment cited as "persuasive" authority may be followed while a "binding" precedent must be, so a court can admire a decision from another jurisdiction and still decline to apply it.**

Binding precedent operates through the court hierarchy: a decision of a superior court on the same point obliges the lower court to follow it whatever the judge thinks of the reasoning. Persuasive authority carries only the weight of its argument, and it includes decisions of foreign courts, of courts at the same level and of bodies with no jurisdiction over the matter at all. Judgments regularly praise reasoning they are free to set aside.

Obligation and influence are separate sources of authority, and the sentence lets admiration stop short of compulsion, exactly as the doctrine allows.

**E) "Compensate" pays for a loss that has already occurred while "indemnify" promises in advance to cover a loss if it arises, so an indemnity in a museum's loan agreement may never be called on at all.**

Compensation responds to something that has happened and is measured against the loss suffered. An indemnity is a forward-looking allocation of risk: one party undertakes to bear specified losses should they occur, and the undertaking has value from the moment it is given, whether or not anything goes wrong. Lending institutions insist on it precisely because the harm they fear is unlikely but ruinous.

Payment after the event and a promise made before it are different commitments, so an unused indemnity is a working clause rather than a dead one, just as the sentence suggests.
tasks.solution_overview: Terms of art in procedure and contract describe what a party may do next, so translate each pair into consequences: no obligation ever arose against one that can be undone, permission withdrawn against permission altered, obligation to follow against freedom to be convinced. Where one word names a category and the other a member of it, check which way the nesting runs before accepting the definition. The final line rewards noticing whether a promise looks backwards at a loss or forwards at a risk.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five statements about words whose specialist senses cut across, or even reverse, what a general reader would expect. Judge whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Sanction" can both authorise and punish, so an ethics committee that sanctions a trial has approved it while a state under sanctions is being penalised, and only the surrounding words separate the senses.
In British parliamentary usage "tabling" a motion puts it forward for debate while the American sense sets it aside, so the same verb reports opposite fates for a proposal depending on the chamber.
In reactor physics "critical" names the steady self-sustaining state rather than a dangerous one, so a reactor reported as having gone critical is running exactly as designed.
A "positive" laboratory result reports that the target was detected rather than that the news is good, so a positive result on a tuberculosis test is the one a patient least wants to hear.
A "conservative" estimate in a risk assessment is one deliberately set to understate the benefit or overstate the danger, so the word marks caution in the arithmetic rather than a political leaning.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Sanction" can both authorise and punish, so an ethics committee that sanctions a trial has approved it while a state under sanctions is being penalised, and only the surrounding words separate the senses.**

As a verb with a person or body as subject, sanction usually means to give official approval, which is how it appears in ethics, licensing and church usage. As a plural noun in international relations it means the penalties imposed to coerce a state, and the verb has followed the noun into that sense as well. Nothing in the word itself resolves the ambiguity, so readers rely on the object and the setting.

**Tip:** Approval takes a singular verb and an institution behind it; punishment almost always arrives in the plural.

A single word carrying opposite forces is unusual but real, and the sentence names the two contexts that keep them apart, so the description is accurate.

**B) In British parliamentary usage "tabling" a motion puts it forward for debate while the American sense sets it aside, so the same verb reports opposite fates for a proposal depending on the chamber.**

At Westminster, tabling means placing an item on the table of the House so that it enters the order of business, which is a step towards discussion. In American legislative practice, a motion to table postpones consideration indefinitely and is a recognised way of killing a proposal without a vote on its merits. Reporters covering both systems have to be explicit, since the bare verb tells a reader nothing about the outcome.

One convention advances a proposal and the other shelves it, so the sentence is right that the verb's meaning depends entirely on which chamber is speaking.

**C) In reactor physics "critical" names the steady self-sustaining state rather than a dangerous one, so a reactor reported as having gone critical is running exactly as designed.**

A reactor is critical when each generation of fissions produces exactly one further fission on average, so the chain reaction sustains itself at a constant power. Subcritical means the reaction is dying away and supercritical that power is rising, which is a normal condition during start-up. The everyday sense of critical as perilous belongs to a different family of uses and misleads badly in this context.

**Trap:** News coverage often treats going critical as an emergency, which reverses the meaning the operators intend.

Steady operation rather than crisis is what the physics term reports, so the sentence describes the technical usage correctly.

**D) A "positive" laboratory result reports that the target was detected rather than that the news is good, so a positive result on a tuberculosis test is the one a patient least wants to hear.**

In diagnostics positive and negative describe the presence or absence of the analyte the assay looks for, and they carry no evaluation whatever. The ordinary senses of the two words point in the opposite direction, which is why clinicians take care when giving results and why patient information leaflets often spell out what each term means. The same reversal appears in screening, toxicology and microbiology.

Detection and desirability are separate matters, so the sentence is right that the technically positive result is the unwelcome one.

**E) A "conservative" estimate in a risk assessment is one deliberately set to understate the benefit or overstate the danger, so the word marks caution in the arithmetic rather than a political leaning.**

In assessment work a conservative assumption is one chosen to err on the safe side, so that if the estimate is wrong it is wrong in the direction that protects people. That may mean assuming the worst plausible exposure, the shortest tolerable margin or the least favourable weather. The political sense of the adjective is entirely unrelated and never governs its use in a technical annex.

Erring towards safety is the whole content of the term here, so the sentence separates the methodological sense from the political one exactly as a risk assessor would.
tasks.solution_overview: Specialist registers sometimes keep a sense that ordinary usage has lost or reversed, so read each line for the setting that fixes the meaning: a committee, a chamber, a control room, a laboratory or a risk annex. Ask what the word is doing for the professional who chose it rather than what it suggests to a general reader. Where a term seems alarming or evaluative, check whether the technical use is in fact neutral or even reassuring.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five statements about adjectives of praise and reproach that are close enough in form or sense to be exchanged by mistake. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Iconic" claims that an image has come to stand for something beyond itself while "celebrated" claims only wide admiration, so a photograph can be celebrated for decades without ever becoming iconic.
"Seminal" merely records that a paper has been widely read, so any heavily cited study can properly be called seminal.
"Ingenuous" describes clever contrivance, so an ingenuous solution to a drainage problem is the inventive one.
A witness described as "credulous" is one whose account the tribunal found believable.

"Eccentric" reports a harmless departure from the norm while "erratic" reports unpredictable variation that undermines reliance, so an eccentric filing system is a curiosity and an erratic one is a problem.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Iconic" claims that an image has come to stand for something beyond itself while "celebrated" claims only wide admiration, so a photograph can be celebrated for decades without ever becoming iconic.**

Celebrated is a measure of reputation: the work is widely known and widely praised. Iconic makes a stronger and stranger claim, that the image now functions as a sign for an event, a person or an era, so that showing it evokes the whole thing it condenses. Plenty of admired photographs never acquire that representative function, which is why the words are not interchangeable however loosely the second is used.

Standing for something and being admired are different achievements, and the sentence lets a picture reach the second without the first, which is the honest description of most famous images.

**B) "Seminal" merely records that a paper has been widely read, so any heavily cited study can properly be called seminal.**
