Seminal means generative: the work opened a line of inquiry, supplied the framework or method that others then built on, and the field looks different afterwards. Citation counts measure attention, and a paper can accumulate thousands of references as a convenient source of data or as a standing target for criticism. Influence and originating power are related but not the same, which is why review articles distinguish foundational studies from heavily cited ones.

Being read widely is not the same as founding a line of work, so the equivalence fails — a much-cited paper is influential, and only a paper that started something is seminal.

**C) "Ingenuous" describes clever contrivance, so an ingenuous solution to a drainage problem is the inventive one.**

Ingenious is the adjective for cleverness and inventive design, and it is the one an engineer would want attached to a scheme. Ingenuous means artless, open and unguarded, describing a person too candid to suspect deception, and it survives most visibly in its negative form disingenuous, meaning insincere. The two differ by a letter and by nearly everything else.

**Trap:** The pair looks like a spelling variant, which is exactly how the wrong one slips into technical prose.

The adjective for inventiveness is the other member of the pair, so the sentence does not hold — the clever scheme is "an ingenious solution to a drainage problem."

**D) A witness described as "credulous" is one whose account the tribunal found believable.**

Credible describes the account or the person as worthy of belief, and it is the word a tribunal uses when it accepts what it has heard. Credulous describes someone too ready to believe others, which is a comment on the witness's judgement and, if anything, a reason to treat their account with care. The suffixes divide the pair neatly once noticed: one invites belief, the other extends it too freely.

Being believed and being easily taken in are opposite postures, so the description misfires — a witness the tribunal accepted would be called credible.

**E) "Eccentric" reports a harmless departure from the norm while "erratic" reports unpredictable variation that undermines reliance, so an eccentric filing system is a curiosity and an erratic one is a problem.**

Eccentric marks something as unusual and consistently so: the archivist's scheme may be idiosyncratic, but it follows its own rules and can be learnt. Erratic marks the absence of any stable pattern, so users cannot predict what will happen next, and that unpredictability is what makes it a fault rather than a quirk. Consistency is precisely what one word preserves and the other denies.

Oddness and unreliability are separate charges, and the sentence keeps the tolerable one apart from the disabling one, so the contrast is well drawn.
tasks.solution_overview: These adjectives sit close enough to be swapped, so paraphrase each one before testing the example: standing for something rather than merely admired, originating a field rather than widely cited, inventive rather than artless, believed rather than too ready to believe. Two of the lines rely on near-identical spellings, and the surest check is to recall the negative or related form that fixes the meaning. Where a sentence flatters a work or a witness, ask whether the compliment being paid is the one the adjective actually confers.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five statements about adjectives built from the same root that have settled into different jobs. Judge whether each account of the pair is accurate.
statements: "Systematic" describes a fault that runs through an entire structure while "systemic" describes something carried out methodically, step by step.
"Continuous" claims an unbroken run while "continual" allows gaps between repetitions, so a station that records continuously is doing something different from one that is continually being repaired.
"Historic" marks importance in history while "historical" merely places something in the past, so a historical drought recorded in tree rings need not have been a historic one.

"Classical" ties a work to the Greek and Roman world or to a defined period style while "classic" claims enduring exemplary status, so a classic recording of a classical symphony is not a redundant phrase.
"Liquidity" and "solvency" describe the same financial condition, so a firm whose assets comfortably exceed its liabilities can never run short of cash.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Systematic" describes a fault that runs through an entire structure while "systemic" describes something carried out methodically, step by step.**

Systematic describes method: a systematic review, a systematic search, a systematic error that arises from a consistent procedure. Systemic describes the system itself: a systemic weakness affects the whole body, network or institution rather than one part of it. Medicine keeps the second for effects that spread beyond a local site, and the distinction has carried into writing about institutions and finance.

The two definitions have been exchanged, so the line fails — a weakness running through an institution is systemic, while an orderly procedure is systematic.

**B) "Continuous" claims an unbroken run while "continual" allows gaps between repetitions, so a station that records continuously is doing something different from one that is continually being repaired.**

Continuous describes something without interruption in time or space: an unbroken data series, a continuous surface, a continuous supply. Continual describes something that recurs often, with intervals in between, and it frequently carries a note of irritation about the repetition. A logger sampling every second all year is continuous; a run of breakdowns spread across that year is continual.

Unbroken duration and frequent repetition are different patterns, and the sentence gives each adjective the pattern that belongs to it, so the distinction stands.

**C) "Historic" marks importance in history while "historical" merely places something in the past, so a historical drought recorded in tree rings need not have been a historic one.**

Historic singles out events, buildings and moments judged significant enough to be remembered: a historic ruling, a historic site. Historical is the neutral classifier, covering anything belonging to or concerned with the past, including historical records, historical fiction and historical climate data. Almost everything historical fails to be historic, which is why the pair repays care in headlines.

Significance and mere pastness are different claims, and the tree-ring example accepts the second while withholding the first, so the sentence works.

**D) "Classical" ties a work to the Greek and Roman world or to a defined period style while "classic" claims enduring exemplary status, so a classic recording of a classical symphony is not a redundant phrase.**

Classical points at a tradition or period: classical antiquity, classical architecture, and in music the style of the later eighteenth century, though the word is also used loosely for the whole art-music tradition. Classic is an evaluation, marking something as a standard of its kind that has lasted. One phrase therefore names what the symphony is and the other names how the performance is regarded.

Period and verdict are separate pieces of information, so the double description the sentence defends carries two distinct claims rather than one repeated.

**E) "Liquidity" and "solvency" describe the same financial condition, so a firm whose assets comfortably exceed its liabilities can never run short of cash.**

Solvency compares what is owned with what is owed and is a statement about the balance sheet as a whole. Liquidity concerns the ability to meet obligations as they fall due, which depends on how quickly assets can be turned into cash without loss. A business holding valuable property, long-dated receivables or specialised plant can be comfortably solvent and still unable to pay next week's bills.

**Trap:** Both words sound like general financial health, which hides that one measures the stock of value and the other the timing of cash.

A strong balance sheet does not guarantee cash on the day it is needed, so the inference fails — solvency and liquidity are tested separately for precisely that reason.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjective pairs from one root usually divide between a neutral classifier and an evaluative or structural partner, so ask what job each form has taken on. Method against whole-system reach, unbroken against repeated, past against significant, period against verdict: naming the axis first makes a swapped definition easy to see. The financial line works the same way, dividing what a balance sheet shows from what can actually be paid on the day.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five statements about the vocabulary of research ethics and data protection, where each term carries a duty or a safeguard. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: Data described as "pseudonymised" has had every identifier destroyed and cannot be re-linked, which is why regulators treat it exactly as they treat anonymised data.
In research ethics a child gives "consent" while the parent provides "assent" on the child's behalf.
A survey promised to be "confidential" is one in which answers were never linked to names in the first place, which is precisely what "anonymous" also means.

In data-protection reporting an "incident" is any suspected event while a "breach" is the narrower category that triggers a duty to notify, so a laptop briefly mislaid may be logged as an incident without ever becoming a reportable breach.
Files "deleted" from a drive are physically overwritten, which is why deletion and secure erasure are treated as equivalent in equipment disposal policies.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Data described as "pseudonymised" has had every identifier destroyed and cannot be re-linked, which is why regulators treat it exactly as they treat anonymised data.**

Pseudonymisation replaces direct identifiers with a code while a key is kept elsewhere, so the link back to individuals still exists and the data remain personal data with all the obligations that follow. Anonymisation removes that possibility altogether, and only then do the protection rules fall away. The whole point of the intermediate category is that re-identification is possible for those holding the key.

**Trap:** Both terms describe removing names from a dataset, which makes it easy to miss that only one of them destroys the route back.

A surviving key is exactly what distinguishes the weaker safeguard, so the equivalence fails — pseudonymised records remain personal data and stay inside the regime.

**B) In research ethics a child gives "consent" while the parent provides "assent" on the child's behalf.**

Consent is the legally effective authorisation, and for a child it is given by a parent or guardian with the capacity to grant it. Assent is the child's own agreement to take part, sought as a matter of respect even though it carries no legal force on its own, and a refusal to assent is generally honoured. Ethics committees ask for both because the two answer different questions about the child's participation.

The legal authorisation and the child's own agreement have been swapped, so the line does not hold — the parent consents while the child assents.

**C) A survey promised to be "confidential" is one in which answers were never linked to names in the first place, which is precisely what "anonymous" also means.**

An anonymous survey collects no identifying information at all, so not even the researchers can say who returned which questionnaire. A confidential survey may know exactly who said what and undertakes not to disclose it outside the study team, which is what allows follow-up, linkage to records and withdrawal of a specific response. Participant information sheets separate the two because the promises differ in what they can guarantee.

Not collecting identities and promising not to reveal them are different undertakings, so the equation fails — confidentiality protects information the study still holds.

**D) In data-protection reporting an "incident" is any suspected event while a "breach" is the narrower category that triggers a duty to notify, so a laptop briefly mislaid may be logged as an incident without ever becoming a reportable breach.**

Incident is the operational catch-all: anything that might have compromised information gets logged, assessed and closed, and most entries turn out to be nothing. Breach is the defined category involving unauthorised access, loss, alteration or disclosure of personal data, and once it is established the clock starts on notifying the regulator and possibly the individuals affected. Encryption and prompt recovery are exactly the factors that keep an event on the lower rung.

Logging everything and notifying the regulator are different obligations, so the mislaid laptop the sentence describes can indeed stop at the first, which is how incident registers work.

**E) Files "deleted" from a drive are physically overwritten, which is why deletion and secure erasure are treated as equivalent in equipment disposal policies.**

Ordinary deletion removes the pointer to the file and marks the space as available, leaving the content in place until something else happens to write over it, which is why recovery tools succeed so often. Secure erasure overwrites the storage, issues a sanitise command or destroys the key that makes encrypted data readable, and it is verified before a device leaves the building. Disposal policies specify the second precisely because the first is not a safeguard.

Removing a reference and destroying the data are different operations, so the sentence collapses a distinction that disposal procedures exist to maintain.
tasks.solution_overview: Every term here corresponds to a duty, so ask what a regulator or an ethics committee could still require once the word applies. Two lines turn on whether a link back to an individual survives, one on who is legally entitled to authorise participation, and one on whether the data have actually gone. Where a sentence claims two safeguards are equivalent, look for the residue the weaker one leaves behind.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five statements about words that differ by a syllable and by their entire evaluative force. Judge whether each description matches careful usage.
statements: A "venial" official is one open to bribery, while a "venal" fault is a minor one that can readily be excused.
"Luxuriant" describes abundant growth while "luxurious" describes costly comfort, so a luxuriant hedge says nothing about the wealth of the house behind it.

"Officious" condemns someone for asserting authority beyond what the role requires while "official" merely marks the authority as formal, so a request from the registry is neutral where an officious clerk is being criticised.
"Human" classifies while "humane" evaluates, so a mistake can be entirely human without the treatment that followed it being humane.
"Momentary" measures duration while "momentous" measures importance, so a momentary lapse at the signal box can prove momentous.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "venial" official is one open to bribery, while a "venal" fault is a minor one that can readily be excused.**

Venal comes from the language of things for sale and describes people who can be bought: a venal inspector, venal patronage, venal journalism. Venial belongs to the vocabulary of sin and describes an offence slight enough to be forgiven, which is why it pairs with fault, error and transgression. The pair differs by one letter and by the whole weight of the accusation.

**Tip:** Venal keeps the sense of vendor, while venial keeps the sense of pardon.

The corruptible person and the pardonable slip have been attached to the wrong adjectives, so the sentence fails — a bought official is venal and a forgivable error venial.

**B) "Luxuriant" describes abundant growth while "luxurious" describes costly comfort, so a luxuriant hedge says nothing about the wealth of the house behind it.**

Luxuriant reports thick, vigorous, profuse growth and belongs with vegetation, hair and prose that runs to excess. Luxurious reports expense and comfort and belongs with fabrics, hotels and interiors. The shared root in abundance explains the confusion, but a botanical survey using the second word would be commenting on the furnishings rather than the plants.

Growth and expenditure are separate things to be abundant in, and the sentence keeps the hedge on the botanical side of the pair, so it holds.

**C) "Officious" condemns someone for asserting authority beyond what the role requires while "official" merely marks the authority as formal, so a request from the registry is neutral where an officious clerk is being criticised.**

Official is descriptive: the act comes from an office, carries its sanction and appears on its paper. Officious is a reproach, describing someone who interferes, insists on formalities nobody needed and enjoys the small exercise of power. The words share an origin in office and have diverged entirely in tone, one neutral and one hostile.

Description and reproach sit on different sides of this pair, and the sentence attaches the criticism to the person rather than to the paperwork, which is where careful usage places it.

**D) "Human" classifies while "humane" evaluates, so a mistake can be entirely human without the treatment that followed it being humane.**

Human assigns something to the species or to the ordinary condition of people, which is why human error names a category of cause rather than a verdict on anyone. Humane praises conduct as compassionate and marks a standard that can be met or missed, as in humane treatment or humane conditions of detention. An inquiry can accept the first about the cause and still find the second lacking in the response.

Category and standard are answered by different findings, so the sentence is right that recognising an ordinary human failure settles nothing about how people were then treated.

**E) "Momentary" measures duration while "momentous" measures importance, so a momentary lapse at the signal box can prove momentous.**

Momentary means lasting only a moment and says nothing about consequence. Momentous derives from the sense of moment as weight or significance, and it describes decisions, occasions and turning points whose effects are large. Because one measures time and the other measures weight, a very short event can score at the top of the second scale.

Duration and significance are independent, and the sentence uses that independence to make its point rather than tripping over it, so the line is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjectives that differ by a syllable often differ by their entire verdict, so recover the root sense behind each form before judging the example. Ask whether a word describes something for sale or something forgivable, growth or expense, an office or an overreach, a category or a standard, a duration or a weight. Reading each adjective into a sentence of praise and then into a complaint shows quickly which one the writer actually needed.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five statements about verbs and labels that differ over how completely something has been displaced, or over who brought the change about. Decide whether each is accurate.
statements: "Obviate" says a need has been removed altogether rather than merely lessened, so a gravity-fed bypass channel that obviates the need for pumping does more than reduce it.
"Subside" describes something settling of its own accord while "abate" can be brought about by intervention, so a storm subsides while a statutory nuisance is abated by an order.

In corporate reporting a "merger" describes two firms combining into a new entity while an "acquisition" describes one absorbing another, so a deal announced as a merger of equals is often an acquisition in substance.

"Supersede" claims the newer item has displaced the older by authority rather than merely standing in for it, so a revised standard supersedes its predecessor while a stand-in lecturer only replaces a colleague.
"Denote" names what a word points to while "connote" names what it suggests alongside, so "thrifty" and "stingy" can denote the same behaviour and connote opposite judgements.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Obviate" says a need has been removed altogether rather than merely lessened, so a gravity-fed bypass channel that obviates the need for pumping does more than reduce it.**

Obviate means to make something unnecessary, so what follows the verb is a requirement, a difficulty or a risk that no longer has to be dealt with at all. Reduce leaves the requirement in place at a smaller scale, which means pumps must still be bought, maintained and powered. A channel driven by gravity removes the requirement rather than shrinking it, and the capital and running costs disappear with it.

Removing a requirement and shrinking one lead to different designs and different budgets, so the sentence is right to rank the verb above mere reduction.

**B) "Subside" describes something settling of its own accord while "abate" can be brought about by intervention, so a storm subsides while a statutory nuisance is abated by an order.**

Subside is intransitive and agentless: floodwater, swelling and unrest all subside without anyone acting on them. Abate works both ways, so a fever may abate on its own while an authority abates a nuisance by serving a notice and, if necessary, doing the work itself. That transitive use is why abatement appears as a legal term while subsidence never does in this sense.

**Tip:** If you can name someone who did it, the verb has to be the one that takes an object.

One verb admits an agent and the other does not, and the sentence gives the weather the agentless verb and the authority the active one, so the pairing is correct.

**C) In corporate reporting a "merger" describes two firms combining into a new entity while an "acquisition" describes one absorbing another, so a deal announced as a merger of equals is often an acquisition in substance.**

A merger implies parity: the businesses combine, and neither is presented as the survivor swallowing the other. An acquisition names a buyer and a target, and the target's identity, board and often its name disappear into the purchaser. Because the softer word helps with staff, customers and regulators, deals are frequently announced as mergers when the balance of control says otherwise.

Parity and absorption are different structures behind the same headline, and the sentence is right that the label chosen often reflects presentation rather than the substance of control.

**D) "Supersede" claims the newer item has displaced the older by authority rather than merely standing in for it, so a revised standard supersedes its predecessor while a stand-in lecturer only replaces a colleague.**

Supersede carries the sense of sitting above: the new version takes over the authority of the old, which is withdrawn and should no longer be cited or applied. Replace is neutral about authority and covers any substitution, temporary or permanent, of one thing or person for another. Standards bodies use the stronger verb because the earlier document ceases to be current on the day the new one issues.

Displacement by authority and simple substitution are different relationships between old and new, and the sentence assigns each verb to the case it fits, so the line holds.

**E) "Denote" names what a word points to while "connote" names what it suggests alongside, so "thrifty" and "stingy" can denote the same behaviour and connote opposite judgements.**

Denotation is the referential core: the class of things or the behaviour a term picks out, which is what a dictionary's first definition tries to capture. Connotation is the freight the word carries with it, the approval, disapproval, formality or warmth that comes along for the ride. Near-synonyms typically share the first and differ in the second, which is exactly why choosing between them is a choice about attitude.

Reference and overtone are separate layers of meaning, and the pair the sentence offers demonstrates the split it describes, so the account is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Ask two questions of each line: how much of the original has been displaced, and who did the displacing. Removing a requirement outranks shrinking it, taking over by authority outranks standing in, and combining as equals is a different structure from being absorbed. Where a verb can appear with or without an agent, check that the sentence has supplied one for the transitive use and none for the intransitive.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: Five statements about words whose established senses are regularly reversed in careless use. Decide whether each account of the settled meaning is accurate.
statements: "Flaunt" means to treat a rule with open contempt, which is why a laboratory that ignores its containment protocol is said to flaunt it.

"Elicit" reports drawing something out deliberately, usually by asking, while "evoke" reports calling a feeling or memory into being, so an interviewer elicits a date while a photograph evokes a decade.
"Reticent" describes unwillingness to speak while "reluctant" describes unwillingness to act, so a witness can be reluctant to attend an inquiry and perfectly forthcoming once there.
"Fulsome" in careful use marks praise as excessive to the point of insincerity, so a reviewer who calls an acknowledgement fulsome is not paying a compliment.
"Enervate" means to fill with energy, so a bracing walk across the moor enervates the hikers who take it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Flaunt" means to treat a rule with open contempt, which is why a laboratory that ignores its containment protocol is said to flaunt it.**

Flout is the verb for defying a rule, a convention or an order in a way that makes no attempt at concealment. Flaunt means to display something ostentatiously, so what follows it is normally a possession, a talent or wealth rather than a regulation. The confusion is common enough to be listed in every usage guide, and it survives because both verbs suggest a kind of brazenness.

**Trap:** Both words carry an air of showing off, which is why the wrong one slips easily into a sentence about broken rules.

Open defiance belongs to the other verb, so the sentence does not hold — a laboratory that ignores containment rules is flouting them.

**B) "Elicit" reports drawing something out deliberately, usually by asking, while "evoke" reports calling a feeling or memory into being, so an interviewer elicits a date while a photograph evokes a decade.**

Elicit requires an agent working on a source: questions elicit answers, prompts elicit responses, and the object is usually information or a reaction that was there to be drawn out. Evoke needs no questioner and works on the audience, summoning associations, atmospheres and memories that were not being asked for. One is extraction, the other suggestion.

Deliberate extraction and spontaneous summoning are different operations, and the sentence gives the questioner the first verb and the image the second, so the distribution is right.

**C) "Reticent" describes unwillingness to speak while "reluctant" describes unwillingness to act, so a witness can be reluctant to attend an inquiry and perfectly forthcoming once there.**

Reticent is specifically about speech: the reticent person keeps their views, feelings or information to themselves. Reluctant is general unwillingness and takes any action as its complement, from attending to signing to agreeing. The two have converged in loose usage, but the narrower word loses its usefulness once it is allowed to cover every hesitation.

Speech and action are separate things to withhold, and the sentence separates them with a witness who resists one and not the other, so the contrast is well made.

**D) "Fulsome" in careful use marks praise as excessive to the point of insincerity, so a reviewer who calls an acknowledgement fulsome is not paying a compliment.**

The established sense of fulsome is cloying and overdone, which is why fulsome praise traditionally means flattery rather than generous appreciation. The word is now widely used to mean full or lavish in a positive spirit, and that use is spreading, but in edited prose the pejorative reading remains live enough to make the word risky. A reviewer who reaches for it is commenting on excess.

**Tip:** Where a compliment is intended, generous or wholehearted removes the ambiguity that fulsome introduces.

Excess rather than warmth is what the careful sense reports, so the sentence describes the usage correctly.

**E) "Enervate" means to fill with energy, so a bracing walk across the moor enervates the hikers who take it.**

Enervate means to drain of strength and vitality, leaving someone weakened and listless; heat, illness and long confinement enervate. The resemblance to energise is entirely misleading, since the root concerns the removal of sinew rather than the supply of energy. A walk that leaves hikers refreshed calls for the opposite verb.

The verb reports depletion rather than supply, so the sentence inverts it — a bracing walk invigorates the hikers, while a week of humid heat would enervate them.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line offers a definition that either matches the settled sense or reverses it, so state the meaning yourself before reading the example attached to it. Ask whether the verb defies or displays, extracts or suggests, withholds speech or withholds action, and drains or supplies. Where two words look or sound alike, the root is usually the fastest guide back to the sense a careful editor would defend.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five lines name the noun that a verb or an adjective is supposed to yield. Decide whether the form quoted is the one English actually supplies for that slot.
statements: In a paper on peer review, the phrase "the journal's reliance on unpaid referees" uses "reliance", the act noun that "rely" yields with -ance, in the slot a possessive and a following "on" require.
In a museum report, the phrase "the restorative of the canvases took two years" uses "restorative", the noun that "restore" yields for the process of repairing a painting.
In a study of glacier retreat, the phrase "the observance of the ice front over ten years" uses "observance", the noun English forms from "observe" for the act of watching something closely.
In a clinical trial report, the phrase "the site's compliancy with the protocol" uses "compliancy", the standard noun English forms from "comply" for conformity with a rule.
In a history of printing, the phrase "the diffuseness of movable type across Europe" uses "diffuseness", the noun that names the spread of a technology from one region to another.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a paper on peer review, the phrase "the journal's reliance on unpaid referees" uses "reliance", the act noun that "rely" yields with -ance, in the slot a possessive and a following "on" require.**

The verb "rely" gives "reliance" for the act of depending on something, while the rival noun "reliability" is built one step further out, on the adjective "reliable", and names a quality instead. Only the act noun inherits the preposition "on" from the verb, which is exactly what the frame "the journal's ... on unpaid referees" needs. Swapping in the quality noun would claim that the referees are dependable, a different assertion from the one the paper is making.

An act noun that carries its verb's preposition into the slot is precisely what this sentence is built around, so the wording is sound.

**B) In a museum report, the phrase "the restorative of the canvases took two years" uses "restorative", the noun that "restore" yields for the process of repairing a painting.**

"Restore" does produce "restorative", but the -ative ending makes an adjective of function, and where it works as a noun it names a tonic rather than a programme of work. The process noun in this family is "restoration", formed with -ation, and that is what a determiner plus an of-phrase calls for here. Conservation departments accordingly date restorations, never restoratives.

The two-year programme the report is dating has a noun of its own, so the line cannot stand as written: "the restoration of the canvases took two years".

**C) In a study of glacier retreat, the phrase "the observance of the ice front over ten years" uses "observance", the noun English forms from "observe" for the act of watching something closely.**

"Observe" splits its nouns by sense: "observation" covers watching and measuring, while "observance" covers the keeping of a rule, a custom or a holy day. A decade of measurement at an ice front belongs squarely to the first sense, so the -ance form imports an idea of ritual compliance that has no place in glaciology. The two nouns are not interchangeable even though they share a verb.

Watching and measuring is what the study describes, and that sense has its own noun, so the phrase fails: "the observation of the ice front over ten years".

**D) In a clinical trial report, the phrase "the site's compliancy with the protocol" uses "compliancy", the standard noun English forms from "comply" for conformity with a rule.**

Where -ance and -ancy compete, English usually keeps the -ance form for the act or state and lets the -ancy form drift towards a disposition of character. "Comply" follows the pattern: regulators write about compliance with a protocol, whereas "compliancy" survives only in the rare sense of a readiness to give way. The trial report is describing conformity to written procedure, not a temperament.

Conformity to a protocol has a settled noun in regulated research, so the -ancy form misses it: "the site's compliance with the protocol".

**E) In a history of printing, the phrase "the diffuseness of movable type across Europe" uses "diffuseness", the noun that names the spread of a technology from one region to another.**

"Diffuseness" is built on the adjective "diffuse" and names a quality, most often the wordiness of prose that spreads itself too thin. The spread of a technology across a continent is "diffusion", the -ion noun of the verb "diffuse", which historians use for exactly this movement of techniques and ideas. Adjective-based quality nouns and verb-based process nouns are not interchangeable simply because they share a stem.

A quality noun cannot carry a process that travelled across Europe over decades, so the phrase needs the verbal noun: "the diffusion of movable type across Europe".
tasks.solution_overview: Every line here offers a real English word, so the question is never whether the form exists but whether it is the member of the family the sentence needs. Sort the act nouns from the quality nouns, and remember that several bases split their meanings across two rival endings: reliance against reliability, observation against observance, diffusion against diffuseness. Read the frame first, since a possessive or a following of-phrase usually tells you whether an act, a state or a product is wanted.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Each line chooses one adjective out of a competing pair. Judge whether the sense and the stem allow the form that has been picked.
statements: In an essay on quantum theory, the phrase "the historic development of the field between 1900 and 1930" uses "historic" in its ordinary sense of belonging to the past.
In a review of a new Homer translation, the phrase "the translator's classic training in Greek metre" uses "classic" to mean of ancient Greece and Rome.
In a report on flood defences, the phrase "the estuary is navigatable by shallow craft" uses "navigatable", the adjective English builds from the verb "navigate" with -able.
In an ethics paper, the phrase "a distinction that is not defensible on utilitarian grounds" uses "defensible", the -ible adjective English takes from the Latin stem defens- of "defend".
In a report on a vaccine trial, the phrase "the second study was confirmatory rather than exploratory" uses "confirmatory", an adjective of function built from "confirm" on its Latin stem.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In an essay on quantum theory, the phrase "the historic development of the field between 1900 and 1930" uses "historic" in its ordinary sense of belonging to the past.**

The pair "historic" and "historical" divides a single base between two endings: -ic marks something famous enough to make history, and -ical marks anything that has to do with the past. An essay tracing how a field developed across three decades is doing plain historical work, however celebrated those decades were. Reserving the shorter form for landmark moments is what keeps the contrast usable.

The sentence describes a stretch of past time rather than a monument in it, so the shorter adjective misfires: "the historical development of the field between 1900 and 1930".

**B) In a review of a new Homer translation, the phrase "the translator's classic training in Greek metre" uses "classic" to mean of ancient Greece and Rome.**

"Classic" and "classical" have drifted apart: the first now means definitive or typical of its kind, while the second is the adjective that points to Greek and Roman antiquity, as in classical languages and classical archaeology. Training in Greek metre is training in antiquity, so the longer form is the one the review needs. A classic training would instead be an exemplary one, which says nothing about Homer.

Antiquity is what the reviewer means, and only one member of the pair carries that sense, so the line does not hold: "the translator's classical training in Greek metre".

**C) In a report on flood defences, the phrase "the estuary is navigatable by shallow craft" uses "navigatable", the adjective English builds from the verb "navigate" with -able.**

Verbs ending in -ate drop that ending before -able rather than keeping it, which is why "navigate" gives "navigable", "demonstrate" gives "demonstrable" and "tolerate" gives "tolerable". The truncation is regular enough to be predictable, and the untruncated forms sound unmistakably wrong to a fluent ear. Hydrographic writing has used the short form for centuries.

Adding -able to an -ate verb without cutting the stem is what goes wrong here, so the sentence needs the regular form: "the estuary is navigable by shallow craft".

**D) In an ethics paper, the phrase "a distinction that is not defensible on utilitarian grounds" uses "defensible", the -ible adjective English takes from the Latin stem defens- of "defend".**

English attaches -ible to Latin stems rather than to plain English verbs, so "defend" yields "defensible" through its stem defens-, just as "compress" yields "compressible" and "permit" yields "permissible". The form "defendable" survives for physical places that can be held, but an argument or a distinction is defensible. A predicative slot after "is not" wants precisely this adjective.

Latin stem plus -ible is the regular route for abstract argument, and this line follows it exactly, so the phrase stands as written.

**E) In a report on a vaccine trial, the phrase "the second study was confirmatory rather than exploratory" uses "confirmatory", an adjective of function built from "confirm" on its Latin stem.**

The ending -atory turns a Latin verb stem into an adjective meaning serving to do the thing named, so confirmat- gives "confirmatory" and explorat- gives "exploratory". Trial protocols lean on the contrast constantly: an exploratory study generates a hypothesis and a confirmatory one tests it. The linking verb "was" opens a predicative slot, which is where such adjectives belong.

Two adjectives of function set against each other is exactly the pairing the sentence needs, and both are correctly formed, so the wording holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Rival adjective endings rarely mean the same thing, so treat -ic against -ical, -able against -ible, and -ory against nothing at all as genuine choices rather than spelling variants. Ask what the sentence is actually claiming: a period of time wants the ending that means relating to history, while an ending that means momentous will not do. Where the base is a Latin verb, check the stem too, since -ate verbs shed their ending before -able and -ible attaches to stems in -s.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Five lines drop a member of a word family into a particular slot. Decide whether the form quoted is the part of speech the surrounding words demand.
statements: In a paper on Saharan reforestation, the phrase "the aridity of the plateau" uses "aridity", the noun the adjective "arid" yields with -ity, in the slot a determiner and an of-phrase open.
In a catalogue essay on a modernist painter, the phrase "her handling of pigment was highly innovation" uses "innovation" in the slot the sentence requires.
In a seismology bulletin, the phrase "the fault's quiescence since 1957" uses "quiescence", the noun formed from the adjective "quiescent" with -ence.
In a public-health briefing, the phrase "the vaccine's efficacious in the trial was 91 per cent" uses "efficacious" in the noun slot that the possessive opens.
In a bank's annual report, the phrase "the board questioned the sustainability of the payout ratio" uses "sustainability", a noun stacked on "sustain" by way of the adjective "sustainable".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a paper on Saharan reforestation, the phrase "the aridity of the plateau" uses "aridity", the noun the adjective "arid" yields with -ity, in the slot a determiner and an of-phrase open.**

The suffix -ity converts a Latinate adjective into an abstract noun naming its quality, so "arid" becomes "aridity" much as "dense" becomes "density" and "porous" becomes "porosity". The frame "the ... of the plateau" is a noun slot: a determiner in front, an of-phrase behind, and nowhere for an adjective to sit. Physical geography uses the noun as a technical measure of dryness.

Quality noun in a determiner-plus-of frame is a clean fit, so the phrase does what the paper needs it to do.

**B) In a catalogue essay on a modernist painter, the phrase "her handling of pigment was highly innovation" uses "innovation" in the slot the sentence requires.**

"Innovation" is the -ation noun of "innovate" and names the act or its product, whereas the adjective in the family is "innovative". The degree adverb "highly" can only modify a gradable adjective, and the linking verb "was" opens a predicative slot, so the sentence has two independent reasons for refusing a noun here. A noun could follow "was" only in an equative reading, which "highly" rules out.

Nothing gradable can be made of an act noun, so the catalogue sentence collapses as it stands: "her handling of pigment was highly innovative".

**C) In a seismology bulletin, the phrase "the fault's quiescence since 1957" uses "quiescence", the noun formed from the adjective "quiescent" with -ence.**

"Quiescent" is itself built on the Latin root qui- for rest with the inceptive -escent, and adjectives in -ent regularly convert to nouns in -ence: silent gives silence, prevalent gives prevalence. The possessive "the fault's" opens a noun slot, and the time adverbial "since 1957" attaches naturally to a state noun. Seismologists use the word for a period without recorded rupture.

An -ent adjective turning into its -ence noun in a possessive slot is textbook derivation, and the bulletin applies it correctly, so the phrase is sound.

**D) In a public-health briefing, the phrase "the vaccine's efficacious in the trial was 91 per cent" uses "efficacious" in the noun slot that the possessive opens.**

"Efficacious" is an adjective, and the noun the family supplies is "efficacy", formed with -acy and the loss of the adjectival -ious. The possessive "the vaccine's" plus a following prepositional phrase and a percentage figure demand a measurable noun, which no adjective can provide. Trial reports quote efficacy figures precisely because the noun names the quantity.

A percentage has to be predicated of a measure rather than of a quality word, so the briefing sentence fails: "the vaccine's efficacy in the trial was 91 per cent".

**E) In a bank's annual report, the phrase "the board questioned the sustainability of the payout ratio" uses "sustainability", a noun stacked on "sustain" by way of the adjective "sustainable".**

The word is built in two moves: -able turns the verb "sustain" into an adjective meaning able to be kept up, and -ity then turns that adjective into an abstract noun. Stacking in that order is what licenses the noun as the object of "questioned" and as the head before "of the payout ratio". Only the noun can be questioned; the adjective would need a subject to attach to.

Verb to adjective to noun is the route the slot requires, and the report follows it exactly, so the sentence works as written.
tasks.solution_overview: Read the frame before you read the word: a determiner or a possessive followed by an of-phrase opens a noun slot, and a degree adverb such as highly must be followed by a gradable adjective. Then check that the form quoted really carries the ending that produces that part of speech, since -ity, -ence and -ability build nouns while -ive and -ious build adjectives. Where the noun involves a stem change, as with efficacious and efficacy, the shift is a signal rather than an obstacle.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five lines state which negative or privative prefix a word takes. Decide whether English makes that choice.
statements: In a thermodynamics text, the sentence "the compression is unreversible under real conditions" treats "unreversible" as the standard negative of the adjective "reversible".
In a philosophy of science seminar, the claim that "a hypothesis immune to counter-evidence is unfalsifiable" builds "unfalsifiable" by attaching un- to the -able adjective "falsifiable".
In a study of an unreliable narrator, the description of him as "amoral rather than immoral" uses "amoral" with a- for standing outside moral judgement and "immoral" with im- for acting against it.
In an editorial on press regulation, the sentence "the two positions are irreconcilable" builds "irreconcilable" with in- assimilating to ir- before the r of "reconcilable".
In an oncology note, the sentence "the tumour was judged inoperable" builds "inoperable" from in- and the adjective "operable" to say that surgery cannot be performed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a thermodynamics text, the sentence "the compression is unreversible under real conditions" treats "unreversible" as the standard negative of the adjective "reversible".**

"Reversible" comes from a Latinate verb and takes the in- prefix, which assimilates to ir- before the initial r of the base, giving "irreversible". English does allow un- on many -able and -ible adjectives, but not where a settled Latinate negative already occupies the slot, and thermodynamics has used the ir- form since the nineteenth century. Coining a rival with un- produces a word no physicist writes.

Assimilated in- is the prefix this base has long carried, so the coinage cannot stand: "the compression is irreversible under real conditions".

**B) In a philosophy of science seminar, the claim that "a hypothesis immune to counter-evidence is unfalsifiable" builds "unfalsifiable" by attaching un- to the -able adjective "falsifiable".**

Once -able has built an adjective, un- is the prefix English reaches for most readily, which is why we have unworkable, unreadable and unfalsifiable. The base itself is layered: "false" gives the verb "falsify" through -ify, and -able then gives "falsifiable", so the negative sits outermost, over the whole adjective. Popper's usage fixed the term in exactly this shape.

Outermost un- over an -able adjective is the regular pattern, and the seminar's term is built on it, so the wording is correct.

**C) In a study of an unreliable narrator, the description of him as "amoral rather than immoral" uses "amoral" with a- for standing outside moral judgement and "immoral" with im- for acting against it.**

Greek a- marks the absence of a property, while Latin in-, here assimilated to im- before the lip consonant m, marks contrariety. That gives two genuinely different readings: an amoral narrator has no moral framework in play, an immoral one breaks a framework he recognises. Literary criticism relies on the contrast to describe narrators who report cruelty without evaluating it.

Absence set against opposition is exactly what the two prefixes encode, and the study uses each in its own sense, so the description holds.

**D) In an editorial on press regulation, the sentence "the two positions are irreconcilable" builds "irreconcilable" with in- assimilating to ir- before the r of "reconcilable".**

Latin in- adapts to the first sound of its base: it becomes il- before l, im- before m, b and p, and ir- before r, giving illegal, impossible and irreconcilable. The base is itself derived, since "reconcile" takes -able to form an adjective before the negative is added. Pronunciation drives the change, and spelling records it.

Assimilation before r is a rule rather than an accident, and the editorial's adjective displays it exactly, so the sentence is well formed.

**E) In an oncology note, the sentence "the tumour was judged inoperable" builds "inoperable" from in- and the adjective "operable" to say that surgery cannot be performed.**

"Operate" loses its -ate before -able, giving "operable", and the Latinate negative in- then attaches without assimilation because the base begins with a vowel. The resulting adjective sits predicatively after "was judged", where a quality of the tumour is being reported. Clinical writing keeps the word for cases where surgery is not technically possible rather than merely unwise.

Latinate base, truncated stem and unassimilated in- all line up here, so the note's wording is exactly right.
tasks.solution_overview: Negative prefixes are not interchangeable, and the base usually decides which one appears: in- and its assimilated forms attach to Latinate stems, un- attaches freely to adjectives including those already carrying -able, and Greek a- marks absence rather than opposition. Watch for assimilation, since in- becomes ir- before r, il- before l and im- before a lip consonant. Where two prefixes are both possible, the meanings diverge, so let the sense the sentence needs settle the choice.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Each line takes apart a word built on a Latin root that never stands alone in English. Decide whether the analysis of root and ending is accurate.
statements: In a report on concert-hall acoustics, the word "audible" is taken apart as the bound root aud-, meaning hear, plus -ible, giving an adjective for what can be heard.
In a handbook on debating, the word "tenable" is taken apart as the root ten-, meaning hold, plus -able, giving an adjective for a position that can be maintained.
In a forensic report, the noun "credence" is taken apart as the root cred-, meaning believe, plus -ence, giving the abstract noun used in the phrase "lend credence to".
In a history of protest, the adjective "vociferous" is taken apart as voc-, meaning voice, plus -fer-, meaning carry, plus -ous.
In a chemistry note, the adjective "insoluble" is taken apart as in-, plus the root solu-, meaning loosen, plus -ble, giving what cannot be dissolved.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on concert-hall acoustics, the word "audible" is taken apart as the bound root aud-, meaning hear, plus -ible, giving an adjective for what can be heard.**

No English word "aud" exists, yet the root is unmistakable across audience, audition, auditory and audible, all of them turning on hearing. The ending -ible carries the passive potential sense, so the whole means capable of being heard, and it functions as an adjective wherever the sentence needs one. Acoustic reports use it for sound that reaches a listener above the noise floor.

Root and ending together deliver the meaning the acousticians are after, so the analysis of the word is right.

**B) In a handbook on debating, the word "tenable" is taken apart as the root ten-, meaning hold, plus -able, giving an adjective for a position that can be maintained.**

The root ten- for holding surfaces in tenure, retain, tenacious and tenant, none of which leaves it standing alone. With -able the sense is able to be held, which transfers from ground held in war to an argument held under challenge. Debating handbooks use the transferred sense almost exclusively, and its negative "untenable" is even commoner.

Holding a position rather than a place is the natural extension of the root, so the handbook's analysis stands.

**C) In a forensic report, the noun "credence" is taken apart as the root cred-, meaning believe, plus -ence, giving the abstract noun used in the phrase "lend credence to".**

Cred- runs through credible, credit, incredulous and creed, always with belief at its centre, though it never appears as a word on its own. The ending -ence builds an abstract noun, and this one names the belief accorded to a claim rather than the claim's own quality, which is "credibility". Forensic writing exploits the difference when one piece of evidence lends credence to another.

Root of belief plus an abstract ending is exactly what the fixed phrase draws on, so the report's analysis is accurate.

**D) In a history of protest, the adjective "vociferous" is taken apart as voc-, meaning voice, plus -fer-, meaning carry, plus -ous.**

Two bound elements combine here: voc- gives vocal, vocation and evoke, while -fer- for carrying gives transfer, conifer and pestiferous. The adjectival -ous rounds the compound off, producing a word for protest that carries its voice loudly and insistently. Historians reach for it when they want the volume of a campaign rather than its argument.

Two roots and an adjectival ending account for the whole word, and the meaning falls out of them, so the analysis holds.

**E) In a chemistry note, the adjective "insoluble" is taken apart as in-, plus the root solu-, meaning loosen, plus -ble, giving what cannot be dissolved.**

Solu- for loosening lies behind solve, dissolve, solution and absolute, and it retains the sense of coming apart in liquid. The passive ending -ble supplies able to be, and the Latinate negative in- reverses the whole, so the salt in question stays undissolved. The same word serves for a problem that will not come apart under analysis, which is the metaphor made literal.

Negative, root and passive ending stack in the order the meaning requires, so the chemistry note's analysis is correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Bound roots carry the meaning of these words even though none of them is an English word by itself, so the test is whether the gloss offered for the root really matches how the whole word behaves. Aud-, ten-, cred-, voc- and solu- all recur across large families, and recognising them turns unfamiliar vocabulary into something you can read off. Check the ending too, since -ible and -ence assign a part of speech that the sentence around the word has to accept.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Five lines undo something with a prefix. Decide whether the prefix quoted is the one English uses to reverse the action in question.
statements: In a report on nuclear power, the sentence "the reactor was decommissioned over eleven years" builds "decommissioned" with de-, the prefix that reverses the state of being in commission.
In a marine mammal report, the sentence "the whale was misentangled from the fishing gear" builds "misentangled" with mis-, treated as the prefix that reverses the action of entangling.
In a data-management guide, the sentence "the archive was unzipped and then uncompressed by the utility" uses "uncompressed" as the verb that names the reversal of compression.
In a note on state archives, the sentence "the cabinet files were declassified in 2019" builds "declassified" with de-, reversing the act of classifying a document as secret.
In a museum conservation note, the sentence "the frame was unassembled for cleaning" builds "unassembled" with un-, treated as the prefix that reverses the act of assembling.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on nuclear power, the sentence "the reactor was decommissioned over eleven years" builds "decommissioned" with de-, the prefix that reverses the state of being in commission.**

The prefix de- takes a noun or verb of installed condition and runs it backwards, which is why we have deregulate, defrost and decommission. Here the base is the noun "commission", the state of being in active service, and the derived verb names the whole programme of shutting a plant down and making it safe. Nuclear engineering has no rival term, and the eleven-year span fits a process verb rather than a simple negation.

Undoing a state that was formally entered into is precisely what de- encodes, so the report's verb is the right one.

**B) In a marine mammal report, the sentence "the whale was misentangled from the fishing gear" builds "misentangled" with mis-, treated as the prefix that reverses the action of entangling.**

The prefix mis- says that an action was performed wrongly, as in misdiagnose, misquote and misfile; it never says that the action was undone. Reversal of "entangle" belongs to dis-, which strips away a state in disconnect, disarm and disentangle. Rescue teams disentangle whales, and a misentangled whale would, if the word meant anything, be one that had been tangled up incorrectly.

Faulty performance and undoing are different jobs, and only one prefix does the second, so the sentence needs repair: "the whale was disentangled from the fishing gear".

**C) In a data-management guide, the sentence "the archive was unzipped and then uncompressed by the utility" uses "uncompressed" as the verb that names the reversal of compression.**

As a past participle used adjectivally, "uncompressed" describes a file that was never compressed in the first place, since un- on a participle simply negates. The verb that reverses a completed technical process is "decompress", built with the de- that also gives decrypt, defragment and deduplicate. The guide is describing an operation the utility performed, so it needs the process verb rather than the state adjective.

A word that means never compressed cannot name the act of undoing compression, so the line has to read: "the archive was unzipped and then decompressed by the utility".

**D) In a note on state archives, the sentence "the cabinet files were declassified in 2019" builds "declassified" with de-, reversing the act of classifying a document as secret.**

"Classify" here means to assign a security grade, and de- reverses that assignment rather than denying it, exactly as it does in denaturalise and demobilise. The point is that the files were once secret and have now been released, which a plain negative could not convey. Archive notes rely on the verb because it dates the release as an event.

An earlier state formally cancelled by a later act is what de- is for, and the archive note uses it in that sense, so the sentence stands.

**E) In a museum conservation note, the sentence "the frame was unassembled for cleaning" builds "unassembled" with un-, treated as the prefix that reverses the act of assembling.**

On a participle, un- again gives a state rather than an action: an unassembled frame is one that arrived in pieces and was never put together. Taking apart something already built calls for dis-, which gives disassemble alongside disconnect and dismantle. The conservators plainly worked on a completed frame, so the reversative is required.

Never put together and taken apart again are opposite descriptions, and the note means the second, so the wording fails: "the frame was disassembled for cleaning".
tasks.solution_overview: Reversing an action is not the same as denying it, and the two jobs use different prefixes: de- and dis- undo a state that was brought about, while un- mostly negates and mis- only says that something was done badly. Latinate verbs of process, especially those ending in -ise, -ify or -ate, usually take de- when the process is run backwards. Ask what has actually been undone in each sentence, then check whether the prefix chosen can carry that reversal.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five lines name the noun that goes with a verb whose stem shifts on the way. Decide whether the form quoted is the one English settles on.
statements: In a highways report, the phrase "the bridge's maintainance schedule" treats "maintainance" as the standard noun that "maintain" yields with -ance.
In a phonetics handbook, the phrase "the pronounciation of the reduced vowel" treats "pronounciation" as the noun English forms from "pronounce" with -ation.
In a physics tutorial, the phrase "the explanation of the anomaly" uses "explanation", the noun of "explain" with the ai of the verb reduced to a.
In an account of a Security Council vote, the phrase "the abstention of three permanent members" uses "abstention", the noun of "abstain" with the stem reduced before -tion.
In a study of medieval philosophy, the phrase "the conception of time as circular" uses "conception", the noun of "conceive" with -ceive replaced by -cep- before -tion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a highways report, the phrase "the bridge's maintainance schedule" treats "maintainance" as the standard noun that "maintain" yields with -ance.**

The verb "maintain" does take -ance, but the stem shortens as the suffix goes on, so the noun is "maintenance", with an e where the verb has ai. The same reduction shows up in sustain beside sustenance, and it reflects the Latin tenere that lies under both. Writing the noun with the verb's vowel intact is one of the commonest slips in engineering prose.

The suffix is right but the stem has not been adjusted, so the phrase misses the standard form: "the bridge's maintenance schedule".

**B) In a phonetics handbook, the phrase "the pronounciation of the reduced vowel" treats "pronounciation" as the noun English forms from "pronounce" with -ation.**

"Pronounce" loses the o of its diphthong before -ation, giving "pronunciation", which is why the noun has four syllables with a short u where the verb has a long ou. The pattern parallels denounce beside denunciation and renounce beside renunciation. A phonetics handbook of all places has to keep the spelling that matches the sound.

The stem shift the suffix triggers has simply not been made, so the handbook's noun is wrong: "the pronunciation of the reduced vowel".

**C) In a physics tutorial, the phrase "the explanation of the anomaly" uses "explanation", the noun of "explain" with the ai of the verb reduced to a.**

The verb "explain" and its noun "explanation" differ in the stem vowel because the suffix pulls the stress forward and shortens what follows, exactly as in maintain beside maintenance. The noun names both the act of explaining and the account produced, and the frame of determiner plus of-phrase requires a noun. Physics tutorials use it for the account that makes a measurement intelligible.

The stem reduction is real and the form quoted records it correctly, so the tutorial's phrase is exactly as English has it.

**D) In an account of a Security Council vote, the phrase "the abstention of three permanent members" uses "abstention", the noun of "abstain" with the stem reduced before -tion.**

"Abstain" behaves like its relatives detain and retain, whose nouns are detention and retention, so the ai of the verb becomes a short e before the ending. The result names a single act of declining to vote, and it pluralises freely when several members do so. Diplomatic reporting distinguishes abstentions from votes against precisely because the noun is countable.

Stem reduction before -tion is the regular path for this family, and the account follows it, so the phrase is well formed.

**E) In a study of medieval philosophy, the phrase "the conception of time as circular" uses "conception", the noun of "conceive" with -ceive replaced by -cep- before -tion.**

Verbs in -ceive all shift to -cep- when they take -tion, giving receive and reception, perceive and perception, deceive and deception. "Conception" therefore names the act or product of conceiving, here the way a period understood time rather than any biological sense. The determiner and the following of-phrase make the noun slot unmistakable.

The -ceive to -cep- shift is exactly what the form displays, and the sense fits the history being written, so the phrase holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Many Latinate verbs do not keep their shape when they become nouns, and the change is regular enough to check: -ain often reduces to -en, -ceive becomes -cep-, and pronounce loses its o before -ation. Because the shifted forms look like misspellings and the unshifted ones look reasonable, spelling and morphology are being tested together here. Say the noun aloud, since the vowel you hear usually confirms the written stem.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Five lines turn on the choice between -ance and -ence or between -ant and -ent. Decide whether the form quoted is the one English writes.
statements: In a soil ecology paper, the phrase "the persistence of the pathogen in cool soils" uses "persistence", the abstract noun "persist" takes with -ence.
In a metallurgy note, the phrase "the alloy's resilience under repeated loading" uses "resilience", the noun that goes with the adjective "resilient".
In an immigration policy note, the phrase "the applicant's dependants" uses "dependants" with -ant to name the people who rely on the applicant rather than the abstract state of relying.
In a study of Victorian science, the phrase "the correspondence between the two naturalists" uses "correspondence" for the letters themselves rather than "correspondent" for a person.
In a cosmology essay, the phrase "the existance of a fourth generation of neutrinos" treats "existance" as the standard spelling of the noun formed from "exist".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a soil ecology paper, the phrase "the persistence of the pathogen in cool soils" uses "persistence", the abstract noun "persist" takes with -ence.**

Verbs in -sist all build their nouns in -ence: insist gives insistence, consist gives consistence and persist gives persistence. The noun names how long something continues rather than any quality of the thing itself, which is exactly what a study of a pathogen's survival is measuring. The of-phrase after the determiner confirms a noun slot.

Family pattern and sense agree on the -ence form here, so the ecologists' phrase is correctly built.

**B) In a metallurgy note, the phrase "the alloy's resilience under repeated loading" uses "resilience", the noun that goes with the adjective "resilient".**

Adjectives in -ent take nouns in -ence as a matter of course, so resilient pairs with resilience just as prudent pairs with prudence. The base is the rare verb "resile", from Latin salire for leaping, so the noun names a springing back rather than mere toughness. Materials science uses it as a measurable capacity to recover shape after strain.

An -ent adjective with its matching -ence noun, used in its technical springing-back sense, is what the note supplies, so the phrase is right.

**C) In an immigration policy note, the phrase "the applicant's dependants" uses "dependants" with -ant to name the people who rely on the applicant rather than the abstract state of relying.**

This family splits its endings by job: -ence gives "dependence", the state of relying, while -ant gives a countable noun for the person in that position. British legal drafting keeps the noun with an a and the adjective "dependent" with an e, which makes the contrast visible on the page. The possessive plus plural marks a set of people, not a condition.

People rather than a condition is what the policy note is counting, and the -ant form is what names them, so the phrase is accurate.

**D) In a study of Victorian science, the phrase "the correspondence between the two naturalists" uses "correspondence" for the letters themselves rather than "correspondent" for a person.**

The verb "correspond" yields the abstract noun "correspondence" through -ence, and English has extended that noun to the body of letters produced by corresponding. The rival form "correspondent" uses the agentive -ent to name the writer, which would leave the between-phrase without anything to link. Historians of science quote from a correspondence and cite each correspondent by name.

The between-phrase needs an exchange rather than a person, and the -ence noun supplies exactly that, so the study's phrase works.

**E) In a cosmology essay, the phrase "the existance of a fourth generation of neutrinos" treats "existance" as the standard spelling of the noun formed from "exist".**

"Exist" comes from Latin existere, whose present participle gives the -ent adjective "existent", and English accordingly writes the noun with -ence. The pull towards -ance is strong because the ending is unstressed and inaudible, but no dictionary records the a-spelling as an alternative. Related forms such as "coexistence" and "non-existent" all confirm the e.

The suffix that this base has always taken is the one with an e, so the essay's noun is misspelt: "the existence of a fourth generation of neutrinos".
tasks.solution_overview: The -ance and -ence endings sound identical in unstressed position, so the choice has to be made on the Latin conjugation behind the base rather than by ear. It helps to think in families, since persist and existence pattern together while resile and dependence do not, and it helps to notice that -ant often names a person or an agent where -ence names the abstract quality. When a line offers a noun for a human being, check whether the abstract form has been used by mistake, and vice versa.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Five lines gloss a word built from Greek or Latin elements. Decide whether the meaning assigned to the element really produces the meaning of the word.
statements: In a note on language teaching, a pupil described as "a polyglot" is said to be a speaker of one tongue, since "polyglot" is analysed with -glot carrying the sense of many.
In a company's human resources report, the firm's promotion system is called "a meritocracy", and "meritocracy" is glossed as a scheme for measuring merit, since -cracy means measurement.
In a hospital referral letter, the department of "hepatology" is described as the branch of medicine dealing with the kidneys.
In a seismology bulletin, the instrument called a "seismograph" is analysed as seismo-, meaning shaking, plus -graph, meaning something that writes or records.
In a university prospectus, "philology" is glossed as the study of sound in language, on the ground that phil- means sound.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a note on language teaching, a pupil described as "a polyglot" is said to be a speaker of one tongue, since "polyglot" is analysed with -glot carrying the sense of many.**

The elements have been swapped: poly- is the Greek for many, as in polygon, polymer and polyphony, while -glot is the tongue, as in the glottis and in isogloss. A polyglot is therefore a speaker of many languages, which is why the word is a compliment in language teaching rather than a description of the monolingual. Reading the parts in the right order also gives the right sense of the whole.

Many belongs to the first element and tongue to the second, so the gloss inverts the word and cannot be accepted.

**B) In a company's human resources report, the firm's promotion system is called "a meritocracy", and "meritocracy" is glossed as a scheme for measuring merit, since -cracy means measurement.**

The element -cracy comes from Greek kratos for power or rule, which is why it gives democracy, autocracy and bureaucracy, each naming who governs rather than how anything is counted. A meritocracy is thus a system in which merit rules, whatever measurement it happens to use. Measurement would call for -metry, as in symmetry and telemetry.

Rule rather than measurement is what the ending contributes, so the report's gloss of its own promotion system misses the word.

**C) In a hospital referral letter, the department of "hepatology" is described as the branch of medicine dealing with the kidneys.**

Hepat- is the Greek for liver, which is why hepatitis is inflammation of the liver and a hepatic artery supplies it. Kidney medicine is nephrology, from nephros, and the two departments treat different organs and different diseases. The ending -logy names a field of study in both cases, so it is the root that decides the referral.

The root points to the liver and only to the liver, so the letter has sent the patient to the wrong specialty in name at least.

**D) In a seismology bulletin, the instrument called a "seismograph" is analysed as seismo-, meaning shaking, plus -graph, meaning something that writes or records.**

Seismos is the Greek for a shaking of the ground, and it recurs in seismic and seismology, while -graph names either a writing instrument or its written product, as in telegraph and photograph. A seismograph therefore writes a record of ground motion, and the trace it produces is a seismogram, with -gram for the thing written. The bulletin's analysis fits both elements and the machine itself.

Shaking plus recording is exactly what the instrument does, so the analysis in the bulletin is sound.

**E) In a university prospectus, "philology" is glossed as the study of sound in language, on the ground that phil- means sound.**

Phil- is love, as in philosophy, philanthropy and bibliophile, so philology is literally the love of words and in practice the historical study of texts and languages. Sound belongs to phon-, which gives phonetics, phonology and telephone, and that is the field the gloss actually describes. A prospectus that confuses the two misdirects applicants to the wrong course.

Love of language rather than the study of sound is what the first element gives, so the prospectus gloss does not survive inspection.
tasks.solution_overview: Neoclassical words are assembled from elements that keep their meaning across dozens of formations, so a wrong gloss on one element usually shows up as a clash with how the whole word is used. Test each analysis twice: once against the element as it appears elsewhere, and once against the sense the sentence itself gives the word. Poly-, -cracy, hepat-, -graph and phil- are all frequent enough that a single familiar cousin will settle the question.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five lines identify the suffix that names a person, an agent or an instrument. Decide whether the account of the ending and its role is accurate.
statements: In a conveyancing file, the party receiving the land is called the "transferee", the ending -ee marking the one to whom the action is done.
In a pharmacology note, a drug that widens blood vessels is a "vasodilator", where -or names the agent even though the agent is a substance rather than a person.
In a study of Georgian scholarship, a collector of coins and inscriptions is called an "antiquarian", the ending -arian naming someone occupied with a field.
In a water-treatment protocol, the chemical added to make suspended particles clump is a "coagulant", with -ant naming the substance that brings the process about.
In an ethics seminar, someone who judges acts by their outcomes is called a "consequentialist", the ending -ist naming the adherent of a doctrine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a conveyancing file, the party receiving the land is called the "transferee", the ending -ee marking the one to whom the action is done.**

English uses -ee for the passive participant, in contrast with the -or or -er that names the actor, which is why legal drafting pairs transferor with transferee and lessor with lessee. The base is the verb "transfer", and the ending picks out its indirect object, the party the property moves to. Nothing about the ending suggests activity, which is precisely why conveyancers rely on it.

The receiving end of a verb is what -ee singles out, and the file uses it for exactly that party, so the account is correct.

**B) In a pharmacology note, a drug that widens blood vessels is a "vasodilator", where -or names the agent even though the agent is a substance rather than a person.**

The word joins vaso-, from Latin vas for vessel, to the verb "dilate", whose stem takes the Latinate agentive -or. That ending is not restricted to human beings: it gives generator, resistor and radiator as readily as it gives inventor. Here it names the substance that performs the widening, which is how prescribing guidance classifies the drug.

An agentive ending doing duty for a chemical rather than a person is standard in pharmacology, so the note's analysis holds.

**C) In a study of Georgian scholarship, a collector of coins and inscriptions is called an "antiquarian", the ending -arian naming someone occupied with a field.**

The suffix -arian attaches to a noun or adjective and names a person defined by an interest or a doctrine, as in disciplinarian, librarian and utilitarian. Built on "antiquary" and ultimately on the Latin for ancient things, it names the scholar who collects and studies the material remains of the past. The same form serves as an adjective for the trade in old books.

A person defined by the field they pursue is exactly what the ending delivers, so the study's label is properly formed.

**D) In a water-treatment protocol, the chemical added to make suspended particles clump is a "coagulant", with -ant naming the substance that brings the process about.**

The base is the verb "coagulate", which loses its -ate before the ending, and -ant then names what does the coagulating, exactly as it does in lubricant, disinfectant and pollutant. The ending began as the Latin present participle, so it still carries an active sense whether the agent is animate or not. Treatment plants distinguish the coagulant from the flocculant by the stage at which each acts.

An active participial ending applied to a working chemical is what the protocol needs, so the term is correctly analysed.

**E) In an ethics seminar, someone who judges acts by their outcomes is called a "consequentialist", the ending -ist naming the adherent of a doctrine.**

The suffix -ist attaches to a noun or an -ism to name the person who holds the position, giving empiricist, federalist and consequentialist alongside their doctrines. The chain here runs from "consequence" through the adjective "consequential" to the doctrine "consequentialism" and then to its adherent. The same form works attributively, as in a consequentialist argument.

Doctrine first and adherent second is the order the ending assumes, and the seminar's term follows it, so the description is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Agent endings are not all alike: -er and -or name the one who acts, -ee names the one acted upon, and -ant slides between people and substances that bring an effect about. Two further endings, -ian and -ist, attach to fields and doctrines rather than to verbs, which is why they name practitioners and adherents. Read the base first, then ask whether the person or thing named stands at the giving or the receiving end of it.
