tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five lines make a verb out of a noun or an adjective. Decide whether English builds the verb in the way described.
statements: In a cryogenics note, the sentence "the gas was liquidified at low temperature" treats "liquidified" as the standard verb English forms from the adjective "liquid".
In a survey methods guide, the sentence "the analyst stratificated the sample by region" builds "stratificated" by adding -ate to the noun "stratification".
In a soil science manual, the sentence "lime is added to sweeten acid soils" uses "sweeten", where -en turns an adjective into a verb of causing.
In a note on the history of publishing, the verb "edit" is described as a back-formation, cut down from the earlier noun "editor" rather than built up from a base.
In a laboratory protocol, the sentence "the samples were centrifugated for ten minutes" forms "centrifugated" by adding -ate to the noun "centrifuge".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a cryogenics note, the sentence "the gas was liquidified at low temperature" treats "liquidified" as the standard verb English forms from the adjective "liquid".**

The verb in this family is "liquefy", where -fy attaches to a shortened Latin stem lique- rather than to the whole adjective, and the same shape appears in putrefy, rarefy and stupefy. Building the verb on the full adjective produces a form no laboratory writes, and it also blocks the noun "liquefaction" that goes with it. The e in the middle is the mark of the Latin stem.

The suffix is right but it has been fixed to the wrong stem, so the note misses the established verb: "the gas was liquefied at low temperature".

**B) In a survey methods guide, the sentence "the analyst stratificated the sample by region" builds "stratificated" by adding -ate to the noun "stratification".**

English works the other way round here: the verb "stratify" comes first, and "stratification" is the noun derived from it with -ation. Cutting the noun back and pinning -ate on the result invents a verb where a shorter one already exists, much as "orientate" and "administrate" strain against orient and administer. Sampling manuals speak of a stratified sample and of stratification by region.

Deriving a verb from a noun that was itself derived from a verb doubles the morphology needlessly, so the guide should read: "the analyst stratified the sample by region".

**C) In a soil science manual, the sentence "lime is added to sweeten acid soils" uses "sweeten", where -en turns an adjective into a verb of causing.**

The native ending -en attaches to short adjectives, mostly of one syllable ending in a consonant, and gives a verb meaning to make or become that quality: harden, dampen, widen, sweeten. Agricultural writing has used the last of these for centuries in the specific sense of reducing acidity, where the taste metaphor has hardened into a technical term. The ending will not attach to Latinate polysyllables, which is why we say acidify rather than acid-en.

A short native adjective taking the causative ending in a settled technical sense is exactly what the manual has, so the sentence is well formed.

**D) In a note on the history of publishing, the verb "edit" is described as a back-formation, cut down from the earlier noun "editor" rather than built up from a base.**

The usual direction of derivation is base first, agent noun second, so speakers hearing "editor" naturally assumed a verb behind it and supplied one. That reversal is what back-formation names, and it also produced burgle from burglar, donate from donation and diagnose from diagnosis. The dates confirm the sequence, since the agent noun is recorded well before the verb.

A verb carved out of an agent noun that came first is the textbook case of back-formation, and this is one of the clearest, so the description holds.

**E) In a laboratory protocol, the sentence "the samples were centrifugated for ten minutes" forms "centrifugated" by adding -ate to the noun "centrifuge".**

"Centrifuge" is used unchanged as a verb by conversion, so a technician centrifuges a sample and reports that it was centrifuged. Adding -ate to a noun that already works as a verb produces the same kind of overbuilt form as "orientate" beside orient, and in the laboratory it simply sounds wrong. Conversion is one of the most productive routes into the English verb, and it needs no ending at all.

The noun already does duty as a verb without any suffix, so the protocol should say: "the samples were centrifuged for ten minutes".
tasks.solution_overview: English has several ways of making verbs, and they are not freely interchangeable: -ise and -ify attach to nouns and adjectives, -en attaches to short native adjectives, and a good many verbs are simply nouns used unchanged or shortened back from a longer noun. The traps here run in both directions, since a verb can be invented by adding an ending that the language never added, or by keeping an ending the language strips away. Check whether a shorter verb already exists before accepting a longer one.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five lines pick an adjective out of a family where more than one ending competes. Decide whether the form quoted is the one careful English keeps.
statements: In a public health plan, the phrase "preventive care in primary settings" uses "preventive", the shorter of the two adjectives the verb "prevent" supports.
In a note on academic writing, the phrase "an assertative style of argument" treats "assertative" as the adjective English forms from the verb "assert".
In a report on jury directions, the phrase "the judge's admonitory tone" uses "admonitory", built on the Latin stem of "admonish".
In a chemistry paper, the phrase "an exothermal reaction" treats "exothermal" as the standard adjective for a reaction that gives out heat.
In a study of autobiographical memory, the phrase "an odour that proved evocative of early childhood" uses "evocative", the adjective of "evoke" formed on the stem evoc-.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a public health plan, the phrase "preventive care in primary settings" uses "preventive", the shorter of the two adjectives the verb "prevent" supports.**

The Latin stem prevent- takes -ive directly, giving "preventive", while the longer "preventative" adds an extra syllable that the stem does not require. Both are recorded, but health policy and clinical writing have settled firmly on the shorter form, as in preventive medicine and preventive services. Where two forms mean the same thing, the one without the redundant syllable is the safer choice in formal prose.

The shorter form is both regularly built and the established term of art in this field, so the plan's wording is right.

**B) In a note on academic writing, the phrase "an assertative style of argument" treats "assertative" as the adjective English forms from the verb "assert".**

The stem here is assert-, which takes -ive straight off to give "assertive", the form that pairs with the noun "assertion". Inserting an extra -at- imitates families such as authoritative, where the -at- belongs to the Latin stem itself, and produces a word English does not have. Checking the noun is a reliable cue: assertion has no -at-, so neither does the adjective.

The stem never carried the syllable that has been added, so the note needs the regular form: "an assertive style of argument".

**C) In a report on jury directions, the phrase "the judge's admonitory tone" uses "admonitory", built on the Latin stem of "admonish".**

English takes the adjective from the stem admonit-, the same stem that gives the noun "admonition", and adds the functional ending -ory meaning serving to do the thing. The verb's own English shape in -ish never carries the adjective, which is why we have no form in -ishing here. Legal reporting uses the adjective for a tone that warns without yet punishing.

Latin stem plus an ending of function gives the exact shade the courtroom description needs, so the phrase is properly built.

**D) In a chemistry paper, the phrase "an exothermal reaction" treats "exothermal" as the standard adjective for a reaction that gives out heat.**

The settled term is "exothermic", where the Greek therme for heat takes the Greek-derived ending -ic, matching endothermic, isothermic and thermodynamic. English does form some adjectives in -al on Greek stems, but this family has fixed on -ic, and journals treat the -al form as an error rather than a variant. Its counterpart noun, exotherm, confirms the shape of the stem.

Greek stems in this family take the Greek ending, so the paper's adjective is not the accepted one: "an exothermic reaction".

**E) In a study of autobiographical memory, the phrase "an odour that proved evocative of early childhood" uses "evocative", the adjective of "evoke" formed on the stem evoc-.**

The verb "evoke" shows its Latin stem in the noun "evocation", and the adjective is built on the same stem with -ative, meaning tending to call something up. The predicative slot after "proved" needs an adjective, and this one takes the preposition "of" to name what is called up. No adjective is formed from the English verb directly, which is why there is no form in -oking here.

Stem, ending and complement all fit together in the memory researchers' phrase, so the description is exactly right.
tasks.solution_overview: When two adjectival endings compete, one of them is usually either the settled form or the only one carrying the sense that is wanted. Latinate verbs supply their adjectives from the same stem that gives their nouns, so admonition sits beside admonitory and evocation beside evocative, and an ending pinned to the plain English verb instead will not sound right. Scientific vocabulary adds a further constraint, since Greek-derived terms take -ic where a native-looking -al is not available.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Each line reads a word off its Latin root. Decide whether the root really yields the sense the sentence gives the word.
statements: In an account of a treaty, the statement that a state "acceded to the convention" is glossed as meaning that it went beyond its obligations, since "acceded" and "exceeded" are said to share a root meaning to surpass.
In an anatomy text, the muscle called an "abductor" is read as ab-, meaning away, plus duct-, meaning lead, giving a muscle that draws a limb away from the midline.
In a materials note, the adjective "intractable" is read as in-, plus tract-, meaning draw or handle, plus -able, describing a material that cannot be worked.
In a philosophy paper, the noun "introspection" is read as intro-, meaning within, plus spect-, meaning look, plus -ion, naming the act of looking inward.
In a court order, the verb "desist" is read as de-, meaning off or away, plus sist-, meaning stand, giving a command to stand off from an action.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In an account of a treaty, the statement that a state "acceded to the convention" is glossed as meaning that it went beyond its obligations, since "acceded" and "exceeded" are said to share a root meaning to surpass.**

The root ced- means to go or to yield, not to surpass; the sense of going beyond comes from the prefix ex- in "exceed", where ex- supplies the beyond. With ad- assimilated to ac-, the verb means to go towards and so to join or agree, which is why a state accedes to a convention and a monarch accedes to a throne. Reading the surpassing sense back into the root wipes out the contribution of the prefix.

The prefix, not the root, carries the idea of going beyond, so the gloss misreads the word: a state that acceded to the convention has joined it.

**B) In an anatomy text, the muscle called an "abductor" is read as ab-, meaning away, plus duct-, meaning lead, giving a muscle that draws a limb away from the midline.**

The root duct- for leading runs through conduct, aqueduct and induction, and ab- for away appears in abstain, absent and abrasion. Put together with the agentive -or, they give a muscle that leads the limb away, which is precisely how anatomists define it against the adductor, built with ad- for towards. The pair differs by a single consonant and by the whole direction of movement.

Prefix, root and agent ending combine to name the movement the muscle makes, so the anatomy text's reading is correct.

**C) In a materials note, the adjective "intractable" is read as in-, plus tract-, meaning draw or handle, plus -able, describing a material that cannot be worked.**

Tract- for drawing or handling gives traction, tractor, contract and, through the sense of handling, treatise and treatment. With -able the adjective means able to be handled, and the negative in- turns it into what resists working, whether the resistant thing is an alloy, a disease or a dispute. The metaphorical uses grow directly out of the physical one.

Root of handling under a negative prefix is what the word is made of, and it fits the resistant material exactly, so the note's reading holds.

**D) In a philosophy paper, the noun "introspection" is read as intro-, meaning within, plus spect-, meaning look, plus -ion, naming the act of looking inward.**

Spect- for looking is unmistakable in spectator, inspect, prospect and circumspect, and intro- for inward appears in introduce and introvert. The ending -ion turns the compound verb stem into the act itself, so the noun names the mind's inspection of its own contents. Nineteenth-century psychology coined its method around exactly this analysis.

Direction, seeing and an act ending together produce the philosophers' term, so the analysis in the paper is sound.

**E) In a court order, the verb "desist" is read as de-, meaning off or away, plus sist-, meaning stand, giving a command to stand off from an action.**

The root sist- for standing gives consist, insist, resist and subsist, in each case with the prefix setting the direction of the standing. With de- the sense is to stand away from what one has been doing, which is why the injunction pairs it with "cease" in a formula that covers both stopping and staying stopped. The doubling is legal caution rather than redundancy.

Standing away from an action is what the parts add up to, and that is exactly the conduct the order requires, so the reading is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Roots such as ced-, duct-, tract-, spect- and sist- appear in dozens of words and keep a constant core meaning, so a prefix plus a root is often enough to compute the whole. Work outwards from the root, add the prefix, and then check the result against the way the sentence uses the word. Similar spellings are the trap, since -cede and -ceed look alike but pull in different directions once the prefix is in place.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five lines separate two nouns or two forms that grow from the same base but do different work. Decide whether each division of labour is drawn correctly.
statements: In a note on observatory instruments, "refraction" is said to name the bending of light while "refractor" names the telescope that exploits it, both from "refract".
In a paper on measurement error, "variance" is described as the technical statistical quantity while "variation" names the general fact of differing, both from "vary".
In a note on oral history, "transcription" is said to cover both the act and its result while "transcript" names only the finished document.
In an audit file at an accountancy firm, "valuation" is described as the exercise carried out by the valuer while "value" names the figure that exercise produces.
In a clinical article, "dilatation" is described as the longer form of "dilation" that has survived in medical usage, both built on the verb "dilate".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a note on observatory instruments, "refraction" is said to name the bending of light while "refractor" names the telescope that exploits it, both from "refract".**

The ending -ion turns the verb into the name of a process or its result, while the Latinate agentive -or names the thing that performs it, a division that also gives conduction beside conductor and projection beside projector. A refracting telescope bends light through a lens, so the instrument takes the agent noun even though it does nothing on its own. Astronomers set the refractor against the reflector on exactly this basis.

Process noun and instrument noun dividing one base between them is standard, and the note assigns each correctly, so the account stands.

**B) In a paper on measurement error, "variance" is described as the technical statistical quantity while "variation" names the general fact of differing, both from "vary".**

English has kept both nouns and given them different lives: -ance supplies a form that statistics has fixed as the mean squared deviation, while -ation supplies the ordinary noun for the fact or the range of differing. That is why a paper reports the variance of a set of readings but discusses variation between sites. The specialised sense does not displace the general one; it sits alongside it.

Two nouns from one verb, one narrowed to a defined quantity and one left general, is exactly the split described, so the paper's account is accurate.

**C) In a note on oral history, "transcription" is said to cover both the act and its result while "transcript" names only the finished document.**

Nouns in -ion characteristically cover an act and, by extension, what the act produces, so a scholar may spend a week on transcription and then quote from a transcription. The shorter form comes straight from the Latin participle and names only the object, the written-out text itself. Oral historians rely on the longer noun when they mean the labour and the shorter when they mean the file.

Act and product on one side, product alone on the other, is a real difference between the two nouns, so the note draws it correctly.

**D) In an audit file at an accountancy firm, "valuation" is described as the exercise carried out by the valuer while "value" names the figure that exercise produces.**

The verb "value" takes -ation to name the professional process, complete with method, assumptions and a date, while the base noun names the resulting amount. That is why an auditor can question a valuation without disputing that the asset has a value at all. The agent noun "valuer" fills the third slot, naming whoever performs the exercise.

Process, agent and figure each have their own form in this family, and the audit file assigns them properly, so the description holds.

**E) In a clinical article, "dilatation" is described as the longer form of "dilation" that has survived in medical usage, both built on the verb "dilate".**

The longer noun preserves the full Latin stem dilatat-, while the shorter one has been trimmed by ordinary English shortening, and the two mean the same thing. Medicine kept the long form in fixed terms such as dilatation of the aorta and dilatation and curettage, whereas general and ophthalmic writing has largely gone over to the short one. Register rather than meaning separates them.

A Latin doublet surviving in clinical prose beside its shortened twin is just what the article reports, so the description is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: One base often supplies several nouns, and English rarely wastes them: one names the process, another the instrument, a third the product, and a fourth may survive only as a technical measure. Ask what each form is doing in the sentence before deciding whether the pair has been described accurately, and pay attention to endings, since -or points to instruments and agents while -ion covers acts and results. Doublets that differ only in length, such as dilation and dilatation, usually divide by register rather than by meaning.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five lines describe what happens to a prefix when it meets the first sound of its base. Decide whether the account of the assimilation is right.
statements: In a logic textbook, the sentence "the inference is inlogical" treats "inlogical" as the standard negative of the adjective "logical".
In a hydrogeology report, the phrase "an inpermeable clay layer" treats "inpermeable" as the standard negative of "permeable".
In a note on rhetoric, the phrase "the two conrelative clauses" is said to show "conrelative" keeping con- unchanged before the r of "relative".
In a neurophysiology text, the term "afferent" is explained as ad-, meaning towards, assimilated to af- before the f of the root fer-, meaning carry.
In a note on Latin prefixes, "sufficient" is offered as a case where sub- survives unchanged before the f of its base.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a logic textbook, the sentence "the inference is inlogical" treats "inlogical" as the standard negative of the adjective "logical".**

The negative prefix in- assimilates to the l that follows, giving the doubled consonant of "illogical", exactly as it does in illegal, illegible and illiterate. The unassimilated spelling is not an alternative but a form English never produced, since the change happened in Latin long before the words were borrowed. Hearing the doubled l confirms what the spelling shows.

Assimilation before l is obligatory in this family, so the textbook sentence needs the standard form: "the inference is illogical".

**B) In a hydrogeology report, the phrase "an inpermeable clay layer" treats "inpermeable" as the standard negative of "permeable".**

Before the lip consonants p, b and m, in- becomes im-, which gives impermeable, impossible, imbalance and immobile. The base itself is built from per- and mea- for passing through, with -able adding the potential sense, and the negative then denies it. Groundwater studies use the assimilated form as a technical classification of strata.

The prefix has to adapt to the p that follows it, so the report's adjective is not English: "an impermeable clay layer".

**C) In a note on rhetoric, the phrase "the two conrelative clauses" is said to show "conrelative" keeping con- unchanged before the r of "relative".**

Con- assimilates to cor- before r, producing correlative, correspond, corrode and correct, and to col- before l in collate and collapse. The doubled consonant is the trace of the prefix folding into the base, and no unassimilated variant survives in English. The intended word here, "correlative", names clauses that answer to each other, such as either and or.

Keeping the prefix intact before r is precisely what Latin did not do, so the phrase should read: "the two correlative clauses".

**D) In a neurophysiology text, the term "afferent" is explained as ad-, meaning towards, assimilated to af- before the f of the root fer-, meaning carry.**

The root fer- for carrying gives transfer, confer and fertile, and the prefix ad- regularly assimilates to the following consonant, producing accede, affix, aggression and annex. An afferent nerve therefore carries signals towards the central nervous system, and its counterpart, efferent, built on ex-, carries them away. The single letter of difference encodes the whole direction of traffic.

Prefix, assimilation and root together explain both the spelling and the direction of conduction, so the text's account is correct.

**E) In a note on Latin prefixes, "sufficient" is offered as a case where sub- survives unchanged before the f of its base.**

The word is in fact a clear case of assimilation, since sub- becomes suf- before f, just as it becomes sup- before p in support and suppress and sug- before g in suggest. The base is fic-, a form of facere for making or doing, so the sense is something made up from underneath, enough to meet the need. What looks like an intact prefix is the assimilated one.

The very example chosen shows the prefix changing rather than surviving, so the note has it backwards: sub- has assimilated to suf- here.
tasks.solution_overview: Latin prefixes change shape to suit the consonant that follows, and the spelling records the change: in- becomes il-, im- or ir-, ad- becomes ac-, af- or ag-, con- becomes col- or cor-, and sub- becomes suf- or sup-. The doubled letters that result are the visible sign of assimilation rather than a spelling quirk. When a line leaves a prefix unchanged before a consonant that would normally trigger the shift, treat that as the error to catch.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five lines concern families where a short adjective and a longer one have divided the work between them. Decide whether the division described is the one English observes.
statements: In an essay on cabinet government, the phrase "a politic silence" uses "politic" in its own sense of prudent, distinct from the general adjective "political".
In a review of a repertory season, the claim is made that "a comic actor" and "a comical actor" describe the same performer, "comical" being interchangeable with the shorter adjective.
In a physics tutorial, "electric" is said to describe the phenomenon itself, as in electric current, while "electrical" describes what relates to it, as in electrical engineering.
In a note on adverb formation, "ironicly" is given as the adverb English derives from the adjective "ironic".
In a musicology essay, "harmonic" is said to name the physical partial above a fundamental while "harmonious" describes a sound that is agreeable, both from "harmony".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In an essay on cabinet government, the phrase "a politic silence" uses "politic" in its own sense of prudent, distinct from the general adjective "political".**

The short form has narrowed to mean shrewd or expedient, surviving mainly in phrases such as a politic reply and the impolitic remark that ends a career. The longer form covers everything to do with politics, from parties to institutions, and it cannot mean prudent at all. A silence that is politically motivated and a silence that is politic are therefore different observations.

Prudence belongs to the short adjective alone, and that is the sense the essay is reaching for, so the phrase is exactly right.

**B) In a review of a repertory season, the claim is made that "a comic actor" and "a comical actor" describe the same performer, "comical" being interchangeable with the shorter adjective.**

The short form points to comedy as a genre and a profession, which is why we speak of comic timing, comic opera and a comic actor as a specialism. The longer form means laughable, and it often carries a hint that the effect was not intended, so a comical actor may simply be an unintentionally funny one. Reviewers keep the two apart because one is a job description and the other a verdict.

Genre and unintended absurdity are different things, so treating the pair as interchangeable will not do: a comic actor is not necessarily a comical one.

**C) In a physics tutorial, "electric" is said to describe the phenomenon itself, as in electric current, while "electrical" describes what relates to it, as in electrical engineering.**

The short adjective attaches directly to things that carry or produce the effect, giving electric field, electric charge and electric shock. The longer one covers the wider domain, hence electrical safety, electrical installation and the engineer whose subject is the whole field. Neither form is more correct in the abstract; usage has simply assigned them different territory.

Direct phenomenon on one side and general relation on the other is the working distinction, and the tutorial states it accurately, so the account holds.

**D) In a note on adverb formation, "ironicly" is given as the adverb English derives from the adjective "ironic".**

Adjectives ending in -ic form their adverbs on the extended -ical stem, which is why English has basically, drastically, scientifically and ironically. The rule holds even where the -ical adjective is rare or unused, and the single exception, "publicly", is remembered precisely because it is one. Adding -ly straight to the short adjective leaves a form no dictionary lists.

The adverb has to be built on the extended stem, so the note supplies a word English does not have: the adverb is "ironically".

**E) In a musicology essay, "harmonic" is said to name the physical partial above a fundamental while "harmonious" describes a sound that is agreeable, both from "harmony".**

The Greek-derived -ic gives the technical adjective and, converted to a noun, the partial itself, as in the third harmonic of a vibrating string. The Latinate -ious gives an evaluative adjective about pleasantness, which is why a chord may be harmonious while a spectrum is harmonic. Acoustics needs both, and it needs them not to overlap.

Measurement on one side and judgement on the other is the split the two endings maintain, so the essay's distinction is correctly drawn.
tasks.solution_overview: Pairs in -ic and -ical are not spelling variants: one member usually keeps a narrow, often technical sense while the other does the general work, and a few pairs have drifted so far apart that swapping them changes the claim entirely. The same pressure produces splits between -ic and -ious, as with harmonic and harmonious. One purely formal rule belongs here too, since adjectives ending in -ic build their adverbs on the -ical stem.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five lines name the abstract noun that an adjective yields. Decide whether English takes the ending the line proposes.
statements: In a phonetics paper, "sonority" is described as the technical noun formed from "sonorous", used in preference to a form built with -ness.
In a study of civil service memoirs, "candour" is described as the noun that goes with the adjective "candid", the two differing noticeably in stem.
In a note on measurement terms, "wideness" is given as the noun formed from "wide", the older form "width" having dropped out of use.
In a data protection briefing, "privateness" is given as the abstract noun corresponding to the adjective "private".
In a materials science note, "tenaciousness" is given as the only abstract noun available from "tenacious", there being no shorter Latinate form.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a phonetics paper, "sonority" is described as the technical noun formed from "sonorous", used in preference to a form built with -ness.**

The suffix -ity attaches to the Latin stem sonor-, giving a noun that phonology has made into a defined scale ranking vowels above glides, liquids, nasals and stops. A form in -ness would be readable but would carry only the everyday sense of full-sounding richness, with none of the technical content. Where an -ity noun already exists, it usually takes the specialist ground.

An established Latinate noun that has been given a precise phonological job is exactly what the paper is using, so the description holds.

**B) In a study of civil service memoirs, "candour" is described as the noun that goes with the adjective "candid", the two differing noticeably in stem.**

The pair comes from Latin candere for shining white, which gave both the adjective and an abstract noun in -or that English received directly as candour. The stems no longer match on the page, since the noun has kept the Latin ending while the adjective has kept the participial one. That mismatch is why speakers occasionally reach for "candidness", a form that exists but sounds laboured beside the older noun.

An inherited Latin noun standing beside its adjective with a visibly different ending is just what this family shows, so the study's account is right.

**C) In a note on measurement terms, "wideness" is given as the noun formed from "wide", the older form "width" having dropped out of use.**

English keeps a small group of nouns in -th built on native adjectives with a vowel change: wide gives width, broad gives breadth, deep gives depth, strong gives strength. Far from being obsolete, "width" is the only noun available in technical measurement, and no engineer records the wideness of a beam. A form in -ness is possible in principle but has been squeezed out by the older noun.

The -th noun is alive and doing the work in every measurement context, so the note is wrong to write it off: the noun from "wide" is "width".

**D) In a data protection briefing, "privateness" is given as the abstract noun corresponding to the adjective "private".**

The noun English uses is "privacy", formed with -acy and a shortening of the adjective's ending, on the pattern of intimate and intimacy or accurate and accuracy. It is the word in the legislation, the case law and the ordinary phrase invasion of privacy, so nothing licenses a coinage in -ness. The -acy ending is what marks the abstract state in this family.

A settled -acy noun occupies the ground here, and the briefing needs it: the noun corresponding to "private" is "privacy".

**E) In a materials science note, "tenaciousness" is given as the only abstract noun available from "tenacious", there being no shorter Latinate form.**

The shorter form exists and is the usual one: "tenacity", built with -ity on the stem tenac- from the root ten- for holding. Materials science uses it for the property of resisting fracture, and ordinary prose uses it for stubborn persistence, so both registers are covered. The -ness form is grammatical but redundant, and no technical writer prefers it.

A Latinate noun is available and standard in exactly this field, so the claim that none exists cannot stand: the noun is "tenacity".
tasks.solution_overview: Where a Latinate adjective already has a noun in -ity, -acy or -our, English rarely builds a rival with -ness, and the older noun is normally the one that carries the technical sense. Native adjectives can behave differently again, since a handful still keep the old -th noun that survives in width, depth and strength. Look for the established noun before accepting a regular-looking coinage, and let the stem changes, which can be considerable, confirm what you find.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five lines concern words that change class without changing shape, or that shift their stress instead. Decide whether each account of the process is accurate.
statements: In a note on broadcasting, "record" is described as a pair distinguished only by stress, the noun taking it on the first syllable and the verb on the second.
In a horticulture manual, the verb in "the trays were seeded in March" is said to be formed by adding a suffix to the noun "seed".
In a report on urban policy, the verb in "the council set out to green the eastern wards" is described as the adjective "green" converted to a verb.
In a study of internet access, the noun in "the digital divide widened" is described as the verb "divide" converted to a noun without any ending.
In an aviation maintenance report, the noun "overhaul" is described as a phrasal verb reversed into a compound, with the stress moving to the first element.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a note on broadcasting, "record" is described as a pair distinguished only by stress, the noun taking it on the first syllable and the verb on the second.**

English has a sizeable group of two-syllable Latinate words where the noun is stressed at the front and the verb at the back: permit, conflict, rebel, increase, contrast. No ending marks the difference, so the shift of stress is doing the whole job of derivation, and the vowels reduce accordingly. Broadcasters make the contrast dozens of times a day without noticing it.

Stress placement standing in for a suffix is a genuine derivational device in this family, so the note's description is correct.

**B) In a horticulture manual, the verb in "the trays were seeded in March" is said to be formed by adding a suffix to the noun "seed".**

No suffix has been added: the noun has simply been used as a verb, which is conversion or zero derivation, and the -ed on the participle is ordinary past inflection rather than a derivational ending. English converts nouns to verbs with great freedom, giving us to seed, to water, to bottle and to shelve. The inflectional ending appears only once the verb already exists.

Inflection has been mistaken for derivation here, since the verb was formed with no ending at all: the noun "seed" is simply used as a verb.

**C) In a report on urban policy, the verb in "the council set out to green the eastern wards" is described as the adjective "green" converted to a verb.**

Conversion works from adjectives as well as nouns, giving to empty, to dry, to calm and here to green, all of them meaning to make something take on the quality. No ending is present, which distinguishes this route from the causative -en of sweeten and harden. Policy writing has adopted the converted verb for planting and greenspace programmes.

An adjective doing duty as a causative verb without any ending is exactly what the report shows, so the description is accurate.

**D) In a study of internet access, the noun in "the digital divide widened" is described as the verb "divide" converted to a noun without any ending.**

Conversion runs in the other direction just as readily, producing a noun from a verb with no suffix at all: a divide, a spend, a rise, a find. The noun here names the gap itself rather than the act of dividing, a specialisation that distinguishes it from the -ion noun "division". Social research adopted the phrase in the 1990s and it has kept the converted noun ever since.

A bare verb serving as a count noun with a meaning of its own is genuine conversion, so the study's account holds.

**E) In an aviation maintenance report, the noun "overhaul" is described as a phrasal verb reversed into a compound, with the stress moving to the first element.**

The verb haul over gives the noun overhaul, just as hold up gives holdup, break out gives outbreak and let down gives letdown. Reversing the particle and the verb, then stressing the particle, is a regular way of making nouns out of phrasal verbs. Engineering registers use the resulting nouns as names for defined procedures.

Particle first, verb second and stress at the front is the standard shape of these nouns, so the maintenance report's analysis is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Not every derivation adds an ending, since English turns nouns into verbs and verbs into nouns by conversion, leaving the form untouched, and it distinguishes some noun and verb pairs only by where the stress falls. Phrasal verbs supply a further route, because haul over and hold up can be reversed and compressed into nouns with the stress on the first element. Ask whether an affix is really present before accepting a claim that one has been added.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five lines identify a less common noun-forming ending and the sense it contributes. Decide whether each account matches the word.
statements: In a study of polar exploration diaries, "solitude" is analysed as the Latin base sol-, meaning alone, with -itude forming an abstract noun of state.
In a paper on constitutional crises, "legitimacy" is analysed as the adjective "legitimate" with -acy replacing the adjectival ending to form a noun of condition.
In a study of the medieval manor, "serfdom" is analysed as the noun "serf" plus -dom, an ending that names a condition or a domain.
In a note on maritime training, "seamanship" is analysed as a person noun plus -ship, the ending that names a skill or a standing.
In a history of Greek rhetoric, "sophistry" is analysed as the person noun "sophist" plus -ry, an ending that names a practice or a body of activity.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a study of polar exploration diaries, "solitude" is analysed as the Latin base sol-, meaning alone, with -itude forming an abstract noun of state.**

The ending -itude comes straight from Latin and builds nouns naming a condition: aptitude, fortitude, lassitude, plenitude. Here it works on the base that also gives sole, solo and solitary, so the noun names the state of being alone rather than any act of withdrawing. Diaries of overwintering use it for a condition endured over months.

Base of aloneness plus an ending of state gives precisely the condition the diarists describe, so the analysis is correct.

**B) In a paper on constitutional crises, "legitimacy" is analysed as the adjective "legitimate" with -acy replacing the adjectival ending to form a noun of condition.**

The ending -acy attaches to adjectives in -ate and to some nouns, trimming what precedes it: intimate gives intimacy, accurate gives accuracy, and legitimate gives legitimacy. The resulting noun names the condition of being recognised as rightful, which is the quality a constitutional crisis puts in doubt. A rival form in -ness is available but never used in political theory.

Adjective trimmed and re-ended to name a condition is exactly the derivation at work, so the paper's analysis holds.

**C) In a study of the medieval manor, "serfdom" is analysed as the noun "serf" plus -dom, an ending that names a condition or a domain.**

The native ending -dom names either a realm, as in kingdom, or a status and the condition that goes with it, as in freedom, martyrdom and officialdom. Attached to a person noun it turns the individual into the institution, so serfdom names the whole legal condition of unfree tenure. Historians use it for the system rather than for any one serf.

Person noun turned into a legal condition by a native ending is what the word shows, so the study's analysis is accurate.

**D) In a note on maritime training, "seamanship" is analysed as a person noun plus -ship, the ending that names a skill or a standing.**

The ending -ship attaches to nouns of person or role and names either the office, as in professorship, or the competence that goes with it, as in craftsmanship, workmanship and statesmanship. Applied to the seaman it names the whole body of practical skill involved in handling a vessel. Training manuals use it as an examinable subject rather than as a description of any individual.

Role noun turned into the skill of the role is precisely what the ending does here, so the analysis in the note is sound.

**E) In a history of Greek rhetoric, "sophistry" is analysed as the person noun "sophist" plus -ry, an ending that names a practice or a body of activity.**

The ending -ry, reduced from -ery, names trades and practices, as in husbandry, chemistry, rivalry and archery, and it often carries the tone the speaker takes towards them. Here the practice of the sophists has come to mean argument that is clever rather than sound, so the noun is now almost always disparaging. The neutral term for their teaching is sophism in some histories.

Practitioner turned into practice, with the evaluative colouring the word has acquired, is what the ending has produced, so the analysis stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Beyond the familiar -tion and -ity, English keeps a set of quieter noun endings that each specialise: -itude for a state, -acy for a condition or quality, -dom for a realm or status, -ship for a skill or standing, and -ry for a practice or a body of activity. Because these endings are less productive, the words carrying them are often old and slightly literary, and their bases may be Latin, French or native. Check the base as well as the ending, since several of these nouns are built on forms that no longer stand alone.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five lines propose a derived form that looks plausible. Decide whether English actually has the word, or whether another form already occupies the slot.
statements: In an ornithology paper, "migrance" is offered as the noun English forms from the verb "migrate" for the seasonal movement of birds.
In an air quality report, "toxinous" is offered as the adjective English derives from the noun "toxin".
In a compliance manual issued by a financial services firm, "remunerative" is treated as the adjective from "remunerate" and "remuneration" as its noun.
In a research methods seminar, "analysation" is offered as the noun English forms from the verb "analyse".
In a note on court procedure, "adjournation" is offered as the noun formed from the verb "adjourn".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In an ornithology paper, "migrance" is offered as the noun English forms from the verb "migrate" for the seasonal movement of birds.**

Verbs in -ate build their nouns with -ation, not with -ance, which is why we have migration alongside irrigation, mutation and vibration. The proposed form is transparent but unattested, and ornithology has used the -ation noun since the discipline began, complete with compounds such as migration route and migration season. Nothing in the family supports an -ance form.

An -ate verb has only one regular noun ending available, and it is already in service, so the coinage has no place: the noun is "migration".

**B) In an air quality report, "toxinous" is offered as the adjective English derives from the noun "toxin".**

The adjective in this family is "toxic", formed from the Greek stem tox- with -ic, and it is the form behind toxicity, toxicology and non-toxic. The noun "toxin" is itself a nineteenth-century coinage for a specific poisonous substance, so it is a sibling of the adjective rather than its base. Adding -ous to it produces a word that no monitoring report uses.

The adjective was formed from the stem rather than from the noun, and it is already standard, so the report should read: the adjective is "toxic".

**C) In a compliance manual issued by a financial services firm, "remunerative" is treated as the adjective from "remunerate" and "remuneration" as its noun.**

The Latin stem remunerat- supplies both forms: -ion gives the noun for payment for services, and -ive gives an adjective meaning yielding a return. Compliance and pay documents use the noun constantly and the adjective occasionally, as in remunerative work. The verb itself, built on munus for a gift or duty, is the base of both.

One stem feeding a noun of payment and an adjective of profitability is exactly the pattern here, so the manual's usage is correctly formed.

**D) In a research methods seminar, "analysation" is offered as the noun English forms from the verb "analyse".**

The noun is "analysis", taken over whole from Greek, and it supplies the plural "analyses" as well as the adjective "analytical". Because the noun arrived before the verb, which was back-formed from it, there is no room for a nominalisation in -ation. Similar Greek nouns behave the same way, giving synthesis rather than synthesisation.

A Greek noun already fills the slot and even gave the verb its shape, so the coinage is superfluous: the noun is "analysis".

**E) In a note on court procedure, "adjournation" is offered as the noun formed from the verb "adjourn".**

The noun English uses is "adjournment", with the -ment that also gives judgment, commitment and postponement, all of them at home in legal procedure. The verb comes through French from a phrase about fixing a day, and it has never taken a Latin ending in -ation. Court lists record an adjournment, and no reporter writes anything else.

A French-derived verb with a settled -ment noun leaves nothing for the proposed form to do, so the note is wrong: the noun is "adjournment".
tasks.solution_overview: Regular-looking endings can be attached to almost anything, so the test is not whether a coinage is intelligible but whether the language has already settled on a different form. Latinate bases in particular often reserve their nouns and adjectives for stems you cannot predict from the English verb, which is why analyse yields a noun from Greek and adjourn takes -ment rather than -ation. When a proposed form and an established one compete, the established one wins by occupation.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five lines assign a meaning to a prefix of degree, position or relation. Decide whether the prefix carries that meaning in the word quoted.
statements: In an endocrinology note, "hypoglycaemia" is read as hypo-, meaning below normal, with glyc- for sugar and -aemia for a condition of the blood.
In an architectural history, "antechamber" is read as anti-, meaning against, plus "chamber", giving a room set opposite the main one.
In a virology paper, "intracellular" is read as intra-, meaning within, in contrast with inter-, which would mean between.
In a note on cloud physics, "supersaturated" is read as super-, meaning beyond the normal limit, applied to the participle "saturated".
In a note on legal drafting, "proscribe" is read as pro-, meaning before, plus scrib-, giving the sense of writing something down in advance.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In an endocrinology note, "hypoglycaemia" is read as hypo-, meaning below normal, with glyc- for sugar and -aemia for a condition of the blood.**

Greek hypo- marks something under or below a norm, as in hypothermia, hypotension and hypodermic, and it stands against hyper- for excess. Combined with glyc- and the blood-condition ending, it names blood sugar that has fallen too low, the opposite of hyperglycaemia. Clinical writing depends on the two prefixes being distinguishable at a glance, which is why they are never abbreviated.

Deficiency below a norm is what the prefix contributes, and the condition named is exactly that, so the note's reading is correct.

**B) In an architectural history, "antechamber" is read as anti-, meaning against, plus "chamber", giving a room set opposite the main one.**

The prefix here is ante-, from Latin for before, which also gives antecedent, antenatal and antedate; the room is the one you pass through before reaching the principal chamber. Greek anti- for against is a different prefix altogether, and it gives antibody, antithesis and antifreeze. Position in a sequence rather than opposition is what the word records.

Before rather than against is what the first element means, so the reading fails: the antechamber is the room that comes before the main one.

**C) In a virology paper, "intracellular" is read as intra-, meaning within, in contrast with inter-, which would mean between.**

Intra- marks what happens inside a single unit, giving intravenous, intramural and intracellular, while inter- marks what passes between units, giving intercellular, international and intervene. A virus replicating intracellularly is working inside the host cell, whereas intercellular traffic moves in the spaces between cells. One letter separates two quite different claims about location.

Inside a single cell is precisely what the prefix specifies, and the contrast drawn is the right one, so the paper's reading holds.

**D) In a note on cloud physics, "supersaturated" is read as super-, meaning beyond the normal limit, applied to the participle "saturated".**

Super- means above or beyond, as in supersonic, superstructure and supernumerary, and here it takes an already complete state and pushes it past its usual ceiling. Air that is supersaturated holds more water vapour than equilibrium allows, which is why droplets form as soon as a nucleus is available. The prefix attaches to the participle rather than to the verb, marking degree rather than reversal.

Beyond the ordinary limit is exactly the excess the atmosphere is in, so the reading in the note is accurate.

**E) In a note on legal drafting, "proscribe" is read as pro-, meaning before, plus scrib-, giving the sense of writing something down in advance.**

Writing in advance belongs to "prescribe", where pre- for before combines with scrib- to give a rule laid down beforehand or a medicine ordered. In "proscribe" the prefix carries the Roman sense of publishing a name in public, and the verb has meant to outlaw or forbid ever since. The two verbs are near opposites in effect, since one lays down what must be done and the other bans it.

Publication and prohibition rather than anticipation are what this prefix delivers, so the reading is wrong: to proscribe is to forbid.
tasks.solution_overview: Prefixes of degree and position come in pairs that are easy to mix up on the page: hypo- against hyper-, intra- against inter-, sub- against super-, and ante- against anti-. Two of them differ by a single letter while pulling in opposite directions, so the spelling has to be read closely. Where a prefix has more than one sense, as pro- does, let the settled meaning of the whole word decide which sense is in play rather than guessing from the prefix alone.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five lines pair an everyday noun with the learned adjective that scientific prose uses for it. Decide whether the adjective named is the one English supplies.
statements: In an astronomy text, "lunar" is given as the adjective corresponding to the noun "moon", supplied by Latin luna rather than built on the English word.
In a nephrology article, "renal" is given as the adjective corresponding to "kidney", from Latin renes.
In an oceanography paper, "maritimal" is given as the learned adjective corresponding to the noun "sea".
In a cardiology paper, "hearty" is given as the learned adjective corresponding to the noun "heart".
In an urban policy report, "cital" is given as the formal adjective corresponding to the noun "city".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In an astronomy text, "lunar" is given as the adjective corresponding to the noun "moon", supplied by Latin luna rather than built on the English word.**

English frequently pairs a native noun with an adjective borrowed from Latin, a relationship known as suppletion because the two forms come from unrelated stems. Luna gives lunar, lunation and lunatic, none of which shows any trace of the noun they serve. The native alternative "moony" survives only in a figurative sense, which leaves the Latin form to do all the technical work.

A borrowed adjective standing in for one the native noun never produced is exactly the pattern described, so the text is right.

**B) In a nephrology article, "renal" is given as the adjective corresponding to "kidney", from Latin renes.**

Medicine draws almost all its adjectives from Latin or Greek, so kidney takes renal, lung takes pulmonary and liver takes hepatic. The noun and adjective again share nothing on the page, which is why renal failure and kidney failure name the same condition in different registers. The Greek stem nephr- supplies the specialty name, giving a third form in the same territory.

Latin adjective serving a native noun is the ordinary state of affairs in clinical vocabulary, so the article's pairing is correct.

**C) In an oceanography paper, "maritimal" is given as the learned adjective corresponding to the noun "sea".**

English has two established adjectives here, "marine" for what belongs to the sea itself and "maritime" for what has to do with seafaring and coasts, both from Latin mare. Neither takes a further -al, and adding one produces a form that appears in no dictionary. Marine biology and maritime law show the two adjectives dividing the field between them.

Two Latin adjectives already cover the ground and neither extends with -al, so the coinage fails: the adjectives are "marine" and "maritime".

**D) In a cardiology paper, "hearty" is given as the learned adjective corresponding to the noun "heart".**

The native adjective exists but has drifted well away from the organ, meaning robust, enthusiastic or generously large, as in a hearty welcome and a hearty meal. Medicine uses "cardiac", from Greek kardia, which also gives cardiology, myocardial and tachycardia. Semantic drift in the native form is precisely why the borrowed one was needed.

A native adjective that no longer refers to the organ cannot serve a cardiology paper, so the form required is "cardiac".

**E) In an urban policy report, "cital" is given as the formal adjective corresponding to the noun "city".**

No such word exists; the adjectives available are "urban", from Latin urbs, and "civic", from civis for citizen, each covering a different aspect of city life. Urban describes the built environment and its patterns, while civic describes the community and its institutions, as in urban density and civic pride. Planning documents move between the two without ever needing a form built on the English noun.

Two borrowed adjectives already divide the ground, and neither resembles the coinage offered, so the report needs "urban" or "civic".
tasks.solution_overview: For many common nouns, the technical adjective comes from a different language entirely, so moon takes lunar, kidney takes renal and heart takes cardiac. Because the two words share no letters, there is nothing to build on and nothing to check by eye: you either know the pair or you must recognise the Latin or Greek root behind it. Watch for regular-looking coinages on the English noun, and watch for real words that have drifted away from the sense you want.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five lines take apart an adjective ending in -ible or -ile. Decide whether the root and the ending have been identified correctly.
statements: In a manuscript studies note, "legible" is taken apart as leg-, meaning read, plus -ible, and is distinguished from "readable", which describes what is easy or pleasant to read.
In a note on tax law, "liable" is taken apart as the English verb "lie" plus -able, giving what lies open to a charge.
In a nuclear physics report, "fissile" is taken apart as fiss-, meaning split, plus -ile, an ending of capacity comparable to -able.
In a paper on mystical writing, "ineffable" is taken apart as in-, plus ef- from ex-, plus fa-, meaning speak, plus -able.
In a chemistry note, "volatile" is taken apart as vol-, meaning fly, plus -ile, giving a substance apt to evaporate.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a manuscript studies note, "legible" is taken apart as leg-, meaning read, plus -ible, and is distinguished from "readable", which describes what is easy or pleasant to read.**

The root leg- for reading and gathering gives legend, lecture, lection and legible, none of which leaves it standing alone. The -ible adjective means capable of being deciphered, so a hand may be perfectly legible and still make dull reading, while a readable book may survive in a barely legible copy. Palaeography needs the distinction constantly.

Root plus ending give decipherability, and the contrast with the native adjective is real, so the note's analysis is right.

**B) In a note on tax law, "liable" is taken apart as the English verb "lie" plus -able, giving what lies open to a charge.**

The word comes through French lier from Latin ligare, meaning to bind, the same root that gives ligament, oblige and alliance, so the sense is bound to answer for something. The resemblance to "lie" is coincidental, and the meaning of being bound rather than lying explains why liability is an obligation. False segmentation of this kind is what folk etymology thrives on.

Binding rather than lying is what the root supplies, so the analysis is mistaken: "liable" belongs with ligament and obligation.

**C) In a nuclear physics report, "fissile" is taken apart as fiss-, meaning split, plus -ile, an ending of capacity comparable to -able.**

The stem fiss- comes from Latin findere for splitting and gives fissure and fission as well as this adjective. The ending -ile marks a capacity or tendency, as in ductile, volatile, fragile and tactile, so a fissile nuclide is one capable of undergoing fission. Geology uses the same adjective for rock that splits readily along planes.

A Latin stem of splitting under an ending of capacity accounts for both the physics and the geology, so the report's analysis holds.

**D) In a paper on mystical writing, "ineffable" is taken apart as in-, plus ef- from ex-, plus fa-, meaning speak, plus -able.**

The root fa- for speaking gives fable, fate, infant, meaning one who does not speak, and preface. With ex- assimilated to ef- the sense is speaking out, and -able plus the negative in- yields what cannot be spoken out at all. Writers on mysticism use the word for experience that resists being put into language.

Three prefixed and suffixed layers over a root of speaking give exactly the unsayable quality at issue, so the analysis is correct.

**E) In a chemistry note, "volatile" is taken apart as vol-, meaning fly, plus -ile, giving a substance apt to evaporate.**

The Latin volare for flying gives volley, volatile and, through French, volley's cousins in older sporting vocabulary. The ending -ile again marks a tendency, so a volatile liquid is one inclined to fly off as vapour, and the same word describes a temper or a market apt to move suddenly. The figurative senses grew out of the chemical one rather than the reverse.

Flying plus a tendency ending explains both the laboratory sense and its extensions, so the chemistry note's analysis is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: The endings -ible and -ile both attach to Latin stems and both express capacity, which is why they crowd the same semantic space as -able while behaving quite differently in form. Since the stems they attach to are bound, the way in is to recognise the root: leg- for reading, fiss- for splitting, fa- for speaking, vol- for flying. One line here is a decoy, because a familiar English verb sits invitingly close to a word that has nothing to do with it.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five lines describe an adjective or an agent noun built on a Latin or Greek stem. Decide whether the account of the parts and their effect is accurate.
statements: In a board paper at a retail group, "inflationary" is described as the noun "inflation" plus -ary, giving an adjective meaning tending to cause or characterised by inflation.
In a report on disclosure rules, "exculpatory" is described as ex-, meaning out of, plus culp-, meaning blame, plus -atory, giving evidence that clears the accused.
In a pharmacology text, "analgesic" is described as Greek an-, meaning without, plus alges-, meaning pain, plus -ic, giving a drug that removes pain.
In a study of parliamentary rhetoric, "hortatory" is described as an adjective from the Latin verb hortari, meaning to urge, with -atory marking function.
In a conservation manual, "desiccant" is described as the verb "desiccate" with -ant, naming the substance that performs the drying.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a board paper at a retail group, "inflationary" is described as the noun "inflation" plus -ary, giving an adjective meaning tending to cause or characterised by inflation.**

The ending -ary attaches to nouns and yields adjectives of relation or tendency, as in revolutionary, precautionary and cautionary. Built on the -ation noun, this one describes pressures, spirals and expectations that either produce rising prices or belong to a period of them. The chain runs from the verb "inflate" through the noun and only then to the adjective, which is why the ending sits on -ation rather than on the verb.

Noun of process turned into an adjective of tendency is exactly the derivation involved, so the board paper's usage is properly formed.

**B) In a report on disclosure rules, "exculpatory" is described as ex-, meaning out of, plus culp-, meaning blame, plus -atory, giving evidence that clears the accused.**

The root culp- for fault or blame gives culpable, culprit and mea culpa, and the prefix ex- takes the accused out of it. The ending -atory marks the function performed, so exculpatory material is material that operates to clear someone, in contrast with the inculpatory material that fastens blame on them. Disclosure regimes are built on the distinction.

Prefix, root of blame and functional ending combine into the exact courtroom category, so the report's account is right.

**C) In a pharmacology text, "analgesic" is described as Greek an-, meaning without, plus alges-, meaning pain, plus -ic, giving a drug that removes pain.**

The privative a- takes the form an- before a vowel, as in anaemia, anaerobic and anarchy, and alges- for pain comes from algos, which also gives neuralgia and nostalgia. The ending -ic makes an adjective that has been converted into a class noun, so a drug can be analgesic or an analgesic. The parallel formation "anaesthetic", built on the root for sensation, shows the same shape.

Absence, pain and a class-forming ending give precisely the pharmacological category, so the text's description is accurate.

**D) In a study of parliamentary rhetoric, "hortatory" is described as an adjective from the Latin verb hortari, meaning to urge, with -atory marking function.**

The stem hortat- appears in exhort and exhortation, where the prefix ex- intensifies the urging, but it never stands alone in English. The ending -atory again marks what the thing does, so hortatory language is language that urges its hearers to act rather than merely informing them. Rhetorical analysis sets it against expository and forensic styles.

A bound Latin stem of urging under an ending of function names the style precisely, so the study's description holds.

**E) In a conservation manual, "desiccant" is described as the verb "desiccate" with -ant, naming the substance that performs the drying.**

The verb loses its -ate before the ending, and -ant, originally a Latin present participle, names the agent that acts, whether animate or not: coolant, propellant, sealant, desiccant. Silica gel placed in a display case is therefore a desiccant, while the process it carries out is desiccation. The prefix de- here is intensive rather than reversative, since siccare already means to dry.

Truncated stem plus an agentive participial ending names the working material exactly, so the manual's description is correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjectives of function and nouns of agency are built on the stem a Latin verb shows in its participle, not on the shape the verb has in English, so inflation gives inflationary and culpa gives exculpatory. The endings themselves carry recognisable jobs: -ary and -atory mark tendency or function, -ant marks the thing that acts, and Greek -ic marks the class a substance belongs to. Identify the root, then let the ending tell you what kind of word has been made.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five lines concern verbs and adjectives that describe a gradual change of state. Decide whether the form or the gloss offered is the one English uses.
statements: In a forensic entomology note, "putrify" is given as the verb that goes with the adjective "putrescent" and the noun "putrefaction".
In a paper on survey design, "satisfication" is given as the noun formed from the verb "satisfy".
In a note on star formation, "coalesce" is described as containing -esce, an ending that marks a process of gradually becoming.
In a medical history, "convalescent" is described as con- plus val-, meaning be strong, plus -escent, giving an adjective for someone gradually recovering strength.
In a building conservation note, "effloresce" is glossed as meaning to lose flowers, on the ground that ef- from ex- marks removal.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a forensic entomology note, "putrify" is given as the verb that goes with the adjective "putrescent" and the noun "putrefaction".**

The verb is spelt "putrefy", with the e that marks the Latin stem putre-, and the same e appears in liquefy, rarefy and stupefy. The noun "putrefaction" cited alongside it is itself the strongest evidence, since it shows the stem vowel plainly. Spelling the verb with an i imports the unrelated -ify ending and produces a form dictionaries do not record.

The noun in the same line already displays the correct stem vowel, so the verb has been misspelt: the form is "putrefy".

**B) In a paper on survey design, "satisfication" is given as the noun formed from the verb "satisfy".**

Verbs of this family take -faction rather than -fication for their nouns, so satisfy gives satisfaction, liquefy gives liquefaction and stupefy gives stupefaction. The ending -fication belongs to verbs in -ify, such as classify and classification or purify and purification, which is a different pattern with a different stem. Survey work is full of the correct noun, since it measures satisfaction directly.

The base belongs to the -faction group rather than the -fication group, so the paper needs the established noun: "satisfaction".

**C) In a note on star formation, "coalesce" is described as containing -esce, an ending that marks a process of gradually becoming.**

The Latin inchoative -esce marks the beginning or the gradual unfolding of a state, and it gives convalesce, effervesce, obsolesce and coalesce. The base here is co- with alescere for growing, so the verb means to grow together, which is what gas and dust do as a protostar forms. The matching noun in this family is "coalescence".

An ending of gradual becoming attached to a root of growing describes the astrophysics exactly, so the note is right.

**D) In a medical history, "convalescent" is described as con- plus val-, meaning be strong, plus -escent, giving an adjective for someone gradually recovering strength.**

The root val- for strength gives valid, valour, prevail and value, and -escent turns the verb of gradual change into an adjective describing someone in the middle of it. That is why nineteenth-century hospitals ran convalescent homes for patients no longer ill but not yet strong. The noun "convalescence" names the period itself.

Strength returning by degrees is what the parts add up to, and that is precisely the patient's condition, so the description holds.

**E) In a building conservation note, "effloresce" is glossed as meaning to lose flowers, on the ground that ef- from ex- marks removal.**

The prefix ex- here marks outward movement rather than loss, so the verb means to burst into flower and, in the sense conservators need, to come out on a surface as a crystalline salt deposit. The inchoative -esce again marks the gradual process, and the noun is "efflorescence", the white bloom that appears on damp brickwork. Nothing in the word suggests anything being taken away.

Coming out rather than being stripped away is what the prefix contributes, so the gloss inverts the word: to effloresce is to bloom or to crystallise outwards.
tasks.solution_overview: Two related patterns meet here: -esce and -escent mark a process of becoming, while -efy and its noun in -efaction mark causing a state, and both keep Latin stems that English never shows on their own. The traps are formal as well as semantic, since -efy is regularly misspelt as -ify and its noun is not built on -ation at all. Where a gloss is offered instead of a form, check it against the way the word behaves in the field it belongs to.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five lines gloss a specialist ending inherited from Latin or Greek. Decide whether the ending means what the line says it means.
statements: In a mining survey, "auriferous" is glossed as auri-, meaning gold, plus -ferous, meaning bearing, describing gravels that contain gold.
In an entomology paper, "detritivorous" is glossed as detriti-, from detritus, plus -vorous, meaning eating, describing insects that feed on decaying matter.
In a hospital hygiene protocol, "bactericide" is glossed as an agent that kills bacteria, the ending -cide naming the killer or the killing.
In a veterinary formulary, "vermifuge" is glossed as a preparation that attracts intestinal worms, on the ground that -fuge means to draw towards.
In an archaeology report, "megalith" is glossed as mega-, meaning great, plus -lith, meaning tomb.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a mining survey, "auriferous" is glossed as auri-, meaning gold, plus -ferous, meaning bearing, describing gravels that contain gold.**

The element -ferous comes from Latin ferre for carrying and gives carboniferous, coniferous and pestiferous, in each case naming what a thing bears or brings. Auri- is the stem of aurum, whose chemical symbol Au preserves it, so auriferous gravels are gravels that carry gold. Survey reports use the adjective for deposits worth working rather than for ore already extracted.

Gold plus bearing is exactly what the deposit is being credited with, so the survey's gloss is accurate.

**B) In an entomology paper, "detritivorous" is glossed as detriti-, from detritus, plus -vorous, meaning eating, describing insects that feed on decaying matter.**

The ending -vorous comes from vorare for devouring and gives carnivorous, herbivorous, omnivorous and frugivorous, each naming a diet. Attached to detritus, the worn-down organic debris of a habitat, it names the feeders that break that debris down further. The matching noun is "detritivore", formed with the shorter -vore.

An ending that names diets attached to the material eaten gives precisely the feeding class described, so the paper's gloss holds.

**C) In a hospital hygiene protocol, "bactericide" is glossed as an agent that kills bacteria, the ending -cide naming the killer or the killing.**

The ending comes from Latin caedere for cutting down or killing, and it serves both for the act, as in genocide and homicide, and for the agent, as in pesticide, fungicide and bactericide. Hygiene protocols contrast it with a bacteriostatic agent, which merely stops bacteria multiplying rather than destroying them. The distinction decides which product may be used where sterility is required.

Killing rather than restraining is what the ending contributes, and the protocol relies on that difference, so the gloss is correct.

**D) In a veterinary formulary, "vermifuge" is glossed as a preparation that attracts intestinal worms, on the ground that -fuge means to draw towards.**

The ending comes from fugare, to put to flight, so it names what drives something away: a centrifuge throws matter outward from the centre, a febrifuge drives down fever, and a vermifuge expels worms. Verm- is the Latin for worm, as in vermin and vermiform. Attraction is the opposite of what the preparation is prescribed to do.

Driving out rather than drawing in is the ending's whole contribution, so the gloss reverses the drug: a vermifuge expels intestinal worms.

**E) In an archaeology report, "megalith" is glossed as mega-, meaning great, plus -lith, meaning tomb.**

The element -lith is the Greek for stone, which is why it gives monolith, neolithic, lithography and the lithosphere. A megalith is therefore simply a great stone, whether it stands alone, forms part of a circle or roofs a chamber; the tomb sense belongs to words such as cenotaph and mausoleum. Some megaliths are indeed funerary, but that comes from the archaeology rather than from the word.

Stone rather than tomb is what the second element means, so the report's gloss overreaches: a megalith is a great stone.
tasks.solution_overview: Technical vocabulary leans on a small stock of endings that behave almost like words in their own right: -ferous for bearing, -vorous for eating, -cide for killing, -fuge for driving away and -lith for stone. Each recurs across a whole field, so one familiar cousin is usually enough to test a gloss. Beware of endings whose sense is directional, since driving away and drawing towards are easy to reverse if the Latin verb behind the ending is unfamiliar.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five lines pair a word with the meaning its shape seems to promise. Decide whether the word has kept that meaning or drifted away from it.
statements: In a report on court delays, "dilatory" is glossed as meaning expanding, on the ground that it is the adjective of the verb "dilate".
In a study of Restoration comedy, "ingenuous" is offered as the adjective corresponding to the noun "ingenuity".
In a note on Victorian sanitary reform, "noisome" is glossed as meaning noisy, formed from "noise" with the ending -some.
In an art history essay, "fulsome" is glossed as meaning generously abundant, a straightforward -some derivative of "full".
In a study of cavalry manuals, "restive" is said not to mean restful, describing instead impatience under restraint, from Latin restare, to remain or hold back.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on court delays, "dilatory" is glossed as meaning expanding, on the ground that it is the adjective of the verb "dilate".**

The adjective belongs to Latin differre in its participial stem dilat-, meaning to put off, and it reached English through dilatorius for a delayer. Its settled sense is causing delay, as in dilatory tactics and dilatory pleading, both terms of art in procedure. The verb about widening is a separate line of descent that happens to share the same letters.

Delay rather than expansion is what the word has always meant in court, so the gloss cannot stand: dilatory conduct is conduct that drags things out.

**B) In a study of Restoration comedy, "ingenuous" is offered as the adjective corresponding to the noun "ingenuity".**

The noun goes with "ingenious", meaning clever and inventive, while "ingenuous" means artless, open and unguarded, and its own noun is "ingenuousness". The two adjectives descend from different Latin words, ingeniosus for talented and ingenuus for freeborn and hence frank, and their similarity is an accident of English spelling. Restoration comedy trades on the difference, since the ingenuous heroine is precisely the one without ingenuity.

Cleverness and artlessness belong to different adjectives, so the pairing is wrong: the adjective matching "ingenuity" is "ingenious".

**C) In a note on Victorian sanitary reform, "noisome" is glossed as meaning noisy, formed from "noise" with the ending -some.**

The base is not "noise" but the older verb "annoy", shortened to noy, so the word means harmful or offensive, and it attaches above all to smells. Sanitary reformers used it constantly for the noisome effluvia they blamed for disease, with no reference to sound at all. The ending -some does mean tending towards, as in troublesome and burdensome, but it is working on a different base here.

The base has been misidentified, and with it the whole sense, so the gloss fails: noisome smells are offensive rather than loud.

**D) In an art history essay, "fulsome" is glossed as meaning generously abundant, a straightforward -some derivative of "full".**

The word did begin as full plus -some, but it has carried an evaluative charge for centuries, and in careful modern prose it means excessive to the point of insincerity. Fulsome praise is praise that embarrasses its recipient, which is why editors query the word wherever plain abundance is meant. The transparent reading is available historically and still misfires in current usage.

Excess and insincerity rather than mere abundance are what the word now conveys, so the essay's gloss misses its force.

**E) In a study of cavalry manuals, "restive" is said not to mean restful, describing instead impatience under restraint, from Latin restare, to remain or hold back.**

The word entered English for a horse that refused to go forward, and the sense has widened to any impatient resistance to control, as in a restive crowd or a restive backbench. Sharing a stem with "rest" makes the calm reading tempting, but the ending -ive marks a tendency, and the tendency here is to baulk. Cavalry manuals used it as a fault to be trained out.

A shared stem hiding an opposite sense is exactly the trap the study is warning about, so its account of the word is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Some derived words look transparent and are not, either because the base you recognise is not the base they were built on, or because the sense has moved while the shape has stayed put. Noisome has nothing to do with noise and dilatory nothing to do with dilating, while ingenuous and ingenious have separated so far that only one of them answers to ingenuity. The way through is to test the proposed meaning against a context where the word is at home rather than against its appearance.
