tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five lines work out the meaning of a word from a prefix and a Latin root. Decide whether the computation gives the sense the word actually has.
statements: In a note on constitutional law, "abrogate" is worked out as ab-, meaning away, plus rog-, meaning ask or propose, giving the repeal of a law.
In an epidemiology paper, "attenuate" is worked out as ad-, assimilated to at-, plus tenu-, meaning thin, giving the weakening of a pathogen.
In a note on plain-language drafting, "circumlocution" is worked out as circum- plus loqu-, giving the sense of speaking against a proposal.
In an archaeology field report, "exhume" is worked out as ex-, meaning out of, plus hum-, meaning ground, giving the recovery of a burial.
In an insurer's underwriting note, "indemnify" is worked out as in-, meaning not, plus damn-, meaning loss or harm, plus -ify, giving the undertaking to make good a loss.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a note on constitutional law, "abrogate" is worked out as ab-, meaning away, plus rog-, meaning ask or propose, giving the repeal of a law.**

The root rog- for asking or proposing gives interrogate, prerogative and the older sense of a bill being proposed to an assembly. With ab- for away, the verb takes the proposal back, which is why abrogating a treaty or a statute means annulling it outright. Its relative "derogate" only detracts from a rule in part, which is a difference constitutional lawyers rely on.

Taking away what was formally proposed is exactly what repeal amounts to, so the computation in the note is sound.

**B) In an epidemiology paper, "attenuate" is worked out as ad-, assimilated to at-, plus tenu-, meaning thin, giving the weakening of a pathogen.**

The root tenu- for thinness gives tenuous and, through the same Latin family, tenuity, and the assimilated prefix ad- adds the sense of bringing something to that state. An attenuated strain has been made thin in virulence while remaining alive, which is the principle behind several live vaccines. Physics uses the same verb for a signal reduced in amplitude.

Bringing something to thinness covers both the vaccine and the signal, so the paper's computation is correct.

**C) In a note on plain-language drafting, "circumlocution" is worked out as circum- plus loqu-, giving the sense of speaking against a proposal.**

Circum- means around, as in circumference, circumnavigate and circumspect, and loqu- means speak, as in eloquent, colloquial and soliloquy. The compound therefore names speaking around a subject rather than coming to the point, which is precisely what plain-language guidance tries to remove. Speaking against something would call for contra- or anti-, neither of which is present.

Around rather than against is what the prefix supplies, so the computation misfires: circumlocution is roundabout speech.

**D) In an archaeology field report, "exhume" is worked out as ex-, meaning out of, plus hum-, meaning ground, giving the recovery of a burial.**

The root hum- for earth or ground gives humus, humble and, through the idea of being close to the soil, humility. With ex- the verb means to take out of the ground, and it applies equally to a legal exhumation and to an excavated inhumation. The opposite formation, "inhume", is still used in archaeological description for burial in the earth.

Out of the ground is both the literal sum of the parts and the technical sense, so the field report's computation holds.

**E) In an insurer's underwriting note, "indemnify" is worked out as in-, meaning not, plus damn-, meaning loss or harm, plus -ify, giving the undertaking to make good a loss.**

The root damn- for loss or harm gives damage, damnify and condemn, and the negative in- produces the adjective indemnis, unharmed, from which the verb and the noun "indemnity" are built. The -ify ending adds the causative sense, so to indemnify is to put someone into the condition of having suffered no loss. That is exactly the promise an insurance contract makes.

Negative, root of loss and causative ending together spell out the contractual promise, so the underwriting note's computation is right.
tasks.solution_overview: A prefix plus a bound root can often be added up to something very close to the modern meaning, provided both parts are read correctly. Ab-, ad-, circum-, ex- and in- set direction or relation, while roots such as rog- for asking, ten- for thinness, loqu- for speaking, hum- for ground and damn- for loss supply the content. Add the parts, then check the total against the technical use of the word, since a specialist sense is usually the most literal one left.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five lines describe the order in which a word's affixes were added. Decide whether the layers are set out in the order English builds them.
statements: In a syntax paper, "ungrammaticality" is built in the order grammar, grammatical, ungrammatical, ungrammaticality, with un- attaching to the adjective before -ity.
In a paper on research methods, "irreproducibility" is built from produce through reproduce, reproducible and irreproducible before -ity is added.
In a paper on electoral systems, "disproportionality" is built from proportion through proportional and disproportional before -ity closes the word.
In an energy policy report, "decarbonisation" is built from carbon through carbonise, then de- for the reversal, with -ation last.
In a data protection guide, "anonymisation" is built on the Greek-derived adjective "anonymous", which loses its ending before -ise, with -ation added last.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a syntax paper, "ungrammaticality" is built in the order grammar, grammatical, ungrammatical, ungrammaticality, with un- attaching to the adjective before -ity.**

Each intermediate step is a real word, which is the test that fixes the order: the noun takes -ical, the negative attaches to the adjective, and only then does -ity package the result. Attaching -ity first would give grammaticality and leave no adjective for un- to negate, since the prefix does not attach to abstract nouns of this kind. Syntacticians use the long form for the property a starred example has.

Every layer produces an existing word in the order given, so the paper's account of the build is correct.

**B) In a paper on research methods, "irreproducibility" is built from produce through reproduce, reproducible and irreproducible before -ity is added.**

The prefix re- attaches to the verb, -ible then makes the adjective, the negative in- assimilates to ir- before that r, and -ity finally makes the noun. Each stage exists independently, which is what licenses the next, and the assimilation happens at the moment the negative meets the base rather than later. Methodology papers use the noun for the property of results that will not come out the same way twice.

Verb, adjective, negated adjective and noun follow one another exactly as described, so the analysis holds.

**C) In a paper on electoral systems, "disproportionality" is built from proportion through proportional and disproportional before -ity closes the word.**

The noun "proportion" takes -al to give an adjective, dis- then negates that adjective, and -ity turns the negated adjective into a measurable property. Electoral studies need the final noun because they quantify the gap between vote shares and seat shares, which the adjective alone could not express. The competing form built on "disproportionate" gives the same sense by a parallel route.

Each layer is a word in its own right and the order matches the meaning, so the paper's build is accurate.

**D) In an energy policy report, "decarbonisation" is built from carbon through carbonise, then de- for the reversal, with -ation last.**

The verb "carbonise" is formed with -ise on the noun, de- then reverses that verb rather than negating the noun, and -ation nominalises the reversed verb. Order matters, since a prefix that means undoing has to have a process to undo before it can attach. The report's subject is the removal of carbon from an energy system, which is the reversal made into a noun.

Noun, verb, reversed verb and process noun follow in the only order the meaning allows, so the description is right.

**E) In a data protection guide, "anonymisation" is built on the Greek-derived adjective "anonymous", which loses its ending before -ise, with -ation added last.**

The adjective comes from an- for without and onyma for name, and it sheds its -ous before the verbal ending, giving "anonymise" rather than any longer form. The final -ation then names the process, which is what data protection law regulates and distinguishes from pseudonymisation. Stem shortening of this kind is regular when -ise attaches to a Latinate or Greek adjective.

Adjective trimmed to a verb and the verb turned into a process noun is exactly the sequence the word shows, so the guide's account holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Long derived words are built one layer at a time, and each layer has to be a possible word before the next can attach, which is what fixes the order. A negative or reversative prefix usually goes on at the point where the meaning it negates already exists, and a final -ity or -ation then packages the whole thing as a noun. Test each proposed step by asking whether the intermediate form is itself English, and watch for stems that shorten when a suffix arrives.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: Five lines make a claim about the noun or the adjective that belongs to a difficult base. Decide whether the form named is the one English has settled on.
statements: In a jurisprudence essay, "derogation" is given as the noun of the verb "derogate", which takes the preposition "from" when a rule is partly set aside.
In a note on employment procedure, "aggrievance" is given as the noun formed from the verb "aggrieve".
In a paper on climate modelling, "simulacrum" is given as the noun formed from "simulate" to name the act of running a simulation.
In an infection control guideline, "prophylaxis" is given as the noun and "prophylactic" as the adjective, both from pro- plus phylax- for guarding.
In a paper on memory training, "mnemonic" is given as a word from the Greek stem for remembering, serving as both adjective and noun.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a jurisprudence essay, "derogation" is given as the noun of the verb "derogate", which takes the preposition "from" when a rule is partly set aside.**

The verb is built on de- and rog- for asking or proposing, so it detracts from a rule rather than repealing it outright, and the -ate stem takes -ion to give the noun. Human rights instruments use the noun for a state's partial suspension of an obligation, and the verb keeps its preposition, as in derogating from a right. The contrast with abrogation, which cancels entirely, is exactly why both words survive.

Verb, preposition and noun all behave as the essay reports, and the partial sense is the settled one, so the account is correct.

**B) In a note on employment procedure, "aggrievance" is given as the noun formed from the verb "aggrieve".**

The noun English uses is "grievance", built on the shorter stem griev- and long established in procedure, as in a grievance hearing or a formal grievance. The verb "aggrieve" survives almost only as the participle "aggrieved", describing the party with a complaint, and it produces no noun of its own. Adding -ance to the prefixed verb creates a form that no handbook records.

The shorter noun already occupies the ground in every procedural context, so the coinage fails: the noun is "grievance".

**C) In a paper on climate modelling, "simulacrum" is given as the noun formed from "simulate" to name the act of running a simulation.**

The noun for the act is "simulation", and "simulacrum" names an image or likeness, often one that is hollow or misleading, which is why cultural theory rather than modelling has made a career of it. Both come from simulare, but the -crum ending forms a concrete noun for a thing produced, not a process. A modelling paper describing runs of a model needs the process noun.

The Latin word exists but names a likeness rather than an act, so the paper needs the process noun: "simulation".

**D) In an infection control guideline, "prophylaxis" is given as the noun and "prophylactic" as the adjective, both from pro- plus phylax- for guarding.**

The Greek phylax for a guard supplies the stem, and pro- means beforehand, so the words name protection put in place in advance of exposure. The -sis ending forms the abstract noun, as in diagnosis and analysis, while -tic forms the adjective, which has also been converted into a noun for the measure itself. Guidelines speak of prophylaxis after exposure and of prophylactic treatment.

Noun and adjective divide between the two Greek endings just as the guideline says, so the account is accurate.

**E) In a paper on memory training, "mnemonic" is given as a word from the Greek stem for remembering, serving as both adjective and noun.**

The stem behind it also gives amnesia, amnesty and Mnemosyne, and the ending -ic forms an adjective that English has converted into a count noun for the device itself. That is why a study can describe a mnemonic strategy and then list three mnemonics. The initial m is silent in English, which hides the family resemblance to the words for forgetting.

One Greek stem supplying an adjective that has become a noun is exactly what the paper describes, so the account holds.
tasks.solution_overview: At this level the traps are subtle: a real Latin word may be offered for a job it does not do, a regular-looking noun may be proposed where an irregular one is entrenched, and a Greek pair may divide noun and adjective duty in a way that has to be known rather than guessed. Check whether the form quoted is attested in the field the sentence describes, and test any proposed noun against the stem changes its family normally shows. A word that exists is not thereby the word required.
